items.title: [RFC]: a SGLang attention step to KV cache access benchmark
items.author: CAICAIIs
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Add `benchmarks/sglang_attention_kv/`, a benchmark for what one attention step spends on the paged KV
cache and where inside the step that time goes. It drives SGLang's own structures — the request to
token table, the allocator, the KV writer, the index kernel and the FlashInfer attention wrappers — so
a row describes the path a server takes.

## Motivation

Questions about the KV cache are usually answered with a transfer engine's bandwidth, which prices a
copy the step may not make and says nothing about what the step spends on the cache. That cost is the
attention kernel reading the KV through the page table, and how much of a step it is depends on the
shape: history length, query length, batch shape, page size and pool layout. Comparing two deployments
on this axis needs the step measured, not the bytes moved.

## What it measures

The step is three windows, in the order a forward pass runs them:

| Window | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `indices` | the query offsets and the CSR stream of KV slots the paged side reads (`create_flashinfer_kv_indices_triton`, the kernel `KVIndexTranslator.fill_packed_read_stream` launches) |
| `attention_plan` | the backend compiling that stream into a kernel schedule (the wrappers' `plan`, as `FlashInferAttnBackend` calls it in `init_forward_metadata`) |
| `layer_loop` | one layer's attention and one layer's KV write, layer by layer, in the order the branch runs them |

`phase_sum` is their sum and `step_window` is one window over all three, so a reader sees the interval
between the windows as well. Beside the step, two passes price the write and the read separately
(`MHATokenToKVPool.set_kv_buffer` for the whole step in one window, the branch's attention path for
every layer in another), and a read-only probe moves the same rows of K and V with `index_select` and
no arithmetic. None of the three is added to the step.

Each mode replays one branch of `FlashInferAttnBackend`:

| Mode | Branch | Per layer, in order |
|---|---|---|
| prefill | `ragged_no_prefix` (the default lane) | ragged prefill over the step's own K/V, then the KV write |
| prefill | `paged_extend` (the lane that variable selects) | the KV write, then one causal paged prefill call over those slots |
| extend | `ragged_prefix_merge` (the default: `SGLANG_FLASHINFER_USE_PAGED` is False) | ragged suffix attention, paged history attention, `merge_state`, then the KV write |
| extend | `paged_extend`, the branch that variable selects | KV write, then one paged prefill call |
| decode | `paged_decode` | KV write, then the paged decode call |

Both prefill rows are what `FlashInferAttnBackend` runs: `forward_extend` branches on `use_ragged`
alone, so a prefix-free prefill takes the paged wrapper too when that variable is set.

The read ledger is split by the path that reads it, because the branches read different KV: a merge
step reads its cached history through the paged wrapper and its own tokens through the ragged one, a
ragged prefill step reads the K/V it computes rather than paged KV, and a decode step reads its whole
context through the paged wrapper. Bandwidth and the arithmetic intensity divide the logical bytes of
both paths; the page
capacity is recorded as the allocation figure it is.

## Design

- The token table, the allocator, the writer, the index kernel and the attention wrappers are SGLang's
  own; the benchmark adds timing, a byte and FLOP ledger, and three checks. The allocator is the one the
  pool's page size selects, the token allocator at page size 1 and the paged allocator above it, and the
  index metadata is held and refilled each step the way the backend holds its own buffers.
- History length and query length are separate axes, with ragged batches, five page sizes and two pool
  layouts (a contiguous pool and a churned one).
- A model whose layers do not all keep a full-length KV is refused at load, naming the config field it
  was classified on: MLA, sliding-window or linear hybrids, encoder-decoder models, and dtypes the
  paged kernels cannot run.
- Three checks per step: the index stream has to name exactly the token table rows the branch's paged
  side reads, every token the step reads has to hold what was written for K and V, and the kernel
  output is compared against a causal float32 reference. The same comparison against a reference
  without the mask has to fail.

## Alternatives considered

- Reporting a transfer engine's bandwidth for the cache. Rejected: it prices a copy the step may not
  make, and says nothing about the kernel that reads the cache.
- A synthetic FlashInfer replica. Rejected: SGLang plans a token-level stream with `page_size=1` and
  takes a ragged path for a prefix-free prefill, so a replica that feeds a paged wrapper describes a
  path the server does not take.
- An end-to-end tier benchmark (server, hit patterns, TTFT) shipped alongside it. Out of scope for
  this change; the tier behaviour of SGLang's HiCache is a separate benchmark if it is wanted.

## Scope

Single GPU, one step, synthetic shapes, random K/V values. It bounds nothing about a request's latency
and does not measure a serving stack.

The replay fixes four settings, each stated in the record and in the result CSV: the `fa2` FlashInfer
wrapper backend, a wrapper page size of 1 while the pool keeps its own page size, the decode wrapper's
tensor-core path, and the KV writer on the step's stream rather than on `MHATokenToKVPool`'s alternate
stream. They are the benchmark's own choices and not the only paths SGLang runs.

items.title: [Bug] `--enable-deterministic-inference` does not make hybrid Mamba2 models (granite-4.0-h) batch-invariant
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--enable-deterministic-inference`, `ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-tiny` (a hybrid Mamba2 + attention model) fails SGLang's own prefix-mode determinism test: one greedy prompt, batched with other prompts of different lengths, comes back as up to 37 different outputs. Dense `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` on the same GPU, build and test returns exactly one output per prompt. The server accepts the flag for the hybrid model without a warning.

`--test-mode prefix --n-trials 30`, unique outputs per prompt (1 = deterministic), on a RTX 4090, v0.5.21, one fresh server per row (Done by Claude):

| model | server flags beyond `--enable-deterministic-inference --mem-fraction-static 0.70` | prefix 1 | prefix 511 | prefix 2048 | prefix 4097 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| granite-4.0-h-tiny | `--mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer --max-running-requests 256 --max-total-tokens 8000` | 1 | 11 | 30 | 8 |
| granite-4.0-h-tiny | `--max-running-requests 256 --max-total-tokens 8000` (no extra_buffer) | 1 | 9 | 31 | 9 |
| granite-4.0-h-tiny | `--max-running-requests 64 --max-total-tokens 8000` | 1 | 10 | 32 | 10 |
| granite-4.0-h-tiny | `--disable-radix-cache --max-running-requests 64 --max-total-tokens 8000` (mem 0.80) | 1 | 12 | 37 | 8 |
| Qwen3-0.6B (dense) | `--max-running-requests 256` | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

Each prompt got 98 to 135 samples per run. `--test-mode single` (batch sizes 1..30 of one prompt) passes for granite (1 unique).

On main(9e26600f3) the same granite server gives 1 / 44 / 10 / 4 unique outputs (RTX 4090) and 1 / 54 / 14 / 2 (A100 40GB; v0.5.21 on the A100: 1 / 13 / 27 / 11); Qwen3-0.6B and a granite MoE model without Mamba layers (granite-3.1-1b-a400m-instruct) give 1 / 1 / 1 / 1.

In 0.5.21 the deterministic flag is consulted by the attention backends and by the GDN linear-attention backend (`layers/attention/linear/gdn_backend.py`, lines 194 and 239), but nothing under `layers/attention/mamba/` reads it; the same is
true on main. So the Mamba2 prefill path (chunked scan over a packed batch) may not be covered by deterministic mode. We have not verified the mechanism beyond that reading.

We first saw this in a fuzzing cell that a greedy request replayed 5 times inside a batch under `--enable-deterministic-inference` gave 5 different outputs, while the same request alone, twice, was identical.

The same test also fails on gpt-oss-20b (sliding-window attention + MoE, no Mamba), which we reported prior https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/43055; the two share the symptom, but I don't think the same cause, thus seperately reported.


### Reproduction


```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-tiny --port 30000 \
    --mem-fraction-static 0.70 --enable-deterministic-inference --max-running-requests 64 --max-total-tokens 8000

python -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --port 30000 --test-mode prefix --n-trials 30
```

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

### Checklist

- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

We noticed that in the `_get_logits` function of vllm, `gather` instead of `all_gather` will be used under certain conditions (the main condition is that for non-tpu devices):
Code link:

- [logits = tensor_model_parallel_gather(logits)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e1fc61f0fb90c37f0d4a1a8f76235a6e4e1103c/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L101C22-L101C50)

The change from using `all_gather` to `gather` is initially added in this PR for your reference: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/2221.

While in SGLang, we see currently `all_gather` is always used:
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e868d0b60eb2d435c5599165f787bca06bdc9c3d/python/sglang/srt/layers/logits_processor.py#L246

Does SGLang have the plan to add `gather` instead of only `all_gather` when gathering the logits? Per the practice in vllm, using `gather` seems to have better performance than `all_gather` on devices which have `gather` support.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache write_through does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction
items.author: donghyq
items.body_excerpt:
# [SGLang] HiCache `write_through` does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction

## Summary

When `--hicache-write-policy write_through` is used with Mooncake Store, a first-seen prefix can be evicted from L1/L2 before all of its KV is backed up to storage. Replaying that prefix after eviction restores only part of it from L3; the rest is recomputed.

Using `--hicache-write-policy write_back --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` on the same workload restores the full prefix from Mooncake Store, so the storage backend and restore path are functional.

## Environment

- SGLang commit: `bdf8886ad3`
- Branch: `main`
- Model: Qwen3-4B
- GPU: 1 × NVIDIA H20-3e
- Attention backend: Triton
- HiCache:
  - `--enable-hierarchical-cache`
  - `--hicache-size 4`
  - `--hicache-write-policy write_through`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend mooncake`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"standalone_storage": true, "client_server_address": "127.0.0.1:50300", "enable_group_semantics": false}'`
- Mooncake Store:
  - master/client started independently
  - `root_fs_dir` and `cluster_id` configured
  - global segment size: 16 GiB
- Prompt: 5 distinct 16,011-token prefixes, `max_new_tokens=1`
- L1 capacity: 42,763 tokens
- L2 capacity: 27,127 tokens

## Reproduction

1. Start SGLang with the `write_through` configuration above.
2. Flush the cache.
3. Send five distinct 16,011-token prefixes sequentially.
4. Replay prefix A after prefixes B–E have displaced it from L1/L2.

## Expected

Prefix A should be restored from Mooncake Store with roughly:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Actual

Prefix A restores only part of the KV from storage:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 2551,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 2551,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

A second replay then reports a full device hit:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16009,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 16009,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 0,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Control experiment

The same workload with:

```text
--hicache-write-policy write_back
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete
```

returns:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

This indicates that Mooncake Store can persist and restore the full prefix when the write path is forced.

## Possible cause

In `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hiradix_cache.py`:

- `_inc_hit_count()` at line 926 skips chunked requests.
- `write_backup()` at line 856 is only called after `hit_count` reaches `write_through_threshold`.
- For a first-seen prefix, the leaf node may therefore not be backed up before eviction.
- `write_backup()` also requires the parent node to already be backed up, so a long first-seen prefix may only be partially persisted.
- `_evict_write_back()` at line 1105 shows the working control path: it stages the node to host, waits for the backup, and then writes storage.

## Suggested fix

One of the following would make the behavior clearer:

1. Add a true “write-through on insert” mode that persists the full prefix chain when a request finishes.
2. Document that `write_through` means “second-hit persistence” rather than “insert-time persistence”.
3. Keep the current optimization, but add a warning when a first-seen prefix is evicted before its backup completes.

## Impact

This affects long first-seen prompts that are evicted before a second request arrives. It can silently reduce L3 hit rate and make shared-cache routing less effective.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache + hybrid (SSM/Mamba): failed cudaHostRegister on a secondary host pool aborts the whole instance, and the error path throws TypeError thereby hiding the real rc
items.author: flymysql
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On sglang `0.5.19` (torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0, H20), starting a **hybrid SSM/Mamba** model
with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend dynamic` fails during
`attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache` and **kills the entire instance**.

Two coupled defects:

1. **`cudaHostRegister` failure is treated as fatal.** `alloc_with_host_register` raises, which
   aborts scheduler init for all TP ranks. But the failure only means "this host pool is not
   zero-copy registered" — and sglang's own non-zero-copy path (`_generic_page_get/_set`) is
   fully functional without registration. A missing acceleration is escalated into a full outage.
2. **The error path destroys its own diagnostic.** Inside the `raise`, `cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)`
   is called with a **plain `int`**, which raises `TypeError` on this torch build — so the real
   `rc`/`offset`/`size` are swallowed. Operators only see a bare `TypeError`.

Additionally, the failure **leaves a sticky CUDA error**, which then surfaces later at an unrelated
call site (`_create_sync_groups` → `all_gather_object` → `torch.zeros`), which made this
considerably harder to root-cause.

### Environment

- sglang `0.5.19`
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0
- 8 × H20 (96 GiB) / 8 × H20-3e (141 GiB), driver `535.161.08`
- Model: `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` (`Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, pool stack **KV + MAMBA**)
- Backend: `--hicache-storage-backend dynamic` with `interface_v1: 1` in the extra config
  (this selects the zero-copy page functions; the crash itself is in host-pool allocation and is
  not specific to any particular dynamic backend)
- Relevant flags: `--mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct
  --hicache-io-backend direct --tp 8`

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <hybrid SSM/Mamba model, e.g. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8> \
  --tp-size 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 1.0 \
  --hicache-storage-backend dynamic \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct \
  --hicache-io-backend direct \
  --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 \
  --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy \
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"backend_name":"...","module_path":"...","class_name":"...","interface_v1":1,...}'
```

Failures are **not deterministic per machine** — we observed the same config **succeed on a 96 GiB
box and fail on a 141 GiB box**, consistent with a pool-geometry / allocation-order dependence.

### Observed failure trace (verbatim)

```
[TP5] attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1759, in attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache
    result = strategy.build(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1329, in build
    host_pool_group, cache_controller = build_hybrid_mamba_stack(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 735, in build_hybrid_mamba_stack
    kv_host_pool = build_kv_host_pool(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 160, in build_kv_host_pool
    return kv_host_pool_cls(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 89, in __init__
    super().__init__(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/base.py", line 205, in __init__
    self.kv_buffer = self.init_kv_buffer()
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/mha.py", line 191, in init_kv_buffer
    buffer = alloc_func(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 235, in alloc_with_host_register
    _cuda_host_register(buffer, registration_granularity_bytes)
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 163, in _cuda_host_register
    f"{cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)}) at offset={offset} size={size} "
       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: cudaGetErrorString(): incompatible function arguments. The following argument types are supported:
    1. (arg0: torch._C._cudart.cudaError) -> str
Invoked with: 1                      <-- the real rc is only visible here, by accident
```

A second, later-surfacing variant of the same root cause (sticky CUDA error), reached when the
first pool *does* register successfully:

```
[TP6] Scheduler hit an exception: ...
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_cache_controller.py", line 161, in attach_storage_backend
    super().attach_storage_backend(
  File ".../managers/cache_controller.py", line 590, in attach_storage_backend
    self.prefetch_hits_sync_groups = self._create_sync_groups()
  File ".../managers/cache_controller.py", line 415, in _create_sync_groups
    create_custom_parallel_group(
  File ".../distributed/parallel_state.py", line 2762, in create_custom_parallel_group
    torch.distributed.all_gather_object(gathered_configs, local_config)
  File ".../torch/distributed/distributed_c10d.py", line 3506, in all_gather_object
    object_sizes_tensor = torch.zeros(
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: invalid argument
```

Note `cache_controller.py:590` calls `_create_sync_groups()` **immediately** after the storage
backend is attached — i.e. right where the sticky error from a failed registration lands.

### Minimal evidence that this is the registration call

Instrumenting `_cuda_host_register` on the failing box (141 GiB) shows the KV pool registers fine
and a **secondary** pool is the one that fails:

```
reg#1 total=49676820480 (46.27GiB) granularity=3840        -> OK
reg#2 total=17765498880 (16.55GiB) granularity=11796480    -> FAILED rc=1 (cudaErrorInvalidValue) at offset=0
reg#3 total=623738880  ( 0.58GiB) granularity=414720       -> (never reached)
```

`offset=0`, the size is page aligned, and `chunk_limit=256 GiB` (i.e. a single call) — so this is
**not** an alignment, chunking, or size problem. The same three pools register fine in an
otherwise-idle process, so it is state/order dependent within the real

### MOTIVATION.

8. Follow up on docstrings not being up-to date in the opt-out configs

always print hashed configs into cache_key_factors.json

items.title: [RFC]: Streaming Derender for Disaggregated Serving
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

The batch derender endpoints (`/v1/chat/completions/derender`, `/v1/completions/derender`) landed in #43606 (detokenization) and #45919 (non-streaming reasoning/tool parsing). They consume `GenerateResponse` and emit a complete `ChatCompletionResponse`.

Many real world disaggregated consumers cannot use a batch only post processing tier:

- **Interactive serving** (llm-d, Dynamo) returns tokens to end clients as they are generated. Streaming is a **hard gating requirement** (ref: @bbrowning in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/42729#issuecomment-4631310758).
- The producer side already streams e2e. `/inference/v1/generate` returns an SSE `StreamingResponse` when `request.stream` is set (`scale_out/token_in_token_out/api_router.py`), emitting `GenerateStreamResponse` chunks whose `GenerateResponseStreamChoice` carries the delta token IDs per step (`scale_out/token_in_token_out/serving.py`). `/render` already forwards `stream` / `stream_options`. **It therefore needs to be implemented on the  derender side.**

This RFC specifies a streaming derender that is the inverse of the streaming render path.

Partial:
- #34407
- #22817

Companion to:
- #42729

#### Why is this not a flag on the derender batch endpoint?

1. **Different input type.** The batch path (#42729) consumes a complete `GenerateResponse`. Streaming consumes `GenerateStreamResponse` *deltas*. It is therefore a distinct request shape and not a parameter on the existing endpoint.
2. **Incremental detokenization is stateful.** `IncrementalDetokenizer` carries `prefix_offset` / `read_offset` / prior tokens across `update()` calls. A naive per chunk `tokenizer.decode()` produces wrong spacing and can split multi-byte characters (see #44620). The per step delta `token_ids` are the right incremental input. `GenerateStreamResponse` however does **not** carry the detokenizer offsets and that state has to come from somewhere.
3. **Streaming parsers are stateful too.** Reasoning/tool parsers maintain incremental parse state across deltas (the reasoning to content/tool transition, partial tool call JSON). This compounds the state transport question below.

### Proposed Change.

#### New endpoints

| Method | Path | Input | Output |
|--------|------|-------|--------|
| `POST` | `/v1/chat/completions/derender` (`stream: true`) | `DerenderChatStreamRequest` | JSON `{ "chunk": ChatCompletionStreamResponse, "stream_state": DerenderStreamState }` |
| `POST` | `/v1/completions/derender` (`stream: true`) | `DerenderCompletionStreamRequest` | JSON `{ "chunk": CompletionStreamResponse, "stream_state": DerenderStreamState }` |

> [!NOTE]
> Streaming reuses the same `derender/` path with a `stream: true` flag, mirroring the producer (`/inference/v1/generate`). FastAPI validates a typed union discriminated on the `stream` literal and the handler dispatches with `isinstance`. The existing non-streaming types keep `generate_response` required.

Both endpoints run on the existing render server (GPU-free, only the `Renderer`/tokenizer) and are **stateless**.

#### Response format: plain JSON per call, not SSE

The derender is a **stateless per chunk translator**: one request in to one `{ "chunk", "stream_state" }` out. SSE out was rejected because it requires either a long lived connection or buffering all chunks before calling derender. This both conflict with the stateless design (Option A). The SSE protocol lives on the generate side and the final usage chunk are the client's responsibility.

#### Core design decision: incremental state (Option A, stateless)

The server returns updated state in each chunk. The client echoes it back on the next chunk. Server stays stateless and idempotent. There is no `request_id` keyed session and no lifecycle/eviction on the render tier.

Other design decision considered:

- **Option B (server-side session keyed by `request_id`)**: rejected because it breaks statelessness and adds session lifecycle + eviction + memory pressure.
- **Option C (shm state transport)**: deferred as a future optimization for large round tripped state on long generations. Only consider after Option A's payload cost is measured.

#### Parser state: replay (no opaque serialization)

Tool parsers hold internals we can't cheaply round trip (`prev_tool_call_arr`, `current_tool_id`, `streamed_args_for_tool`, engine lexer buffers). Rather than serialize them, the streaming chat derender **rebuilds a fresh parser each chunk by replaying the output tokens through it**, then feeds the new chunk and emits whatever the parser hands back.

Replay keeps the producer's chunk boundaries. `stream_state` carries `output_chunk_lens` (the token count of each chunk as it arrived) next to `output_token_ids`. Every chunk, replayed or live, goes through one `parse_delta` call. That matches standard serving which calls `parse_delta` once per engine step, so a multi-token step (e.g. speculative decoding) rebuilds the same parser state. Per token replay could diverge because some parser state (e.g. `history_tool_call_cnt`) advances once per `parse_delta` call. Text comes from a throwaway incremental detokenizer with `skip_special_tokens=False`, so the parser sees `</think>` / `<tool_call>` markers exactly as generate emits them.

Here are a few things to be aware of:

- **Cost:** transport is O(n) per chunk → O(n²) over a generation. Replay is one `parse_delta` call per prior chunk → O(n²) calls over a generation. `parse_delta` is itself O(n) for parsers that re-scan the accumulated text (Hermes tool call JSON, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning), so compute is O(n³) character work. `prompt_token_ids` is also sent and re-scanned on every chunk, so on long prompts it dominates the payload. Prompt + history + delta is bounded by `max_model_len` and rejected past it. Replay runs off the event loop on the renderer's executor (`renderer_num_workers`, default `1`), so size it for concurrent parser configured streams. Documented in `derenderer.md`.
- **Measured

comments.author: hickeyma
comments.body:
#50550 has merged, so streaming chat derender now does reasoning and tool call parsing. Thanks @sagearc, @chaunceyjiang, @NickLucche  and @bongwoobak for the reviews.

### What landed in #50550

- Replay through `parse_delta` on a fresh parser each chunk. It emits the same `reasoning` / `content` / `tool_calls` deltas that `/v1/chat/completions` streams for the same tokens.
- Replay keeps the producer's chunk boundaries. `DerenderStreamState` now carries `output_chunk_lens` alongside `output_token_ids`, so a multi-token step (e.g. spec decode) goes through one `parse_delta` call on replay, just like in serving. 
- `prompt_token_ids` on the request, so the parser knows whether the prompt left reasoning open.
- Tool call ID pinning, the `finish_reason` rewrite to `tool_calls` and parallel tool call filtering.
- Fail closed 400s for:
  - a parser configured without `chat_request` (the batch path now checks this too)
  - missing `prompt_token_ids`
  - more than one choice per chunk
  - prompt + history + delta over `max_model_len`
- `model_config` passed to the batch parser, so it knows the model's `tool_call_id_type`. Batch derender still discards the parser's tool call ID, though. That's tracked under #42729.
- A "Streaming cost" section in `derenderer.md`.

### The replay cost has been measured

@shimib benchmarked the derender tier with #50550 applied (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56851#issuecomment-5685698033), on 1×A100-40G with Qwen3-8B and the hermes + qwen3 parsers. At matched load, detokenizing and parsing on the derender tier cost ~9× the in-process CPU. E2E p50 rose 15% on multi-thousand-token reasoning outputs. With the default `renderer_num_workers=1`, the tier also saturated under concurrent parsed streams until the pool was made bigger.

This RFC deferred a parser cache and parser state serialization "until the cost is shown to matter". For latency sensitive interactive traffic, it matters. Rather than add server side state to the render tier, I propose:

- **Latency sensitive P/D (llm-d):** #56851. Detokenization and parsing move onto the decode pool per request and the parser lives as long as the request does. There's no replay, no echoed state and no extra hop per chunk.
- **Stateless consumers (RL, batch, gateways that own postprocessing):** streaming derender as it is. An LRU of live parsers keyed by `(request_id, choice_index)` stays an optional optimization with no protocol change (#57571).
- Serializing parser state was tied to #32713 which was closed as not planned. I'm therefore  dropping it for now.

### Remaining to close this RFC

- [x] **PR3: streaming parity CI.** Extend `test_derender_parity.py` to the chunked path (plain, reasoning, tool, reasoning + tool) including a multi-token chunk and a finish only final chunk.
- [x] **PR3: docs.** A streaming example, the client loop contract and the `stream: true` symmetry with `/inference/v1/generate`. The client loop contract covers echoing `stream_state`, one choice per chunk, `n > 1` as N streams and the client sending the final usage chunk.
- [ ] **Streaming logprobs.** #55029 (@shimib) covers the plain path. It does conflict and needs a rebase onto #50550 and the parsed path needs the same treatment, including dropping logprobs when reasoning is hidden, as batch does. I'd like to bring this into scope instead of leaving it as a known limitation. Batch already has logprobs and the parity plan in #56851 depends on them.
- [x] **Plain path off the event loop.** #57528 (fixes #57350) moves `_detokenize_delta` onto the renderer executor, so raising `renderer_num_workers` actually helps the plain streaming path.
- [x] **Tracking issues for deferred work:** the parser cache / server side state (#57571), including tool call ID stability across retried calls. Shared per choice `ChatStreamProcessor` used by both chat serving and derender (#57572). Integer token IDs for logprobs in `/inference/v1/generate` responses (`GenerateLogProbs`) (#57574)

#

comments.author: hyeongyun0916
comments.body:
Parser path logprobs. #55029 covers the plain path, and the remaining list just says "then the parsed path". Will the parsed path be a separate PR? I couldn't find an issue for it.

Streaming stop strings. #42729 tracks this as #57052 bug A, and the two fixes listed there — #47313's `stop_reason`, or a derender-side stop string pass — both assume you already have the whole text. Streaming doesn't: `stop_reason` only arrives on the final chunk, and by then a prefix of the stop string may already have been emitted. So it seems to need the hold-back buffer the coupled path has, and since derender is stateless that buffer would have to ride in `DerenderStreamState`. That would be a protocol change. What do you think?

comments.author: hickeyma
comments.body:
@hyeongyun0916 on (a), who owns parsed-path logprobs? I think we need to settle which code produces the token strings before anyone writes that path. Right now there are three candidates and they already disagree. #59241 is one case where derender drops the SentencePiece leading space that the engine restores.

My proposal is the same rule we're using for text. The engine is the reference.
  
- `output_mode=text / derender`: use the engine's `Logprob.decoded_token as-is` and don't re-resolve.
- Standalone /derender, including the parsed path: one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens `plus a shared `_correct_decoded_token`, with parity tests against the engine.

If that works for you and others, I'll open a separate issue for parsed path logprobs, blocked on this. Any per chunk cursor it needs would go into `DerenderStreamState` but I'd like to agree on how that state evolves before adding fields to it.

On (b), agreed that streaming stop strings need a hold-back. I'd rather not build it into derender yet, though. Stop strings only matter when the engine has a tokenizer (#57058 already rejects `stop` on `--tokens-only`), so the engine can apply them itself through `output_mode` (#56851) with the hold-back it already has. For now I'd have streaming `/derender` reject `stop` and point people at `output_mode=text`. If a tokens-only consumer turns up that really needs it, the pending text can be one more optional `DerenderStreamState`  field.

Let me know what you think.

On (b), agree with rejecting `stop` on streaming `/derender` for now. The cursor and any future stop hold-back are the two fields waiting on the state struct, so I'd design them together and change it once.

items.title: [Bug][MP] "full" prefetch drops columns that are partly in L1 when an L1 reservation fails
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `fetching_policy="full"`, if any L1 staging reservation fails, the prefetch controller trims the request to whole columns (Step 3.5 in `_transition_to_load_phase`, added in #5434). The trim only looks at `l1_reserved_keys`, so rows of a column that are already in L1 (`l1_locked_keys`) don't count. A column that is partly in L1 and partly loaded from L2 is never seen as whole, gets released, and turns into a miss.

`_finish_request` does count L1 rows when it picks the whole columns, so the same column is a hit when every reservation succeeds and a miss when some other column's reservation fails.

This affects the "full" callers: the blend sparse leg, warm prefetch and P2P. It shows up under L1 pressure, which is also when some rows of a chunk tend to get evicted.

**To Reproduce**

Three rows, two columns. Column 0 is in L1 for rows 0 and 2 and only in L2 for row 1. Column 1 is only in L2. L1 has room for three staging buffers, so the last row's reservation fails.

```python
rows = [make_group([make_object_key(i, gid=g) for i in range(2)], gid=g) for g in range(3)]
write_keys_to_l1(l1_manager, [rows[0].keys[0], rows[2].keys[0]], layout)
store_keys_in_l2(adapter, [rows[1].keys[0]] + [r.keys[1] for r in rows], layout)
# L1Manager sized for 5 objects
```

(helpers from `tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_controller.py`)

| case | hits |
| --- | --- |
| `full`, L1 big enough | `[[0, 1], [0, 1], [0, 1]]` |
| `full`, one reservation fails | `[[], [], []]` |
| `prefix`, one reservation fails | `[[0], [0], [0]]` |

**Expected behavior**

Column 0 is complete (two rows in L1, one loaded from L2), so the second case should return `[[0], [0], [0]]`.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at 6448b447. Adding `l1_locked_keys` to the cells the trim checks fixes it.

items.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
items.author: mrBenBern
items.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

items.title: [Feature] Implement Image Number Limitation for Image Processors
items.author: JustinTong0323
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

At present, there is no limitation on the number of images during the processing of mm data. It is necessary to impose such a limitation to prevent potential OOM and other problems.

(When using fast image processor, the GPU memory usage is roughly **1GiB** for each **4K** image)

### Related resources

Implementation Steps:
1. Define a constant, such as `IMAGE_NUM_LIMITATION = 5`, for each processor.
2. Modify the `baseprocessor` to utilize this constant for request validation.
3. Incorporate a server argument to enable modification of this numerical value.

In case you lack familiarity with the mm data processing pipeline, it is advisable to first refer to [here](https://github.com/zhaochenyang20/Awesome-ML-SYS-Tutorial/blob/main/sglang/code-walk-through/multimodal_request_lifecycle.md)

items.title: [Bug]: ngram_gpu crashes with num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size (assert num_speculative_tokens == self.k)
items.author: shijieheping
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0` (V1 model runner, defaults)
- GPU: 1× NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`ngram_gpu` accepts `num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size` (Dynamic SD) at config time, but the engine dies as soon as the scheduler picks a K different from `num_speculative_tokens`.

Repro:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --speculative-config \
  '{"method":"ngram_gpu","num_speculative_tokens":4,"prompt_lookup_max":5,"prompt_lookup_min":2,
    "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size":[[1,16,4],[17,256,0]]}'
# then send > 16 concurrent chat completions
```

Result (EngineCore fatal error, every in-flight request returns 500):

```
File "vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py", line 5014, in propose_draft_token_ids
    draft_token_ids, num_valid_draft_tokens = self.drafter.propose(
File "vllm/v1/spec_decode/ngram_proposer_gpu.py", line 340, in propose
    assert num_speculative_tokens == self.k
AssertionError
...
vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError
```

The same happens with a schedule that is K=0 everywhere (`[[1,256,0]]`), so it is not about the specific ranges.

`main` still has `assert num_speculative_tokens == self.k` in `NgramProposerGPU.propose`, while CPU `NgramProposer.propose` asserts `<= self.k` and works with the same schedule (including K=0). The Dynamic SD doc says only Eagle / Eagle-3 / DFlash were tested, so this may be expected, but then the combination should probably be rejected in `SpeculativeConfig` validation instead of crashing the engine at runtime.

Why it matters: `ngram_gpu` is the only n-gram method that keeps async scheduling, and CPU `ngram` disables it. For small models in large-batch offline runs, that loss is about 15–22% of steady throughput even when no drafts are produced (K=0 throughout). Dynamic SD on `ngram_gpu` (K=0 at large batch, K>0 for the low-concurrency tail) would be the draft-model-free way to get both.

Suggested options:
1. Validate: reject `num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size` with `method="ngram_gpu"` with a clear error; or
2. Support variable K in `NgramProposerGPU.propose` (e.g. allow `num_speculative_tokens <= self.k` and slice the kernel output / zero-length when K=0).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched existing issues for `ngram_gpu` + dynamic speculative decoding; found none.

items.title: [RFC]: CPU backend support for the vLLM connector + Mooncake Store L2 for multi-instance CPU serving
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes upstreaming two related contributions that enable **LMCache on the vLLM CPU backend** and make **cross-instance KV reuse** work for CPU serving:

1. **A CPU GPU-connector** (`VLLMCPUConnector`): a pure-torch gather/scatter path between vLLM's paged CPU KV cache and an LMCache `MemoryObj`, handling vLLM's 4D fused K/V CPU layout. This is the missing piece that lets LMCache run at all on `device=cpu`.
2. **Fixes to the Mooncake Store L2 connector** so it works on the CPU backend and shares KV **across instances** (fork-safe per-process client init, a correct `exists()`/lookup path, and a config-key alias).

Together these let multiple vLLM CPU instances behind a load balancer share one KV cache (SHM on a single box, or Mooncake Store over TCP across a cluster), instead of each instance recomputing the same prefixes.

Note that the CPU connector (contribution 1) is **backend-agnostic**: it is the shared foundation that unlocks the *entire* LMCache backend ecosystem on CPU (local DRAM L1, the shared SHM server, pickle, and remote L2s). Contribution 2 is one representative distributed L2 (Mooncake). We enable and validate **both** the default (SHM) and Mooncake paths because they target different deployment scopes (see §3.4).

We propose **two stacked PRs** (CPU connector, then Mooncake-on-CPU) plus this RFC to tie them together.

## 2. Motivation

- **CPU inference is growing** (cost, availability, disaggregated/CPU-tier deployments), and vLLM has a maturing CPU backend.
- **Multi-instance CPU serving needs *shared* KV.** vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is **per-instance**: behind a load balancer, instance B cannot reuse instance A's prefix KV, so shared system prompts / few-shot / documents are recomputed on every instance.
- **LMCache already solves cross-instance reuse**, but had **no CPU connector**, so it could not run on vLLM CPU at all; and the **Mooncake Store L2** path did not work on CPU or across instances (fork-safety + lookup bugs).
- **Measured impact** (Section 5): on a single-socket AMD EPYC, an external shared KV cache gives **+27-31% aggregate throughput at 3 instances** and **-28%/-34% p95/p99 tail latency** vs APC.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Topology

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LB[NGINX load balancer] --> V1[vLLM CPU inst 1]
    LB --> V2[vLLM CPU inst 2]
    LB --> V3[vLLM CPU inst 3]
    V1 <-->|store / load KV| L[(LMCache)]
    V2 <-->|store / load KV| L
    V3 <-->|store / load KV| L
    L <-->|put / get| S{{Shared KV: SHM  or  Mooncake Store L2 / TCP}}
```

### 3.2 CPU connector (`VLLMCPUConnector`)

**Why a CPU connector is needed.** Every existing GPU connector relies on CUDA custom ops (`c_ops`) and CUDA streams and assumes the GPU KV memory layout. None of that exists on CPU, so LMCache previously could not run on vLLM's CPU backend at all. `VLLMCPUConnector` fills that gap.

**What it implements.** The same connector interface, using **plain PyTorch tensor operations** (indexing + copy) with no CUDA kernels or streams:

- `from_gpu(...)` (**STORE / gather**): copy the KV for tokens `[start, end)` out of vLLM's paged CPU buffer into a contiguous `MemoryObj`.
- `to_gpu(...)` (**LOAD / scatter**): copy KV from a `MemoryObj` back into vLLM's paged buffer, placing each token's K/V into the slot given by vLLM's slot mapping.
- `batched_from_gpu(...)` / `batched_to_gpu(...)`: batched variants that handle several token ranges in one call.

**Handling vLLM's CPU KV layout.** vLLM's CPU backend stores each layer's cache as a single **4D fused K/V tensor** (K and V packed together), which is laid out differently from the GPU cache. For each layer the connector derives logical views shaped `[num_blocks, block_size, num_heads, head_size]` for K and for V (`_kv_token_views`), then uses the request's block/slot offsets to move exactly the right rows. This keeps gather/scatter correct without copying the whole buffer.

**Selection.** The connector is picked automatically when the device is CPU (`torch_device_type == "cpu"` in `CreateGPUConnector`), so no user config change is required.

**Plugging in as a `GPUConnectorInterface`.** So the CPU connector can subclass `GPUConnectorInterface` without importing the CUDA-heavy `gpu_connectors`/`utils` modules (which import `c_ops`, absent in NO_GPU_EXT builds), the interface ABC is extracted into a small `c_ops`-free `interface.py` that `gpu_connectors.py` re-exports. Existing GPU connectors are unaffected.

### 3.3 Mooncake Store L2 on CPU

The Mooncake client (Go runtime + multithreaded C++) is **not fork-safe**, and vLLM forks its scheduler/worker processes. Fixes:

- **Fork-safe, lazy per-process init**: the store/lookup client is created inside each process on first use (`_ensure_store()`), never inherited across a fork.
- **Correct lookup path**: `exists()`/`exists_sync()` now call `_ensure_store()` first (the contains/lookup path can run before any put/get on an instance) and compare `is_exist() == 1` (it returns `1/0/-1`) so an error never reads as a cache hit. Without this, cross-instance lookups were swallowed as misses and the instance recomputed.
- **Config-key alias**: accept `master_server_address` as an alias for `master_server_addr` in dict-based setup.

**Cross-instance key consistency (usage requirement, not connector code):** for a prefix computed on instance A to be found by instance B, the KV keys must hash identically across processes. Python's default randomized hashing breaks this; deployments must use a stable algorithm (e.g. `LMCACHE_PRE_CACHING_HASH_ALGORITHM=sha256` with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`). This will be documented.

### 3.4 Why enable both paths (default SHM and Mooncake L2)

The CPU connector is transport/backend-agnostic, so a natural question is *why validate two L2 paths instead of one*. Because they are **complementary, not competing**: the right choice is dictated by deployment topology, and we want CPU users to be able to pick either without changing the connecto

items.title: [Bug][S3] Connector errors raised on CRT threads are swallowed; circuit breaker ignores HTTP failures
items.author: aryangorde8
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/s3_connector.py` has two independent
error-handling defects. Both reproduce against any failing remote backend, and
both are visible in the log attached to #3376.

**Defect 1 — the PUT and GET completion callbacks raise on aws-crt threads**

`_s3_upload.on_done` and `_s3_download.on_done` raise a `RuntimeError` when the
request completes with an error or a non-success status. Those callbacks run on
aws-crt threads, as the `NOTE(Jiayi)` comment above `_s3_download.on_done`
already points out, and `awscrt.s3._S3RequestCore._on_finish` resolves
`finished_future` *before* it invokes `on_done`. The raise therefore cannot
reach the coroutine awaiting the future. It is handed to Python's unraisable
hook, which prints:

```
Exception ignored in: <awscrt.s3._S3RequestCore object at 0x...>
```

Two consequences:

* When aws-crt does report an error code, the future rejects and `_put` / `get`
  do enter their `except` branch — but with the crt error, while the message
  that carried the HTTP status is lost as untraceable noise. This is the
  "hundreds of identical `Exception ignored in:` lines" in #3376.
* When aws-crt reports no error code but the status is not a success — exactly
  the case these callbacks test for — the failure is lost completely. The
  `await` returns normally, so `_put` records the chunk in `object_size_cache`
  as if the upload had landed, and `get` hands back a `MemoryObj` that was
  never written. A later lookup then treats the key as a hit that S3 cannot
  serve.

**The file already contains the correct pattern.** `_get_object_size.on_done`
and `_get_object_size_async.on_done` only record into a `got` dict and let the
caller inspect it once the future has resolved. The HEAD path is right; the PUT
and GET paths are not.

**Defect 2 — the circuit breaker cannot trip on HTTP errors**

`_update_connection_failures(error_msg: str) -> bool` decides whether a failure
counts toward the breaker by substring-matching the message against
`CONNECTION_REFUSED`, `SOCKET`, `DNS` and `TIMEOUT`.

A persistent HTTP 400/401/403 — that is, any misconfiguration — matches none of
them. `connection_failures` never increments, `connection_disabled` never flips,
and LMCache reissues a guaranteed-doomed PUT for every single chunk,
indefinitely. That is why the log in #3376 contains hundreds of identical errors
within seconds. The breaker exists precisely to stop this, and it is blind to
the most common cause.

**To reproduce**

No object store, credentials, GPU or network are needed — stub the
`s3.S3Request` boundary and drive `on_done` directly:

1. Replace `awscrt.s3.S3Request` with a stub that resolves `finished_future`
   and *then* calls `on_done(error=None, status_code=400)`, mirroring
   `_S3RequestCore._on_finish`.
2. `await connector.put(key, memory_obj)`.
3. The `RuntimeError` raised inside `on_done` never reaches the coroutine;
   `connector.object_size_cache` contains the key as though the upload
   succeeded, and `connector.connection_failures` is still `0`.

The same stub with `status_code=403` on a GET makes `get()` return a
`MemoryObj` that was never filled.

**Expected behavior**

* A PUT or GET that completes with an error or a non-success status surfaces on
  the asyncio side, where `_put` / `get` / `batched_get` already have `try` /
  `except` blocks that log and feed the breaker.
* A repeated, non-retryable HTTP status trips the breaker, so LMCache stops
  hammering a backend that is guaranteed to reject every chunk.

**Additional context**

This is independent of the bucket-addressing question that caused the 400 in
#3376; that is being handled separately in #2624. These two defects are about
what the connector does with *any* failure, whatever produced it.

I have a fix with unit tests and will open a PR referencing this issue.

items.title: [Bug] Mamba hybrids without --separate-object-groups: prefix hits restore a state vLLM never computed
items.author: shawnguyen-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

Under vLLM `--mamba-cache-mode align`, a Mamba/linear-attention layer writes its recurrent state only at the end of a scheduler step. A step longer than one block leaves vLLM's null block in the state slot of every earlier block of that step. The attention blocks of those positions are real.

When the server runs without `--separate-object-groups` (the default), one object per chunk holds both the attention pages and the state page. `all_null_chunk_masks` skips a chunk only when **every** kernel group of the object is null. The attention groups never are, so the chunk is stored, with the null block's contents as its state.

The lookup then treats that object like any other. A later request sharing a prefix that ends on such a chunk gets a hit there, loads the null block's contents as the recurrent state, and continues from a state that was never computed. Nothing reports an error; the answers are wrong.

`docs/source/mp/hybrid_models.rst` says `--separate-object-groups` is required for these hybrids. Nothing enforces it: the vLLM connector cannot see the server flag, and only allows `--max-num-batched-tokens >= block_size`.

With `--separate-object-groups` the state object is skipped for those chunks and the lookup stops at the last chunk that has one. That path is correct.

**To Reproduce**

1. `lmcache server --chunk-size 2176 ...` (no `--separate-object-groups`).
2. vLLM with `nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16`, `--mamba-cache-mode align --enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-batched-tokens 8704 --block-size 2176`, and `LMCacheMPConnector` (or any client of the MP server).
3. Send `P + D0 + D1 + D2 + D3 + Q1` (P, D0..D3 one chunk each). vLLM prefills `[2176, 10880)` in one step, so only the state after 10,880 tokens is real.
4. Send `P + D0 + X + ... + Q2`. LMCache reports a 4,352-token prefix hit, and the request continues from the null block's contents.

The server's store for step 3 shows the state kernel group's block ids `[0, 0, 0, 4]` for chunks 1-4, and all four chunks committed.

**Measured** on the `lmcache/vllm-openai` nightly with vLLM 0.31.1rc1 (installed LMCache = `dev` at e64b43ef), Nemotron-3-Nano TP 1, 8,704-token steps, chunk 2,176. The client was a CacheBlend vLLM connector, whose prefix leg uses the same store and fold as the standard lookup. 27 reordered prompts over 3 runs; each needs a 6-digit code from the last document:
- 10 prompts got a prefix hit ending at 4,352 or 6,528 tokens. All 10 answered wrong.
- The other 17 answered right. So did every prompt with fresh documents (54/54).

**Expected behavior**

A prefix hit never ends on a chunk whose recurrent state was not computed.

**Additional context**

Fix: a chunk is not stored for an object when any of its recurrent-state kernel groups has only null block ids in it. Separated layouts and models without recurrent state are unchanged.

items.title: [Perf][MP] The ZMQ server reads one request per poll() and stops scaling under concurrent load
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`MessageQueueServer._main_loop` calls `poll()`, reads one request, and goes back to `poll()`. Responses from blocking handlers also wait until the notifier wakes the loop up again. Under concurrent load this per-request overhead adds up, and the server stops scaling at around 2,000 lookups/s.

**To Reproduce**

Start a CPU `lmcache server` and drive it from several client processes, each with a few threads running `lookup` → `query_prefetch_status` (polling every 1 ms) → `end_session`. From 4×2 up to 8×4 client threads, throughput stays flat at about 2,000 lookups/s while p50 latency climbs from 3.6 ms to 15.7 ms.

**Expected behavior**

The server keeps up with concurrent clients until the handlers themselves become the bottleneck.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at 7d7ca470, macOS, CPU only. I have a fix ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug] First-rank MLA retrieval stages the whole cache hit on the device
items.author: orthur2
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `save_only_first_rank` (the default for MLA models), a non-layerwise retrieve stages the entire cache hit on the device before any of it is written to the KV pages. `_broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs` copies each hit chunk to the device on rank 0, broadcasts it, and keeps every device copy alive until the single `batched_to_gpu` call at the end. A hit of N chunks therefore costs N chunk-sized device allocations on every rank, all live at the same time.

These allocations happen at serving time, after vLLM has planned and allocated its KV pool, so no budget covers them. They come out of whatever headroom `gpu_memory_utilization` leaves, which is a few GB at most, and a hit longer than that kills the engine. We ran into it with a hit of about 500k tokens: staging grew to several GB per rank and every rank died with an OOM raised from `_broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs`.

**To Reproduce**

Run an MLA model with LMCache in-process, keep `save_only_first_rank` at its default, and disable vLLM prefix caching so the hit goes through LMCache. Then make the hit larger than the device memory left after startup, either by raising `gpu_memory_utilization` or by storing a longer prompt. Send the prompt once so it is stored, then send the same prompt again. TP=1 is enough: the first rank stages every chunk on the device whether or not there is anyone to broadcast to.

Expected: the hit is written into the KV pages with bounded temporary device memory.

Actual: device memory grows with the hit, the retrieve fails with an OOM in `_broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs`, and the engine dies.

<details>
<summary>Verified example: DeepSeek-V2-Lite on one 32 GB card</summary>

vLLM 0.28.0, one RTX 5090 (32 GB), DeepSeek-V2-Lite with fp8 online quantization so it fits on the card. Its KV is about 30 KB per token, so a 256-token chunk is about 8 MB on the device and a 160k-token hit stages about 5 GB, well above the headroom that `gpu_memory_utilization` 0.85 leaves.

```bash
LMCACHE_CHUNK_SIZE=256 LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True LMCACHE_MAX_LOCAL_CPU_SIZE=20 \
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-model-len 163840 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --quantization fp8 \
  --enforce-eager \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_both"}'
```

Startup reports a KV pool of 10.08 GiB (347,984 tokens). A 160k-token completion request with `max_tokens=1` is stored in 89 s. The same request again is looked up as `LMCache hit tokens: 160000, need to load: 159999`, device memory climbs for about 36 s, and the engine dies with:

```
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 20.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total
capacity of 31.36 GiB of which 10.00 MiB is free. Including non-PyTorch memory, this process
has 31.30 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated memory 29.74 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, and
932.15 MiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.
  File "lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_v1_adapter.py", line 852, in start_load_kv
  File "lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py", line 859, in retrieve
  File "lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py", line 1863, in _broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs
```

followed by `EngineDeadError`. PyTorch had 29.74 GiB allocated against a 0.85 budget of 26.66 GiB; the difference is the staging that had accumulated before the allocation failed.

</details>

**Expected behavior**

Retrieval should stream the hit through a fixed, configurable device buffer, so that the device memory a retrieve needs depends on that buffer rather than on the hit size. That budget should also be something vLLM can account for, or at least be documented as living outside its KV plan.

**Additional context**

#5292 implements this with a fixed per-engine staging buffer and a windowed broadcast. Layerwise and multiprocess retrieval do not go through this path.

items.title: CUDA illegal memory access in cudaStreamSynchronize (flash-attn path) with Qwen3.6-35B MoE + partial expert offload — deterministic, cross-build (b10107, b10243); disappears with -fa off
items.author: GiulianoBonaventura
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`llama-server` crashes with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` in `ggml_backend_cuda_synchronize` (`cudaStreamSynchronize`, `ggml-cuda.cu:2485` on b10107 / `:2499` on b10243) while processing the **second** request of a specific two-request sequence. The crash is **deterministic** (reproduced 5+ times across two builds) and **disappears with `--flash-attn off`**.

### Environment

- Windows 11 Pro, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 12 GB, driver 610.47
- Builds tested: **b10107** and **b10243** (both `win-cuda-13.3-x64` release binaries, cudart DLLs present, GPU active and verified via VRAM usage ~11.5 GiB)
- Model: `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf` (unsloth repo, arch `qwen35moe`, MoE A3B)

### Server args (frozen across all probes unless noted)

```
--ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 --n-gpu-layers 99 --flash-attn on
--cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --no-mmap --jinja
--batch-size 1024 --ubatch-size 512 --no-context-shift
--override-tensor "blk\.(16|17|...|39)\.ffn_.*_exps\.=CPU"
```
(partial MoE expert offload to CPU: model is 22 GB, VRAM is 12 GB)

### Symptom

First request (RAG-style prompt ~900-7000 tokens, JSON-schema constrained output, `enable_thinking=false`) completes normally (~50 tok/s). The second request of the sequence crashes the server immediately after slot selection:

```
slot get_availabl: id 0 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, sim_best = 0.114 (> 0.100 thold)
slot launch_slot_: id 0 | task 853 | processing task, is_child = 0
E CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
E   current device: 0, in function ggml_backend_cuda_synchronize at D:\a\llama.cpp\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-cuda\ggml-cuda.cu:2485
E   cudaStreamSynchronize(cuda_ctx->stream())
```

### Variable isolation (one change per probe, same request sequence)

| probe | change vs frozen args | result |
|---|---|---|
| control | none (b10107) | **crash** (3/3) |
| A | `--slot-prompt-similarity 0` | crash (slot-reuse hypothesis refuted) |
| B | client sends `cache_prompt: false` | crash |
| C | build **b10243** (same args) | crash (same signature, `:2499`) |
| D | ALL experts to CPU (`blk\..*\.ffn_.*_exps\.=CPU`) | crash |
| E | no `--override-tensor`, `--n-gpu-layers 20` (whole-layer offload) | crash |
| F | `--cache-type-k/v f16` (fa still on) | crash |
| **G** | **`--flash-attn off`** (+ KV f16, required) | **no crash — same 2-request sequence and an 87-request campaign complete cleanly** |

CPU-only inference (no CUDA DLLs) also never crashes.

So: not the build, not prompt-cache/slot reuse, not the MoE offload pattern, not KV quantization — the crash tracks the **CUDA flash-attention path** on this arch/input, across at least b10107→b10243.

Also note: earlier probes with a different input showed the crash is input-dependent (a ~900-token prompt passes, a ~1200-token variant of the same content crashes), which is why we can reproduce it deterministically with our fixed sequence but cannot yet provide a minimal public prompt (the content comes from proprietary documents). Happy to run instrumented builds / additional probes on request, and to share token counts, sampling params, and full server logs.

### Expected behavior

No illegal memory access with `--flash-attn on`; or, if the configuration is unsupported for `qwen35moe` + partial expert offload, a graceful error instead of a crash.

items.title: [RFC]: Hot Standby Mode for Master Service Metadata High Availability
items.author: Libotry
items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Core Component Design #### (1) OpLogManager (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Record all state change operations (PUT_END, PUT_REVOKE, REMOVE) - Generate global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id - Maintain memory buffer (for fast queries) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogManager { uint64_t Append(OpType type, const std::string& key, const std::string& payload = ""); std::vector GetEntriesSince(uint64_t since_seq_id, size_t limit = 1000) const; uint64_t GetLastSequenceId() const; }; ``` #### (2) EtcdOpLogStore (Primary Side) **Responsibilities**: - Write OpLog to etcd - Update latest sequence_id - Record snapshot corresponding sequence_id - Clean up old OpLog **etcd Key Design**: - OpLog Entry: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/{sequence_id}` - Latest Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/latest` - Snapshot Sequence ID: `mooncake-store/oplog/{cluster_id}/snapshot/{snapshot_id}/sequence_id` #### (3) OpLogWatcher (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Watch etcd OpLog changes - Read historical OpLog (for initial synchronization) - Process Watch events and pass to OpLogApplier **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogWatcher { void Start(); void Stop(); bool ReadOpLogSince(uint64_t start_seq_id, std::vector& entries); }; ``` #### (4) OpLogApplier (Standby Side) **Responsibilities**: - Apply OpLog Entry to local metadata store - Check global and key-level order - Handle sequence number discontinuities and out-of-order cases - Periodically clean up key_sequence_map_ (memory optimization) **Key Methods**: ```cpp class OpLogApplier { bool ApplyOpLogEntry(const OpLogEntry& entry); bool CheckSequenceOrder(const OpLogEntry& entry); void CleanupStaleKey

comments.body: ### 1. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. Data Model Changes #### 3.1 Version Type ```cpp using Version = uint64_t; ``` Version can be constructed as: - High bits: timestamp (e.g., microseconds since epoch). - Low bits: per-node monotonic sequence ID. Requirements: - For a single master process, each successful `Put` for a given key gets a **unique, monotonically increasing** version. - Version collisions are practically impossible within a process lifetime. #### 3.2 Replica Descriptor Extension Extend `Replica::Descriptor` (or equivalent) to carry version information: On `PutStart`, the master generates `version`, stores it in metadata, and includes it in each replica descriptor. --- ### 4. Write Path (Put) Design #### 4.1 Master: PutStart 1. Client invokes `Put(key, slices, config)`. 2. `MasterService::PutStart(key, slice_lengths, config)`: - Validates input. - Allocates replicas as it does today (segments, buffers, etc.). - Generates a new `Version version = MakeVersion()` for this key. - Stores `version` in `ObjectMetadata` for this key. - Fills `ReplicaDescriptor.version = version` for each allocated replica. - Returns the list of descriptors to the client. All replicas of the same key for this `Put` share the same version. #### 4.2 Client: Writing to Store We enhance `TransferWrite` to enforce the following **write order** per replica: 1. Write **8-byte version header** at `buffer_address`. 2. Write **payload** at `buffer_address + 8` for length `size`. There are two implementation options: - **Option A: Two-step write** (simpler): - First,

comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

items.title: [Roadmap] sglang auto tuner
items.author: sglang-bot
items.body_excerpt:
Now we have many kernel backends for moe (e.g., triton, cutlass), attention, and allreduce. For each kernel, we can also tune some configs (e.g., the tile sizes in triton fused moe). Tuning these kernels and choosing dispatching heuristics can be non-trivial. We would like to build a simple command that auto-tune all the kernels and dispatch heuristic for a model.

## Todo
1. Implement a script sglang.auto_tune to tune the kernels and hyperparameters for a specific model. It should dump the optimal tile sizes/dispatching heuristics for all kernels used in this model. Example usage:
    - `python3 -m sglang.auto_tune --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 --tp 8`
    - `python3 -m sglang.auto_tune --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 --tp 4`
2. Start from tuning the triton fused moe https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/tree/main/benchmark/kernels/fused_moe_triton
3. Implement a github action workflow that tunes 20 popular models on 5 common platforms.
    - The workflow should take in two arguments: a list of model names, and a list of runner names
    - Our CI has H100, H20, H200, B200, GB200
4. Auto choose allreduce algorithms (custom allreduce, nccl, nccl symmetric memory, torch symmetric memory).
5. Auto choose attention kernel backend and moe runner backend.
6. Auto tune the cutlass gemm kernels (with cutlass profiler)
7. Auto choose speculative decoding parameters for different batch sizes.
