items.title: [Bug] Hybrid-SWA + radix cache: admission livelock when the SWA prefix lock pins a finished request's untrimmed last chunk
items.author: bill-h-lin
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With a hybrid-SWA model, the radix cache on and a tight SWA pool, the scheduler can stop admitting a request forever: 1 waiting, 0 running, GPU idle, no log line. We hit it on MiMo-V2.6-Flash (sliding window 128, page size 1) and traced it to `SWAComponent.acquire_component_lock` pinning a whole tree node that holds a finished request's untrimmed last chunk of SWA, instead of one window.

**Sequence** (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, `--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.06448` → SWA pool 8,451, `--context-length 131072`, `--max-running-requests 1`, overlap scheduler on):

1. A 32,768-token request with `max_new_tokens=1` (it finishes at its first token).
2. A request with the same 32,768 tokens, a different next token, then 4,999 more (37,768 in all).

Request 2 matches 32,768 cached tokens, needs 5,001 SWA slots and never runs. `/v1/loads` stayed at 1 waiting, 0 running for 43 minutes. The same sequence runs fine with `--chunked-prefill-size 4096` or with a 16,643-token SWA pool.

### Root cause (line numbers on `main` @ 6624999385)

1. Under the overlap scheduler, a request that finishes at its first token still gets one decode step prepared before its prefill result is processed: `alloc_for_decode` (`allocation.py:587`) commits one more token, and `release_kv_cache` → `insert_req(req, up_to=req.owned_kv_len())` keys `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)[:kv_committed_len]`. So it is cached with 32,769 tokens, its output token included.
2. `cleanup_after_caching_req` (`swa.py:1011`, the `not is_finished` guard at `:1023`) frees out-of-window SWA only for unfinished requests. So the request's final 8,192-token chunk keeps its SWA live. In the tree that is a node `[24,576, 32,641)` holding 8,065 live SWA slots, then the 128-token window leaf that `_maybe_split_leaf_for_swa_lock` (`swa.py:555`) capped "so locking it pins only one window".
3. Request 2 diverges at position 32,768, so its match splits the window leaf into 127 + 1. `acquire_component_lock` (`swa.py:811`) pins whole nodes until it has covered 128 tokens: the 127-token node, then the whole 8,065-token parent. **8,192 slots pinned** for a 128-token window.
4. `SWAPrefillBudget.check_prefill` (`prefill_budget.py:213`) sees 5,001 needed and 259 available. Since 5,001 fits an empty pool, it is not a permanent shortfall ("Transient pressure waits"), so the request waits for running requests to free slots. None exist.

The bound: only an untrimmed final chunk holds more than about one window of live SWA, so the lock over-pins by at most one chunk, while a request needs at most one chunk + 1. A pool of 2 × chunk + window + slack therefore always leaves enough (by 258 slots here), and one of chunk + window + slack, as above, can deadlock whenever a request reuses the path of one that finished at its first token (`max_tokens=1`, an immediate EOS or stop) and diverges inside its last window.

### Reproduction

- End to end: on a GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) with SGLang at 542a043, reproduced with the sequence above. That build carries local changes (an MoE expert-offload tier, and #41263's chunked-prefill SWA free order); none of them changes the radix tree, the SWA lock or `check_prefill` (#41263 only moves when a chunked request's out-of-window SWA is freed).
- On CPU, on the same build: the same four steps, with the scheduler's own `UnifiedRadixCache`, SWA allocator and `PrefillAdder` plus the orphan decode step, give 259 / 5,001 available / needed (not admitted) at chunk 8,192 / pool 8,451, and admit at chunk 4,096 (4,355 / 4,097) and at pool 16,643 (8,451 / 5,001).
- On `main`: the unit test in the linked PR builds a live parent + capped window leaf, matches a key that diverges on the last page and locks it; the lock pins the whole parent. Links 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged in the code on `main`; we have not run the end-to-end sequence on `main`.

### Proposed fix

In the lock walk, split a live, unlocked device-SWA node that is longer than what the window still needs, so only the in-window tail is pinned (the same idea as the leaf cap, applied to whatever node the walk reaches). PR: #41580.

Related: #27210 caps compute locks by splitting the lock's endpoint node. It does not cover this case: at page size 1 the match ends inside the capped leaf, the endpoint is shorter than a window, and the over-pin comes from its parent. #32379 fixed a different SWA admission livelock (decode headroom double-counted for cached resumes).

### Environment

SGLang 542a043 (end to end) and `main` 6624999385 (unit test), CUDA 13.0, torch cu130, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120), `--tp-size 1`, radix cache on, overlap scheduler on.

items.title: [Bug][KV Cache] nvfp4 KV silently reuses the checkpoint's fp8-calibrated k/v_scale as NVFP4 global scale → deterministic long-context corruption (single-variable proof, sm_120)
items.author: chengye75-star
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

Serving an NVFP4 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) on a checkpoint whose `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme` says `num_bits: 8` (e.g. unsloth's NVFP4 quants, which ship fp8-calibrated `k_scale`/`v_scale`) silently corrupts the KV cache: 32 tiny `[1]` bf16 scalars are loaded verbatim and consumed as the NVFP4 **global scale**. Removing exactly those 64 **bytes** flips long-context needle from 1/4 to 4/4 on an otherwise bit-identical 22.5 GB checkpoint. No log line ever mentions scales. Related but distinct: [#36121](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36121) (fp4 scales not traveling through HiCache host transfers; footnote has our hybrid-path measurement), [#39942](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39942) (fp8 KV scales silently *dropped* — opposite failure, same blind spot: nothing validates KV scale provenance).

## Setup

SGLang 0.5.21 (official PyPI wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu130, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (sm_120, TP2), driver 595.91.07. Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid 16 full-attention + 48 GDN layers, head_dim 256, compressed-tensors). Flags: `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --prefill-attention-backend flashinfer --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --context-length 195000 --page-size 64`, greedy, chat format. (Same rig as my [#36010 evidence post](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36010#issuecomment-5788493111); this bug is **independent of spec decode** — it hits the plain no-spec nvfp4 path.)

## Symptom

With scales as shipped, long-context retrieval collapses: needle **1/4 (d50) / 0/4 (d500)**; answers degenerate into question-echoing after a short thinking block. Everything else looks healthy — boot logs clean, short prompts / tool calls / vision normal. Deterministic: completion tokens reproduce byte-for-byte across boots and repeats.

## Root cause (source walk; mechanism marked as inference)

1. The checkpoint carries 32 per-layer `*.self_attn.{k,v}_scale` tensors — `[1]` bf16 scalars calibrated for **fp8** KV (`config.json → kv_cache_scheme: {num_bits: 8, static_minmax, symmetric}`).
2. *(inference, from source)* At load, `weight_utils.maybe_remap_kv_scale_name()` attaches them to the attention modules unconditionally; the fp4 path (`layers/attention/kvfp4_tensor.py`, comment: *"The KV cache path passes preloaded per-layer scales already on device"*) consumes them as the NVFP4 `global_scale` in `x_fp4 * block_scale * global_scale`.
3. *(inference)* Nothing validates the checkpoint's KV scheme against the runtime `--kv-cache-dtype`. An fp8-geometry scalar (amax/448 family) applied under NVFP4 geometry (amax/6 family) is off by ~75× → every stored K/V is systematically mis-scaled.

## Single-variable proof (same box, same day, same prompts)

| config (one variable per row) | needle d50 | needle d500 |
|---|---|---|
| unsloth + nvfp4, scales as shipped | 1/4 | 0/4 |
| **unsloth + nvfp4, 32 scale tensors stripped (64 bytes total), `kv_cache_scheme=null`** | **4/4** | **4/4** |
| unsloth + fp8_e4m3 (scale geometry matches dtype) | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| `sakamakismile/Qwen3.8-27B-MTP-NVFP4` + nvfp4 (checkpoint ships no scales) | 4/4 | 1/4 |

The stripped copy is a hardlink farm with only `model.safetensors` rewritten (header offsets recomputed; post-check: 0 leftover scale tensors) — the rest of the ~22.5 GB is byte-identical. Same-checkpoint before/after is the control: 64 bytes of metadata move the score by three needle questions.

## Why this is not an edge case

The filename pairing (`…-NVFP4` weights + `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) is the natural reading, and unsloth's NVFP4 releases ship fp8-calibrated KV scales as a matter of their recipe. Everyone doing that pairing gets silently wrong KV with zero log evidence; needle-style evals are the only thing that notices, and most people don't run those. Checkpoints without shipped scales (dynamic path, row 4) are unaffected — which is presumably why this hasn't surfaced loudly.

## Asks

1. **Validate at load**: if the checkpoint carries `k_scale`/`v_scale` and `kv_cache_scheme.num_bits` disagrees with `server_args.kv_cache_dtype`, warn loudly and skip them (fall back to dynamic scales) instead of reinterpreting an fp8 scalar as an fp4 global scale.
2. Checkpoints whose scheme says `num_bits: 4` (e.g. NVIDIA/ModelOpt NVFP4-KV exports) *should* consume their scales — the bug is specifically the mismatched pair, not scale loading per se.
3. Optional `--load-kv-scales {auto,never}` for quick A/B without safetensors surgery (our workaround rewrites a 22 GB file's header — works in 3 minutes, but terrifying to recommend).

## Verified workaround & production numbers

Drop the 32 `*.self_attn.[kv]_scale` tensors from `model.safetensors`, rewrite header offsets, set `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme = null`. The healthy config now serves our production: 185K-token cold prefill ~176 s, decode ~25 tok/s; with HiCache L2 (20 GB host, `write_through`, `page_first`, slru) a post-eviction 185K re-ask lands in **2.4–5.5 s** (vs 178 s cold) with the secret code word intact across the L2 round-trip (2/2 rounds, backup counters confirm real transfers); needle 4/4+4/4; tool-calls live. sm_120 hybrid-attention reference points are thin here — happy to post logs/transcripts.

Footnote re #36121: its fail-fast covers paths our hybrid assembly doesn't traverse (UnifiedRadixCache picks host pools in `hybrid_pool_assembler`), and in our exact combo (nvfp4 + HiCache + page_first + write_through) the fp4 block scales evidently *do* survive L2 as measured above — so the guard as drafted wouldn't cover this configuration either way. Full hybrid-path measurements posted as a review note on that PR.

- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

Version coverage: SGLang source inspected at `234ccba7f625e12639e621044496bcc6197c3758`; GPU reproduction with FlashInfer `0.7.0.post1` and CUTLASS DSL `4.8.0`. The original server used this SGLang base plus downstream patches. A pristine latest-main server was not rerun.

### Describe the bug

With FlashInfer KDA prefill selected, SGLang can pass a packed EXTEND batch with **FP32 SSM state** to a **recurrent implementation that requires BF16 state**. The batch shape changes which implementation FlashInfer selects; the state remains FP32 throughout.

The minimal triggering batch contains two sequences, each with one new token:

```text
q.shape      = [1, 2, 12, 128]
cu_seqlens   = [0, 1, 2]
total_tokens = 2
num_sequences = 2
initial_state.dtype = torch.float32
```

For this input, the dispatch proceeds as follows:

1. SGLang's [FlashInfer fallback condition](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/234ccba7f625e12639e621044496bcc6197c3758/python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/linear/kda_backend.py#L394-L427) checks whether the **total packed token count is at most 1**. Here it is 2, so the batch reaches `FlashInferKDAPrefillKernel`.
2. FlashInfer's [ordinary packed-prefill predicate](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.0.post1/flashinfer/kda_prefill.py#L572-L584) requires **total tokens > number of sequences**. Here `2 > 2` is false. With `backend="cute-dsl"`, the [public facade](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.0.post1/flashinfer/kda.py#L411-L638) therefore takes the recurrent path.
3. The [grouped recurrent kernel](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.0.post1/flashinfer/kda_kernels/recurrent_kda.py#L696-L708) copies the initial state into a register buffer whose element type is hard-coded to `cutlass.BFloat16`. It cannot perform that copy from FP32 state. Its later FP32 accumulation does not provide FP32 state-storage support.

The ordinary CuTe prefill implementation **does support FP32 state**: its [eligibility check](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.0.post1/flashinfer/kda_prefill_cute.py#L227-L241) accepts it and its [compiler specializes on the state dtype](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.0.post1/flashinfer/kda_prefill_cute.py#L321-L327). The integration must preserve that state contract when the batch shape selects a different path.

There is also a layout incompatibility on the selected recurrent path. SGLang supplies `[H, 128]` `dt_bias`. This is valid input for the public prefill API, which [accepts both flat and 2-D bias](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/v0.7.0.post1/flashinfer/kda_prefill_cute.py#L177-L188). The grouped recurrent compiler instead requires dimension 0 to have stride 1. Consequently, the 2-D bias raises a stride error before compilation reaches the state copy. Supplying flat bias exposes the FP32-state error.

The GPU reproducer below gives:

| SSM state storage | `dt_bias` layout | Observed result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FP32 | `[12, 128]` | `Expected strides[leading_dim] == 1, but got 128` |
| FP32 | `[1536]` | `autovec_copy ... got Float32 and BFloat16` |
| BF16 | `[12, 128]` | Same stride error |
| BF16 | `[1536]` | Call completes; output shape `[1, 2, 12, 128]`, finite values |

Expected behavior: packed EXTEND batches must use an implementation compatible with their existing SSM state dtype and accepted bias layout. For the FP32 configuration, short batches need a compatible path or fallback. The BF16 control demonstrates kernel-call compatibility only; it does not establish that changing the serving state's precision preserves model accuracy.

The integration and total-token fallback were introduced in #41400 (`fc3385d53005945473bca42ae62e9635cea1d6ca`). #43246 subsequently made FlashInfer prefill the default for eligible safe-gate KDA models on SM100/SM103.

<details>
<summary>Original serving observation</summary>

The initial failure occurred on Kimi-K3 with P=TP8 and D=TP8, each role on 2 nodes x 4 GB300, FP32 SSM state, EAGLE3, prefix caching, and FlashInfer prefill. The deployment used SGLang base `234ccba7f625e12639e621044496bcc6197c3758` plus downstream EAGLE3/DCP patches; its KDA prefill adapter was unchanged. The prefill schedulers failed at `2026-10-10 21:39:07 UTC` during a 48-concurrency stage, after warmup and earlier requests had succeeded. Decode then reported `Lost connection with prefill instance, 48 requests affected`.

Relevant traceback, with intermediate frames omitted:

```text
kda_backend.py:417, extend
  return kernel.extend(...)
kda_flashinfer_prefill.py:117, extend
  result = self._recurrent_kda(...)
flashinfer/kda.py:638, recurrent_kda
  return _kda_decode._run_recurrent_kda(...)
flashinfer/kda_kernels/recurrent_kda.py:2532, run_recurrent_kda
  compiled_grouped = _get_grouped_compiled(...)
flashinfer/kda_kernels/recurrent_kda.py:1009, _get_grouped_compiled
  dyn(dt_bias, 0)
RuntimeError: Expected strides[leading_dim] == 1, but got 128.
```

The original failing batch's sequence lengths were not captured. The two-token reproducer establishes a sufficient trigger for the same path and stride error; it does not establish that the original batch had exactly that shape. The FP32 state-copy error was observed in the isolated reproducer after flattening the bias, not in the original server traceback.

</details>

Save the following as `repro.py`. It calls the public FlashInfer API with the argument shapes supplied by the SGLang adapter. It requires one

items.title: [RFC]: KV cache grouping for hybrid models with speculative drafters
items.author: LucasWilkinson
items.body_excerpt:
**Status:** Draft · **PRs:** #58207 (group size), #58380 (prefer `BLHNC`, stacked on #58207)

## TL;DR

Speculative drafters on hybrid models add a small KV cache bucket of their own, which breaks vLLM's KV cache grouping heuristic in two ways:

- **Too many groups (Qwen3.5 / 3.6 + DFlash):** a one-layer drafter bucket forces **one group per layer**: Qwen3.5-27B goes from 4 to 70 groups (#49730), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 4 to 46. Each group rebuilds attention metadata every step, so DFlash loses much of its speedup; forcing fewer groups today costs KV cache capacity.
- **Full attention padding (MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash):** the 5-layer drafter bucket sets the group size, which doesn't divide the target's 9 full attention layers, so a full attention padding layer is allocated for the whole context (#58175). Kimi-K3 + DSpark has the same problem: its 5-layer drafter bucket pads the 24 MLA (full attention) layers, with 20 groups.

Checked and unaffected (identical grouping with and without these PRs): GLM-5.3-Flash + DFlash2, MiniMax-M3 + DSpark, DeepSeek-V4-Flash + DSpark.

A two-part proposal fixes both:

| part | problem | fix | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1 · #58207** | small drafter buckets force per-layer KV groups, or full attn padding | pick the group size by worst-case padding **bytes**; `--min-kv-cache-group-layers` (default 3) | 46 → **17** groups, **+54%** tok/s @c=1, **+36%** @c=32 | 11 → **7** groups, no full attn padding, KV capacity 5.76M → 5.96M |
| **2 · #58380** | `LBHNC` forces padding when drafter bytes/token ≠ target's | prefer `BLHNC` when the backends can run it and it avoids full attn padding or needs fewer groups | **5** groups, no padding, 7.53M tokens (> main's 7.42M); Triton only today | stays `LBHNC` at 7 groups (`BLHNC` would need 12 and has no full attn padding to remove) |

The parts are complementary: part 2 picks the path; part 1 is the fallback path (§5).

---

## 1. Background

**Motivation.** Enabling DFlash on Qwen3.5-27B raises the number of KV cache groups from 4 to **70**. Without a drafter, its 64 layers (48 GDN + 16 full attention) form 4 groups of 16; with DFlash, every layer gets its own group (64 target + 6 drafter). The drafter adds a one-layer full attention bucket, and the grouping heuristic falls back to one group per layer (#49730). Every group rebuilds its attention metadata each step, and GDN (linear attention) metadata builders are expensive, so this becomes per-step host overhead and DFlash runs well below its expected speedup; the effect is larger on Qwen3.5-4B. Forcing a larger group size recovers the throughput but, with today's grouping, costs KV cache capacity.

A drafter can also cost KV cache capacity rather than speed. MiMo-V2.5 + its DFlash drafter has buckets `[9 full, 39 SW, 5 drafter SW]`: the drafter bucket is the smallest, so the group size becomes 5, and the 9 full attention layers get a padding layer that grows with context (#58175 reports ~10% more KV capacity once it's removed). Kimi-K3 + its DSpark drafter behaves the same way (Case 3).

Related reports:

| report | model | groups | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| #49730 | Qwen3.5-27B / 4B + DFlash (H100) | 4 without DFlash → 70 with (one per layer) | DFlash ITL much slower than expected; forcing gs=16 recovers ~10% tok/s on 27B but shrinks KV capacity 216k → 141k tokens |
| #51742 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash (H200) | 46 | `build_attn_metadata` ~31 ms/step vs ~6 ms at 10 groups; output tok/s ~2× at c=1 with fewer groups |
| #52297 | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | — | one GDN `build()` takes ~900 µs and is repeated per group |
| #58175 | MiMo-V2.5 + DFlash | 11 | 1 full attn padding layer; removing it gives +10.57% KV capacity (their setup); +8.4% in ours (5.76M → 6.25M) |
| this RFC | Kimi-K3 + DSpark (`RedHatAI/Kimi-K3-speculator.dspark`, TP4) | 20 | 1 MLA (full attn) padding layer; #58207: 17 groups, no MLA padding, +0.37% KV capacity |
| #42505, #46462 | Qwen3.5 / 3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash | — | DFlash slower than expected / than baseline at higher concurrency; not root-caused, likely related |

This RFC's own measurement (§4.1): Qwen3.6-35B-A3B + DFlash on B300 goes from 460 → 733 tok/s at c=1 when the 46 groups drop to 17.

### 1.0 Terms

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| bucket | all layers whose KV cache specs merge (same attention type and shape) |
| group / `group_size` (gs) | a KV cache group shares one block table; buckets are split into groups of `group_size` layers |
| page | one layer's slice of a block; its size is that layer's bytes/token × block size |
| padding | layer slots in a group with no layer behind them; allocated but never written |
| manager vs kernel block | the KV manager allocates *manager* blocks; attention kernels may need them split into smaller *kernel* blocks |
| `LBHNC` | layer-outermost `KVCacheLayout` (today's default): every page is resized to one size, each group gets `group_size` pages per block |
| `BLHNC` | block-outermost `KVCacheLayout`: a block is one contiguous run of per-layer pages, so pages of different sizes share a block. `LBNHC`/`BLNHC` group the same way as `LBHNC`/`BLHNC` |

### 1.1 Buckets, groups, padding

```
Legend:  F/f = target/DRAFTER full attn   S/s = target/DRAFTER sliding window   M = mamba/GDN
         ▓ = full attn padding (grows with context, up to max_model_len)
         ░ = SW / mamba padding or idle page (bounded by window / state)

drafter full-attn group, group_size = 5 (one physical block):
│ f │ ▓ │ ▓ │ ▓ │ ▓ │   4 of 5 pages never written

every group's block has the same byte size (block IDs are shared across groups)
```

| cost | grows with | note |
|---|---|---|
| per-step metadata | # groups | one block table + builder call per group; GDN builders are expensive |
| KV capacity | padded slots × bytes/request | full attn slot: up to `max_model_len` tokens; SW / mamba slot: bounded |

### 1.2 Bad cases

```python
group_size = min(bucket sizes)                       # main

items.title: [Bug] DFlash2/DSpark + prefix caching corrupt output after a cache hit on Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (compressed-tensors) on 0.30/0.31; 0.29, FP8 target and MTP are fine
items.author: sinmkd
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.31.0 (also reproduced on 0.30.0). vLLM 0.29.0 passes the same test.
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, flashinfer-python/cubin 0.7.0.post1 (0.6.18.post1 on 0.30.0), CUDA 13.3, driver 610.57.04
- 1× RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell 48 GB (sm_120), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0.0-34
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` NVFP4 checkpoint, compressed-tensors mixed precision (NVFP4 on the MLP projections, FP8 W8A8 on attention / GDN projections / lm_head, `linear_attn.{in_proj_a,in_proj_b,norm}` and `mtp.*` unquantized via `ignore`)
- Drafter: `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (`DFlash2DraftModel`, sliding_window 2048), `num_speculative_tokens: 7`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since 0.30.0, serving Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 with the DFlash2 drafter and prefix caching enabled produces garbage after a prefix-cache hit. The first requests of a conversation are fine. From the third request on, once the prompt resumes from cached blocks, the model emits a single repeated token (`duct`, over and over) with no coherent content, and the drafter accepts nothing (`SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted: 0 tokens`). The same five requests against 0.29.0 come back coherent every time. I have run the comparison twice on each version.

The test is a replay of a real agent conversation: five consecutive chat-completions requests from one session (31,776 / 45,606 / 52,737 / 65,364 / 67,502 prompt tokens, 25 tool schemas, seed 17), sent in order to a fresh engine so each request hits the previous one's prefix. The conversation itself is private, but I can build a synthetic equivalent if that helps.

Serve command (production flags):

```
vllm serve /models/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --max-model-len 250000 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 17379961324 \
  --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7}' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --override-generation-config '{"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":20,"min_p":0.0}' --scheduling-policy priority
```

env: `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0 VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=false`. Prefix caching on (default), `mamba_cache_mode` resolves to `align`.

### What I tried, to narrow it down

All on 0.31.0, same five requests, fresh engine each time:

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| nothing (command above) | fails at request 3 |
| PR #57128 applied (the `MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` / `drop_eagle_block` fix) | fails |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` instead of FlashInfer | fails |
| `--linear-backend cutlass` (in-tree CUTLASS NVFP4 GEMM) | fails |
| `--linear-backend marlin` (weight-only W4A16, no activation quant) | fails |
| smaller KV pool / 180K window / util 0.94 (copied from my FP8 route) | fails |
| `"disable_eagle_block_drop": true` in the speculative config | worse: garbage from request 1, even cold |
| **no speculative config at all** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` (checkpoint's own MTP head)** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"dspark","model":"RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-speculator.dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7}`** | **fails at request 3** |
| **FP8 target (`Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8`, `quant_method: fp8`) with the same DFlash2 config** | **passes 5/5, twice** |

A unique `cache_salt` per request on 0.30.0 also makes requests 3–5 pass, so the failure needs an actual cache hit.

So the NVFP4 GEMM kernels are not involved (three different kernels, including weight-only, all fail), the GDN prefill kernel is not involved, and the KV pool size is not involved. What it needs is: a hidden-state drafter (DFlash2 or DSpark; MTP is fine) + a prefix-cache hit + this compressed-tensors NVFP4 target, on 0.30 or later. The FP8 checkpoint with the identical drafter config is fine. Turning off the EAGLE trailing-block drop makes it strictly worse, which reads to me like the drafter is leaving bad Mamba/GDN state in the cached tail block and the drop normally hides it inside a request but not across requests.

The compressed-tensors checkpoint is the obvious difference from the FP8 one: it has an `ignore` list covering `linear_attn` sub-modules (the bf16 `in_proj_a` / `in_proj_b` / `norm`) alongside `config_groups` that target `linear_attn.{in_proj_qkv,in_proj_z,out_proj}` at FP8. If the drafter path resolves those layers differently from the plain `fp8` loader, that would be where I'd look first, but I haven't gone further than the table above.

Related: #53912 and #55766 describe neighbouring hybrid-GDN prefix-cache corruption with speculative decoding.

### What I can provide

Per-request replay output (prompt token counts, finish reasons, draft metrics), engine logs for every ablation above, and a synthetic reproducer on request.

items.title: [Bug]: Gemma 4 encoder CUDA graph capture allocates `max_frames_per_batch` full-image rows per budget (38.5 GiB with `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096`) and OOMs
items.author: toan-tq
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM `0.31.1rc1.dev159+g4274ae956` (main @ 4274ae956c), precompiled wheel. The code involved is unchanged on current main (3c062d391d); the links below point to 276fbcff27.
- torch 2.13.0+cu132, torchvision 0.28.0, transformers 5.19.0, CUDA 13.2, driver 595.91.07
- 1× RTX 5090 32 GB (sm_120)
- Model: `nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Turning on encoder CUDA graphs for Gemma 4 with video enabled kills the engine during encoder CUDA graph capture:

```
vllm serve nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-model-len 32768 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --async-scheduling \
  --attention-config '{"backend": "TRITON_ATTN"}' --moe-backend marlin \
  --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": 1, "video": 1}' --media-io-kwargs '{"video": {"num_frames": 32}}' \
  --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mm_encoder": true}'
```

```
INFO [encoder_cudagraph.py:208] EncoderCudaGraphManager initialized with paths={'default': [70, 140, 280, 560, 1120, 2240, 4096]}, max_batch_size=58, max_frames_per_batch=1856, use_dp=False, capture_axes=()
...
  File ".../vllm/v1/worker/encoder_cudagraph.py", line 324, in _capture_budget_graph
    output = self.model.encoder_cudagraph_forward({**values}, path=path)
  File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4_mm.py", line 1994, in encoder_cudagraph_forward
    inputs_embeds = vt.patch_embedder(
  File ".../transformers/models/gemma4/modeling_gemma4.py", line 624, in forward
    pixel_values = 2 * (pixel_values - 0.5)
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 6.69 GiB. GPU 0 has a total capacity of 31.36 GiB of which 4.42 GiB is free.
```

6.69 GiB is exactly one `(1856, 2520, 768)` bf16 tensor, i.e. one copy of the capture dummy for a single budget.

#### Root cause

When nothing is set by the user, [`EncoderCudaGraphManager.__init__`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/276fbcff2717bd934cfa37c8a2e4c391f3e7237b/vllm/v1/worker/encoder_cudagraph.py#L158-L174) infers:

- `max_batch_size = min(max_budget // min_budget, min(budgets)) = min(4096 // 70, 70) = 58`
- `max_frames_per_batch = max_batch_size * max_frames_per_video = 58 * 32 = 1856`

In Qwen2.5-VL / Qwen3-VL / GLM-4.1V, `max_frames_per_batch` only decides how the budget is laid out across frames (`cu_seqlens`, capture grid), so the pixel buffer stays close to the token budget. The Gemma 4 hook ([`prepare_encoder_cudagraph_capture_inputs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/276fbcff2717bd934cfa37c8a2e4c391f3e7237b/vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4_mm.py#L1833-L1858)) instead uses it as the row count of a dense pixel buffer, with every row sized for a full image:

```python
max_size = max(max_batch_size, max_frames_per_batch)          # 1856
per_item_output = min(token_budget, configured_max_tokens)    # 280 for every budget >= 280
per_item_patches = per_item_output * pool_ratio               # 2520
dummy_pixel_values = torch.zeros((max_size, per_item_patches, patch_pixels), ...)
```

As a result:

- **Every budget gets 1856 rows.** The token budget never shrinks the row count, so the 280-token budget would allocate the same `(1856, 2520, 768)` buffer as the 4096-token one.
- **The buffers would add up.** Each budget keeps its own dummy as the graph's `input_buffers` ([L343](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/276fbcff2717bd934cfa37c8a2e4c391f3e7237b/vllm/v1/worker/encoder_cudagraph.py#L343)), so the 7 budgets would hold 38.5 GiB of bf16 dummy input. On this 32 GB card, capture fails before that.
- **The warm-up forward is huge.** Capture starts at the largest budget and first runs one eager forward over the whole dummy ([L324](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/276fbcff2717bd934cfa37c8a2e4c391f3e7237b/vllm/v1/worker/encoder_cudagraph.py#L324)), i.e. 1856 × 2520 ≈ 4.7 M patch tokens through the vision tower in one call. The eager encoder path chunks with `_encoder_chunk`; this path does not.
- **A replay never needs more than `token_budget // 70` rows.** `_execute_local` bills each item by [`get_encoder_cudagraph_item_specs`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/276fbcff2717bd934cfa37c8a2e4c391f3e7237b/vllm/model_executor/models/gemma4_mm.py#L1693-L1737), i.e. by padded slots: 70 per video frame (630 patches) and `max_soft_tokens` (≥ 70) per image. That gives 58 rows at 4096, the inferred `max_batch_size` itself, and 4 rows at 280.

Capture size vs. what a replay can use (1 GPU, video enabled, `max_frames_per_video = 32`, bf16):

| `max_num_batched_tokens` | rows captured | dummy per budget ≥ 280 | all budgets | replay bound (`budget // 70` rows), all budgets |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2048 | 928 | 3.35 GiB | 15.9 GiB | 0.21 GiB |
| 4096 | 1856 | 6.69 GiB | 38.5 GiB | 0.43 GiB |
| 8192 | 2240 | 8.07 GiB | 54.5 GiB | 0.87 GiB |

`tests/models/multimodal/generation/test_vit_cudagraph.py` pins `encoder_cudagraph_max_vision_items_per_batch=1`, `encoder_cudagraph_max_frames_per_batch=16` and budget `[1120]` for gemma4, so CI never runs the auto-inferred sizing.

#### Workarounds (not run, sizing arithmetic only)

- **Images only:** `--limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": 1, "video": 0}'` sets `max_frames_per_batch = 0`, so the buffer becomes `(58, 2520, 768)` (at most 214 MiB bf16 per budget).
- **With video:** pass `"encoder_cudagraph_max_frames_per_batch": N` with `N = max_num_batched_tokens // 70`. The row count becomes `max(max_batch_size, N)`: 58 at 4096 (any `N ≤ 58` gives the same), 117 at 8192. Do not go below `max_num_batched_tokens // 70`. The packer only checks items and tokens ([L510](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/276fbcff2717bd934cfa37c8a2e4c391f3e7237b/vllm/v1/worker/encoder_cudagraph.py#L510)), not frames, so a replay with more frames than captured rows would fail in `pad_pixel_values` (#60112 adds an eager fallback).
- **Video output on main:** #60687 (claim 2) reports that video replay reads the wrong pooled rows from the second frame o

items.title: [Feature] L1/L2/L3 cache hit rate observability — Prometheus metrics, OTel spans & per-request JSONL trace
items.author: grissomsh
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

LMCache's current `PrometheusLogger` provides basic metrics (`time_to_retrieve`, `num_retrieve_requests`), but is missing:

1. **Per-tier cache hit rate** — no way to distinguish whether a hit came from L2 (CPU RAM), L3 (NVMe Disk), or a remote backend.
2. **TTFT decomposition** — `frontend_latency` (API server → engine core) and per-request `kv_lookup_time` / `kv_retrieve_time` are not surfaced.
3. **Per-request tracing** — no way to correlate cache-hit details to an individual request for debugging latency spikes.

These gaps make it hard to answer operational questions like: *"Why did TTFT spike — was it a slow disk read, CPU cache contention, or GPU prefix cache eviction?"*

---

### Design Goals

1. **Three-layer observability model**: throughput → latency → cache hit rate
2. **Minimally invasive**: extend existing `LMCStatsMonitor`, `PrometheusLogger`, and `cache_engine` — no breaking API changes
3. **TP-aware**: cross-process bridge via `/dev/shm` for Worker ↔ EngineCore per-request data relay when TP > 1
4. **Self-verifying**: every trace carries token identity equations for automated correctness validation

---

### Proposed Design

#### Layer 1 — Throughput: Token Source Decomposition

```
Tokens/s = local_compute + L1_hit + L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit
```

**Approach**: Extend `cache_engine.py`'s `retrieve()` / `retrieve_layer()` to classify hit tokens by storage backend. Add a `_BACKEND_NAME_TO_HIT_TIER` mapping:

| Backend | Tier |
|---------|------|
| `LocalCPUBackend` | L2 |
| `LocalDiskBackend` / `GdsBackend` | L3 |
| `RemoteBackend` | Remote |

**New Prometheus metrics** (6 total):

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

#### Layer 2 — Latency: TTFT Decomposition

```
TTFT = frontend_latency + queue_time + prefill_time
prefill_time ⊃ kv_lookup_time + kv_retrieve_time
```

**Approach**: Add `LMCacheKVConnectorStats` (extending vLLM's `KVConnectorStats`) on the vLLM side, and expose per-request timing through `vllm_v1_adapter.py`'s `request_finished()` via `EngineCoreOutput.kv_transfer_params`.

**New Prometheus metrics** (9 bridge metrics + 1 framework metric):

| Metric | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram | KV lookup latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram | KV retrieve latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: process_tokens phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: CPU→GPU DMA phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L2 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L3 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side remote bridge |
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram | API server → engine core latency |

#### Layer 3 — Cache Hit Rate & Per-Request Trace

One JSONL `[trace]` line emitted per request at completion:

```json
{
  "ts": 1782023561.679,
  "rid": "chatcmpl-xxx",
  "prompt_tokens": 3934,
  "output_tokens": 32,
  "TTFT_ms": 169.2,
  "queue_ms": 0.04,
  "prefill_ms": 130.1,
  "decode_ms": 144.6,
  "e2e_ms": 314.3,
  "frontend_ms": 39.0,
  "input_tokens_cache_hit": 3840,
  "L1_hit": 0,
  "external_kv_hit": 3840,
  "L2_hit": 0,
  "L3_hit": 3840,
  "remote_hit": 0,
  "input_tokens_no_cache_hit": 94,
  "kv_transfer_mode": "non_layerwise",
  "kv_lookup_ms": 1.2,
  "kv_retrieve_ms": 101.5
}
```

**Token identity equations** (verifiable by automated scripts at runtime):

```
prompt_tokens = input_tokens_cache_hit + input_tokens_no_cache_hit
input_tokens_cache_hit = L1_hit + external_kv_hit
external_kv_hit ≈ L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit   (≈ due to chunk_size=256 granularity)
```

#### Cross-Process Bridge (TP > 1)

When TP > 1, `retrieve()` runs on Worker_TP0 while `request_finished()` runs on the EngineCore/scheduler process. Per-request data is relayed via file-based bridge in `/dev/shm/lmcache_bridge/` (tmpfs, memory-backed):

- Per-tier counters: file + `fcntl.flock` for atomic cross-process updates
- Timing data: `write-tmp + os.replace` for atomic JSON
- Cleanup: throttled periodic sweep + retry limit (3) to prevent `/dev/shm` exhaustion

#### OTel Span Attributes

8 attributes on the `"llm_request"` span:

| Attribute | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_frontend` | API → engine |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_lookup` | KV lookup |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_transfer` | KV retrieve |
| `gen_ai.usage.l1_hit_tokens` | L1 (GPU prefix cache) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l2_hit_tokens` | L2 (CPU RAM) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l3_hit_tokens` | L3 (NVMe/SSD) |
| `gen_ai.usage.remote_hit_tokens` | Remote backend |
| `gen_ai.latency.kv_transfer_mode` | layerwise / non_layerwise |

---

### Metrics Summary (16 new Prometheus metrics)

**LMCache side (6):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

**vLLM bridge (9):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_transfer_mode` | Info |

**vLLM framework (1):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram |

---

### Verification

The design has been validated end

items.title: [Bug] AsyncPQExecutor shutdown deadlocks: close() awaits a sync shutdown, and shutdown_async cancels workers before draining the queue
items.author: aryangorde8
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`AsyncPQExecutor` in `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/job_executor/pq_executor.py` cannot
be shut down reliably. There are two separate problems, and the correct pattern for
the second one already exists in the same file.

**Problem 1 — `S3Connector.close()` cannot complete**

```python
async def close(self):
    await self.pq_executor.shutdown(wait=True)
```

`AsyncPQExecutor.shutdown` is **synchronous** (it returns `None`), so `await`ing it is
already wrong. More importantly it is implemented as:

```python
def shutdown(self, wait: bool = True) -> None:
    future = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(self.shutdown_async(wait), self.loop)
    if wait:
        future.result()
```

`close()` is a coroutine that runs *on* `self.loop`, so `future.result()` blocks that
loop while waiting for a coroutine that needs the same loop to make progress. It
deadlocks.

Reproduced with a standalone probe: scheduling `await executor.shutdown(wait=True)`
onto the executor's own loop never returns, and the call has to be abandoned by
timeout.

**Problem 2 — `shutdown_async(wait=True)` can hang on `queue.join()`**

In `AsyncPQExecutor.shutdown_async`, the workers are cancelled *before* the queue is
drained:

```python
        # Cancel all worker futures to ensure they stop
        # Even when wait=False, we should cancel workers to prevent hanging coroutines
        for fut in self._workers:
            if not fut.done():
                fut.cancel()          # <-- line 114

        if wait:
            # Let workers drain tasks and exit gracefully
            await self._queue.join()  # <-- line 118
```

A sentinel is pushed per worker just above this, and `_worker` calls
`self._queue.task_done()` when it consumes one. If a worker is cancelled before it
consumes its sentinel, `task_done()` is never called for that item, the queue's unfinished
count never reaches zero, and `await self._queue.join()` waits forever.

**`AsyncPQThreadPoolExecutor.shutdown_async`, in the same file, already does this in the
right order** — it awaits `self._queue.join()` first and only then cancels the worker
futures, with a separate `else` branch that cancels immediately when `wait=False`. The
subclass is correct; the base class is not.

**To reproduce**

Timing dependent, so it is interpreter-sensitive. A test fixture that tears down with
`await executor.shutdown_async(wait=True)` on the executor's loop passes consistently on
Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12, and hangs on **every** test on Python 3.13 (3.13.15), where
it surfaces as a `TimeoutError` from whatever bounds the wait. CI's `Test` matrix covers
3.13, so this is reachable from CI.

**Expected behavior**

`shutdown_async(wait=True)` drains and returns, and `close()` on a connector that owns an
`AsyncPQExecutor` completes rather than deadlocking.

**Suggested fix**

For problem 2, match the ordering the subclass already uses: `join()` first, cancel
after. For problem 1, `close()` should await `shutdown_async` directly rather than the
synchronous `shutdown` wrapper.

**Additional context**

Found while adding tests in #4484 — the fixture there works around this by using
`wait=False`, which cancels the workers without waiting on a drain a cancelled worker can
no longer complete. That is a workaround in test code, not a fix for the executor. I have
not touched `pq_executor.py` in that PR, to keep its scope to the S3 connector.

I am happy to send a PR for this if the suggested direction looks right.

items.title: [Bug] CacheBlend: the blend matcher never reuses compact IDs, so it stops indexing after 2^20 chunks over a server's life
items.author: shawnguyen-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`BlendTokenRangeMatcher` gives every registered chunk a compact ID, and IDs are never reused.
- **Allocation.** A new ID is `len(self._chunk_token_hash)`, a list that only grows (`matcher.py`, `on_new_token_hashes`).
- **Eviction does not free it.** `remove_chunks` marks the ID dead (`_chunk_token_hash[cid] = None`) but leaves the list as long as it was.
- **The cap.** Once 2^20 (1,048,576) IDs have been handed out, every later registration is dropped. The server logs `BlendTokenRangeMatcher compact-ID overflow: ... Skipping.` at ERROR and `on_new_token_hashes` returns 0.

So the limit is on chunks registered over the server's life, not on chunks live in the index. After it, no newly stored content can be blended until the server restarts. Lookups keep working for what was indexed earlier, which hides the problem: hit rate decays as old content leaves the cache.

**How soon.** 2^20 chunks of 256 tokens is about 268M fingerprinted tokens. A server storing 10k tokens/s reaches it in about 7.5 hours. Two things make it sooner:
- With `--enable-dedup-content` off (the default), the same text stored behind a new prefix is a new chunk. A blended request that is stored re-indexes every document it reuses. Registrations grow with request count, not with distinct content.
- The 80% WARNING (`nearing capacity ... Hash collision rate is rising`) also counts lifetime IDs. It fires on every registration from then on, and it names the wrong cause: the table may be nearly empty.

**To Reproduce**

CPU only, with a small table so the cap is reached quickly:

```python
from lmcache.v1.distributed.api import ObjectKey
from lmcache.v1.multiprocess.modules.blend.matcher import BlendTokenRangeMatcher


class Small(BlendTokenRangeMatcher):
    _TABLE_BITS = 3
    _TABLE_SIZE = 1 << 3


m = Small(chunk_size=256)
chunk = lambda s: [s * 256 + i + 1 for i in range(256)]
for s in range(8):  # register and evict 8 chunks
    m.on_new_token_hashes(chunk(s), [ObjectKey.IntHash2Bytes(1000 + s)])
    m.remove_chunks([ObjectKey.IntHash2Bytes(1000 + s)])

# Nothing is live, yet a new chunk cannot be indexed.
print(m.on_new_token_hashes(chunk(99), [ObjectKey.IntHash2Bytes(9999)]))  # 0
print(m.match_sub_sequence(chunk(99)))  # []
```

It logs `compact-ID overflow: 8 chunks registered, cannot add 1 more (limit 8)`.

The allocation code is the same on `dev` at b0b3567b.

**Expected behavior**

The limit applies to live chunks. An evicted chunk's ID is reused, and the capacity warning counts live chunks.

**Additional context**

- A fix needs a free list of evicted IDs, and each per-ID array (`_compact_id_to_slot`, `_chunk_poly_hash`, `_chunk_token_hash`) reset on reuse.
- Freeing alone may not be enough. A chunk leaves the matcher only when a lookup finds it missing twice. A chunk whose KV left the cache and that no lookup touches again keeps its ID. Removing chunks on the cache's eviction events would bound the index by what is actually stored.
- This is separate from #5597 (eviction clearing a slot it does not hold). That fix does not change ID allocation.

items.title: [Feature][CB] Report each blend match's stored predecessor in CBMatchResult
items.author: shawnguyen-tensormesh
items.body_excerpt:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

A CacheBlend client needs to know which matched chunks start a new source context: chunks whose cached KV was computed after a *different* chunk than the one they now follow. Recomputing the first tokens of exactly those chunks greatly improved long-context answer quality in our tests.

**Measured** with a CacheBlend vLLM client: gpt-oss-120b, needle test, ~65k-token prompts that reuse 42 stored documents in a new order, 99.6 % of the prompt blended.

| configuration | needle failures |
|---|---|
| default selection | 13/48 |
| recompute the first 128 tokens of each context-starting chunk | 1/48 |
| control: the same number of rows, 512 tokens into each document | 8/24, against 10/24 for the default on the same 24 prompts |

Today `CBMatchResult` carries only `(old_st, old_ed, cur_st, cur_ed, hash)`. A client can only guess continuity from positions: consecutive matches with equal `cur_st - old_st` offsets. That guess is wrong whenever two *different* stored sequences sit at matching offsets.

**Example.**
- **Stored:** doc A as `[S, Z, A]` and doc B as `[S, Y, B]`, where `|Y| = |Z| + |A|`. So B's stored start equals A's stored end.
- **New prompt:** `[S', X, A, B]` with `|X| = |Z|`. A and B are both non-prefix matches at offset 0, and B starts where A ends.
- **Result:** B looks like a continuation of A, although its cached KV followed Y.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Each match reports the chunk it was stored right after, so a client can test continuity exactly:

```python
continues = b.cur_st == a.cur_ed and b.predecessor_hash == a.hash
```

- **The identity:** the stored predecessor's token hash. Token hashes are prefix hashes, so equal hashes mean equal stored prefixes, and the test above holds exactly when `b`'s KV was computed right after `a`'s.
- **Where:** recorded at STORE, when the matcher indexes a chunk; returned by the matcher with each match.
- **Wire:** an optional trailing field, `predecessor_hash: bytes | None = None` (and `optional bytes` in `blend_service.proto`). Old and new clients and servers keep decoding each other's payloads; `None` means "unknown", and a client falls back to its positional test.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- **Positional continuity (today).** Right in the common case, wrong for equal-offset neighbours from different stored sequences.
- **Recompute every chunk's head.** With 128-token heads on 256-token chunks this recomputes half of every reused row, against ~8 % extra for context starts only.
- **Infer it on the client.** The client sees only match positions and hashes, not what was stored before each chunk, so it cannot recover the predecessor.
- **A stored-sequence id plus chunk index.** Equivalent for this test, but needs a new id space; the predecessor's token hash reuses the existing one.

**Additional context**

- Under `--enable-dedup-content` a match serves the first indexed entry for its text, so the reported predecessor must be that entry's, not the one of the store that was skipped.
- Fleet-coordinator matches (`BlendMatch`) would need the same field in the coordinator's index; reporting `None` for them first is enough for a client to fall back.

items.title: [Bug][MP] The coordinator keeps L1 placements for MP servers that are gone
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

The coordinator can keep L1 placements for an MP server that is gone, so `/directory/lookup` keeps pointing readers at it. I found two ways this happens.

1. Late events after deregistration. `drop_instance` fences the instance and forgets its cursor, so the next batch from it is taken as a fresh stream. The MP server deregisters before it stops its event bus (`http_server.py` shutdown), so its final flush lands after the fence, and with Kafka anything still in the topic does too. Those placements stay, because the instance is no longer in the registry and the health loop never looks at it again.
2. Restore from a checkpoint. Placements and cursors are restored, but the registry isn't checkpointed, and the health loop only evicts registered instances. If a server dies while the coordinator is down, its L1 placements never go away.

**To Reproduce**

Late events, through the HTTP API:

1. `POST /instances` for `mp1`, then `POST /events` with an L1 store at seq 1.
2. `DELETE /instances/mp1`. `/directory/keys` is empty.
3. `POST /events` with another L1 store from `mp1` at seq 2. It's applied, and `/directory/keys` lists the new key on `mp1` while `/instances` is empty.

Restore: start a coordinator with `--checkpoint-path`, register `mp1`, store an L1 key, stop it. Start it again and never register `mp1`. Long after `instance_timeout`, the placement and its bytes in `/instances/usage` are still there.

**Expected behavior**

L1 placements from an instance that left, or that never came back after a restore, are dropped.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at 1fde7bec.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

```shell

# case 1: crashes, no error message

# case 2: silently succeeds with a garbage size limit
llama-gguf-split.exe --split-max-size G test.gguf out2
# exit: 0x00000000
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce


**Description**
I was testing `llama-gguf-split` and noticed it doesn't validate the arguments for `--split-max-tensors` or `--split-max-size`, which causes a few different issues.

For `--split-max-tensors`, passing `0` causes an immediate integer divide-by-zero crash. Passing a negative number like `-5` is silently accepted and treated as 5. 

The bug for `--split-max-size` is worse. If you pass a garbage string like `G` or `xyzM`, the program silently accepts it. Looking at `gguf-split.cpp`, the return value of `sscanf` is dropped, meaning the size variable is left uninitialized. 

Commit: `df03399b8`
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200 

**Steps to reproduce**

<details>
<summary>1. Setup: Generate a dummy GGUF</summary>

You need a file with actual tensors to trigger this (vocab files in `models/` have 0 tensors, so they won't crash). 

```powershell
$S = "$env:TEMP\gguf-split-repro"
mkdir $S
.\build\bin\Release\llama-gguf.exe "$S\test.gguf" w
```
</details>

<details open>
<summary>2. Triggering the crashes and undefined behavior</summary>

**Divide by zero crash:**
```powershell
.\build\bin\Release\llama-gguf-split.exe --split-max-tensors 0 "$S\test.gguf" "$S\out"
"exit: 0x{0:X8}" -f $LASTEXITCODE
```
*Result:* Hard crashes with exit code `0xC0000094` (STATUS_INTEGER_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO) instead of printing a validation error.

**Invalid input accepted:**
```powershell
.\build\bin\Release\llama-gguf-split.exe --split-max-size G "$S\test.gguf" "$S\out2"
```
*Result:* Silently succeeds instead of erroring out on "G". Running this several times produces splits of varying random sizes it exits 0x00000000 and writes the split as if you'd passed a valid limit.
</details>

**Expected behavior**
Malformed inputs and `0` limits should be caught during arg parsing, print a clear error message, and cleanly exit.

items.title: SYCL on Arc B580: ternary weights and q4_0 KV attention on XMX (Bonsai 2 27B, 128K context in 12 GB)
items.author: Torchit1
items.body_excerpt:
I've been working on the SYCL backend for Intel Arc B580 (Xe2), mostly for PrismML's ternary Bonsai 2 27B, and wanted to share the results and a couple of findings in case they're useful to other SYCL work.

Branch: https://github.com/Torchit1/llama.cpp/tree/arc-b580 (guide: docs/bonsai-arc-b580.md)

What's in it:
- Ternary PTQ1_0 weights repacked to 2 bits at load and run on the int8 x int2 DPAS path (Intel's TernSYCL kernels), with round-to-nearest activation quantisation (KL divergence 0.00022 against reference logits).
- Decode and draft-verify attention (1-32 query tokens) straight from the q4_0 KV cache on XMX. Xe2's IGC provides `intel_sub_group_i8_i4_matrix_mad_k32`, which isn't in the public cl_intel_subgroup_matrix_multiply_accumulate list; the raw q4_0 bytes XOR 0x88888888 work as its B operand. It's exact on the B580.
- Full 1024-token prompt batches through oneDNN's int8 GEMM (about 10% faster long prompts).
- Memory changes so MTP drafting fits 128K context in 12 GB (q4_0 KV for the draft context, a smaller draft batch).
- The same attention kernel generalises to Gemma 4 12B (head 512, GQA 16), plus a q4_0 small-batch GEMM on XMX: Gemma 4 12B QAT with Google's assistant drafter goes from about 40 to 100 t/s on new code.

Results on a B580 at 128K context: about 90 t/s writing new code, 250-370 t/s on code edits, 42 t/s plain, 44 t/s with 115K tokens of history. Same card, model and flags against the SYCL support in PrismML's fork: prompt reading 207 vs 895 t/s, plain generation 21 vs 42, generation at 32K context 8 vs 36.

All the XMX paths are gated to Xe2 and fall back to the existing kernels elsewhere. One user report from an A770 (Alchemist): it runs on the fallback kernels but needed -b 256 -ub 256 to avoid a Level Zero ERROR_UNKNOWN, which may be worth a look on the mainline side too.

I'd be glad to help upstream any of the general pieces (the q4_0 KV attention in particular) if there's interest.

items.title: Feature Request: compute buffers are over-allocated ~N× under -sm tensor (N devices)
items.author: mamama1
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Under --split-mode tensor, ggml_backend_meta_buffer_type_get_alloc_size sizes every tensor at its full multi-device shape, so each device reserves the whole tensor rather than the slice it actually holds. Compute scratch is therefore over-allocated by roughly N× on N devices.

Deriving the per-device shape at reserve time and querying each sub-buffer type about that shape (including per-device sources, since backend scratch can depend on them) fixes it. On 4× RTX 5060 Ti running Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K at 262144 context, -ub 1024, with MTP speculative decoding, the main graph’s compute buffer drops from 1736.30 to 874.30 MiB per device and the draft graph’s from 648.03 to 592.03 MiB — 3.6 GiB reclaimed across the four cards. Model, KV and recurrent-state buffers are unchanged, greedy output is byte-identical, and throughput is slightly up (prefill 865 → 955 t/s, decode 51.4 → 55.9 t/s on a 29.5k-token prompt).

Verified with asserts enabled across 206k-token prefill, multimodal (host-view) inputs, and two concurrent 262144-token slots; no reserve-time/compute-time split-state mismatches. I have a working implementation with test coverage if it’s of interest.

Based off of TheBlueMatt’s 39ddae04c and 100% vibe coded by Opus 5.

### Motivation

I now managed to fit 512k context (parallel 2) without unified kv cache + the q6_k_xl unsloth quant of qwen 3.8 27B onto those 4 cards, incl. mmproj offload.

prefill and decode speed actually improved a bit too as a side effect of less data having to be moved around i assume.
nccl was enabled during the build (no p2p though, so shm needs to be 4gb).

I'll locally maintain this until people who know what they're doing do the real work but I'd be happy to share what Claude came up with, if there is interest from the maintainers. I don't know whether my change has impacts on other backends, all I know it works on CUDA (Blackwell).

should i share the code? I can publish it to my public git repo...

items.title: [RFC]: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference（CCF 赛题四）
items.author: Pinoeer-kingxi
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

<!-- GitHub-safe plain Markdown. Copy from the raw .md text, not from Word or a rich-text preview. -->

# RFC: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| RFC | RFC-EPD-Agent-Multimodal-2026 |
| Status | Draft |
| Date | 2026-07-05 |
| Target Project | Mooncake / Mooncake Transfer Engine / MooncakeStore |
| Target Integrations | vLLM, SGLang, Qwen-VL/Qwen3-VL-style multimodal models |
| Scope | Encoder-Prefill-Decode disaggregation, Agent state cloning, cross-step KV reuse, evaluation protocol |
| Primary Audience | Mooncake maintainers, serving-system contributors, vLLM/SGLang integration reviewers |
| Implementation Horizon | One-month prototype milestone, followed by staged hardening |
| Compatibility Target | Preserve existing PD and colocated serving paths; new features must be gated by configuration |

---

## Summary

This RFC proposes an extension to Mooncake for **agentic multimodal inference**. The core idea is to generalize Mooncake's KVCache-centric disaggregated serving capability from a two-stage Prefill-Decode model into a broader **Encoder-Prefill-Decode (EPD)** architecture, while also supporting:

- **Agent state cloning** for multi-branch reasoning;
- **visual feature caching** for repeated image/document contexts;
- **cross-step KV reuse** for repeated workflow prefixes;
- **tool-call offload/restore** to release GPU memory during blocking I/O;
- **A2A handoff** for state transfer among planner, executor, verifier, and domain agents;
- **coordinated scheduling** across Encoder, Prefill, Decode, and storage resources.

The proposal introduces a unified `MultimodalState` abstraction that represents visual feature bundles, textual/multimodal KV pages, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, TTL, and ownership.

The design intentionally avoids a single global strongly-consistent KV registry. Instead, it uses:

1. **KV Directory** for eventually consistent metadata lookup;
2. **Workflow Shards** for per-workflow strong consistency, refcount, CAS, fork, release, and CoW;
3. **Decentralized Scheduler** for admission control, priority scheduling, offload/restore, and A2A-aware routing.

For KV reuse correctness, the RFC uses a conservative default:

> **Exact Prefix Reuse by default; Approximate Reuse only behind validation gates and feature flags.**

Approximate reuse is never required for correctness. If any validation step fails, the system falls back to exact prefix reuse or full Prefill.

---

## Motivation

### Multimodal inference is naturally EPD-shaped

Multimodal inference contains three computationally different stages:

1. **Encoder**: image/video/audio features are produced by a modality encoder.
2. **Prefill**: the language model processes the full multimodal prompt and builds KV cache.
3. **Decode**: autoregressive generation produces output tokens.

Traditional PD disaggregation couples Encoder with Prefill. This becomes inefficient when the same multimodal context appears repeatedly across turns, agent steps, or branch candidates. Separating Encoder from Prefill enables:

- independent scaling of visual encoder workers;
- reuse of visual features across turns and workflows;
- lower repeated prefill cost for multimodal prompts;
- more flexible routing for prefill-heavy versus decode-heavy workloads.

### Agent workflows require persistent state

Agent workloads are not simple one-shot requests. They involve:

- multi-turn conversations;
- external tool calls and long I/O waits;
- multi-branch reasoning such as Tree-of-Thought, beam search, and verifier branches;
- A2A handoff between planner, executor, retriever, tool agent, and verifier;
- repeated prefixes across workflow steps.

These patterns make KV state a first-class runtime object rather than a temporary per-request artifact.

### Mooncake is well positioned for this extension

Mooncake already focuses on disaggregated KVCache management and high-performance transfer. Extending it to EPD and agentic workflows is a natural next step because the same core primitives are needed:

- cross-node tensor transfer;
- distributed KVCache pooling;
- offload and restore;
- memory ownership;
- scheduling across heterogeneous workers;
- efficient movement of large intermediate states.

This RFC defines a practical architecture that can be implemented incrementally and reviewed in stages.

---

## Goals

This RFC has the following goals.

### G1. Support EPD disaggregation

- Separate Vision Encoder, Prefill, and Decode into independently schedulable workers.
- Transfer Encoder outputs to Prefill and Prefill KV pages to Decode through Mooncake Transfer Engine.
- Preserve fallback paths to normal colocated or PD-only execution.

### G2. Introduce a unified multimodal state abstraction

- Represent FeatureBundle, KVPage, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, leases, and TTL.
- Support snapshot-based state reads, page-level refcount, and Copy-on-Write.
- Provide clear lifecycle transitions for active, shared, offloaded, restored, released, and aborted states.

### G3. Support Agent State Cloning

- Enable low-cost fork for multi-branch reasoning.
- Avoid deep-copying full KV state for each branch.
- Make branch writes safe through page-level CoW.
- Make refcount correctness testable and observable.

### G4. Support cross-step KV reuse

- Use exact prefix reuse as the safe default.
- Add approximate or non-contiguous reuse behind validation gates and feature flags.
- Always preserve fallback to full Prefill.

### G5. Reduce control-plane bottlenecks

- Avoid a globally locked GDKR-style metadata service.
- Move refcount and CAS to workflow-local shards.
- Keep cross-workflow metadata eventually consistent with bounded staleness.
- Prevent a single hot workflow or global registry from throttling unrelated workflows.

### G6. Provide a reproducible evaluation protocol

- Define datasets, workload construction, ba

Deterministic shadow-scheduler experiment (2026-07-13) to test the core enforcement hypothesis before touching Admission. This is simulation evidence only.

Environment: Lingjun H20 `lingjun-099`, Python 3.12.7 / NumPy, fixed seed 20260713. Model: 10,000 x 1 ms epochs, capacity 100 work units/epoch; foreground arrivals Poisson(40/epoch), background Poisson(90/epoch), foreground deadline 5 epochs. Compared a single unbiased FIFO against a work-conserving 60/40 class budget; unused foreground capacity was borrowed by background.

Results:

| mode | FG completed / arrived | FG miss | FG P99 wait | BG completed | utilization | final FG/BG backlog |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FIFO | 307,991 / 400,150 | 99.829% | 2,286 epochs | 692,009 | 100% | 92,159 / 207,355 |
| budget | 400,150 / 400,150 | 0.000% | 0 epochs | 599,850 | 100% | 0 / 299,514 |

Conclusion: under sustained aggregate overload, explicit class budgets can protect feasible foreground demand while remaining work-conserving; the benefit is not higher total throughput (both are 100% utilized), but controlled allocation. The cost is explicit: background service fell by 92,159 units and its backlog grew, so aging/reclaim and overload policy are mandatory. This does not validate real TENT timing, hierarchical identity, byte-vs-request accounting or distributed guarantees. A code PR should begin in shadow-accounting mode and reproduce this comparison with tebench and real RDMA before enforcement is enabled.

I am sharing an open research artifact that may be relevant to SGLang's structured-generation path.

GSP (Grammar-Conditioned Sparse Projection) consumes a packed grammar legality mask before/during the target-model LM-head projection instead of computing the full vocabulary projection and masking afterward.

The current artifact includes:
- packed-mask row-sparse Triton projection for latency-oriented decoding
- batched block-GEMM that skips grammar-inactive vocabulary tiles
- density-aware dense fallback for permissive/mixed states
- support/top-1 correctness checks
- raw paired end-to-end Qwen3.5-2B results

On the reference RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, 30 paired AB/BA trials gave median end-to-end ratios of 1.0756x (enum JSON), 1.0642x (tool-call JSON), and 1.0842x (nested-array JSON). The free-string control is not claimed as a reliable mean speedup.

This is not claiming first invention of batch-1 grammar-aware LM-head filtering; the contribution boundary is the packed-mask batched execution, heterogeneous routing, and controlled target-model evaluation.

I would especially value:
- SGLang integration feedback

- heterogeneous-batch measurements

items.author: yangxin-mx

# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python

    arch: str
    warp_size: int

### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`scripts/convert_otel_2_perfetto.py` rejects two supported trace inputs:

1. A JSON array with insignificant leading whitespace is detected as JSONL. A compact array then raises `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str`; a pretty-printed array raises `JSONDecodeError`.
2. A normal OTLP span from `service.name=smg` raises `KeyError: 'child'`. The converter initializes its internal `child` field for engine spans only, while the shared conversion function also expects it on SMG spans.

Both remain present in main commit `c55790d38ba0c41170cec8993e7a85d5c687149c`. JSON whitespace should not change format detection, and an OTLP exporter should not need to provide the converter's internal `child` field.

### Reproduction

Run from the repository root. The converter itself requires only Python's standard library; no model or accelerator is involved.

```python
import json
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

span = {
    "traceId": "00000000000000000000000000000001",
    "spanId": "0000000000000001",
    "name": "smg_request",
    "startTimeUnixNano": "10000000",
    "endTimeUnixNano": "13000000",
    "attributes": [],
}
data = [{"resourceSpans": [{
    "resource": {"attributes": [{
        "key": "service.name", "value": {"stringValue": "smg"}
    }]},
    "scopeSpans": [{"spans": [span]}],
}]}]
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    root = Path(directory)
    for name, text in (
        ("smg", json.dumps(data)),
        ("leading_space", " " + json.dumps(data)),
        ("leading_newline", "\n" + json.dumps(data, indent=2)),
    ):
        source = root / f"{name}.json"
        source.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
        result = subprocess.run([
            sys.executable, "scripts/convert_otel_2_perfetto.py",
            "-i", str(source), "-o", str(root / f"{name}_perfetto.json"),
        ], capture_output=True, text=True)
        print(name, result.returncode)
        print(result.stderr)
```

Actual results: all three cases exit 1, respectively with `KeyError: 'child'`, `TypeError`, and `JSONDecodeError`. Expected: each writes the same complete SMG span to a Perfetto trace.

### Environment

- Source: main `c55790d38ba0c41170cec8993e7a85d5c687149c`.
- Python: CPython 3.11.15.
- OS: macOS 26.6.2, arm64.
- Utility dependencies: standard library only.
- Reproduction uses synthetic OTLP-shaped trace data; no live SMG exporter, inference server, or device run is claimed.
- The requested `PYTHONPATH=python python -m sglang.check_env` cannot complete in this standalone utility environment because the SGLang package initialization imports the uninstalled `torch` package (`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'`). The converter CLI runs independently of that package.
