items.title: [Bug]  DSV4.1 Flash + DSPARK: CUDA caching allocator exhausts GPU memory under sustained max-batch decode (OOM crash every 15–25 min), KV pool only 29% used
items.author: elain
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [ ] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSPARK speculative decoding on a single 8×B200 node is **stable under short benchmark windows (< 6 min) but crashes on a fixed ~15–25 minute cadence under sustained max-batch decode load**. Every crash has the same signature: all 8 TP ranks fail a 20 MB `expandable_segments` mapping with only 4–19 MB free, then the engine kills its own process tree. Docker restarts it, and it crashes again ~15–25 min later. Over a 2-hour sustained soak: **6 crashes, identical signature**.

Crucially this is **not a KV-cache capacity problem** — at crash time `full token usage: 0.29, swa token usage: 0.16` (KV pool `max_total_num_tokens=25,826,048`, ~71% of KV headroom unused). The PyTorch caching allocator's non-KV memory grows unboundedly under sustained load.

**Allocator failure — all 8 ranks within the same second (two shown):**

[rank0]:[W1010 01:38:17.257967532 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:508] expandable_segments: memory mapping failed with OOM on device 0 while trying to map 20971520 bytes (free: 4718592, total: 191502876672).
[rank4]:[W1010 01:38:17.258494500 CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:508] expandable_segments: memory mapping failed with OOM on device 4 while trying to map 20971520 bytes (free: 19398656, total: 191502876672).

**Crash handler immediately after:**

[2026-10-10 01:38:23] kill_process_tree called: parent_pid=1, include_parent=True, pid=1
[2026-10-10 01:38:24] No live scheduler processes found; skipping py-spy and CUDA coredump.
[2026-10-10 01:38:24] SIGQUIT received. signum=None, frame=None. It usually means one child failed.

**KV pool NOT exhausted at crash time** (last scheduler lines before death):

Prefill batch, #new-seq: 1, #new-token: 512, #cached-token: 48896, full token usage: 0.29, swa token usage: 0.16, #running-req: 195, #queue-req: 0

**Mitigation experiments we already ran (both failed, so this looks like unbounded growth, not headroom sizing):**

1. Removing `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` → the server crashes even under trivial load (single-digit concurrent probes) right after startup; the fixed-segment allocator is strictly worse here.
2. Lowering `--mem-fraction-static` 0.75 → 0.73 (frees ~3.8 GB/GPU for the allocator) → **crash cadence unchanged** (4 crashes in 5 sustained windows), same signature.

**Related issues checked and ruled out:**
- #36333 (zombie requests after client disconnect): zero occurrences of `"state was deleted in TokenizerManager"` in our logs.
- #37553 (unbounded `custom_mask` via `torch.cat` in EAGLE/DFlash): DSPARK's verify path passes `custom_mask=None` throughout (`dspark_components/dspark_verify.py`), so it does not use that code path.

Secondary observation: before each crash, sustained throughput degrades ~15–20% vs short-window burst and TTFT/ITL p95 drift up, consistent with growing allocator pressure. This makes the current V4.1 preview unfit for sustained saturated serving on our node (`--restart unless-stopped` recovers in ~8 min per crash as a stopgap). Sustained-load stability may be worth adding to the V4.1 roadmap (#42170) — short-window benchmarks cannot catch this bug class. Happy to provide full container logs / dmesg / workload details on request.

### Reproduction

1. Start the server with the command below.
2. Drive **sustained** saturating decode load at high batch — we replay real SWE agent traces at ~192 concurrent sticky sessions with continuous streaming requests (each request carries its full session prefix, up to ~300K tokens). Any sustained max-batch decode workload with DSPARK on should work.
3. Within 15–25 minutes the process dies with the allocator signature above; docker restarts it; it dies again every 15–25 min.
4. Note: 6-minute benchmark windows never trigger it — the failure only appears under sustained load, so a quick `bench_serving` pass will look clean.

Launch command:

```bash
docker run -d --name sglang_standalone --network host --ipc host --gpus all \
  --shm-size 67108864 --restart unless-stopped \
  -v /data/models/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash:/models:ro \
  -e SGLANG_TIMEOUT_KEEP_ALIVE=60 -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41 python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models --served-model-name deepseek-v4.1-flash \
  --tp 8 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --trust-remote-code \
  --context-length 1048576 --page-size 64 --mem-fraction-static 0.75 \
  --chunked-prefill-size 32768 --max-prefill-tokens 32768 \
  --max-running-requests 256 --enable-cache-report --enable-metrics \
  --enable-decoder-swa-bounded-replay \
  --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --speculative-dspark-block-size 5 \
  --log-level info

Startup reference numbers: max_total_num_tokens=25826048, available_gpu_mem≈20.5 GB after init.

### Environment

```markdown
- Hardware: 8 × NVIDIA B200 (192 GB each, SM100), single node, NVLink, host network
- Driver / CUDA: 580.178.04 / CUDA 13.0.3 (in container); torch 2.13.0+cu130; NCCL 2.30.7
- SGLang: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41@sha256:4a5d132a06a7` (sglang 0.0.0.dev1+gda64c5cbb) — this is still the newest V4.1 preview digest as of 2026-10-10
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (476 GB, bundled 3-stage DSPARK draft, `num_nextn_predict_layers=3`)
- Workload: SWE agent-trace session replay — 400 sticky sessions replayed continuously, ~192 concurrent sessions, streaming (`stream=true`, `include_usage`), per-request prompts carry full session history (up to ~300K tokens)
- Quant/KV defaults: KV dtype fp8_e4m3, attention backend dsv

items.title: [Bug] DFlash + Qwen3.8-27B: speculative decoding accept rate drops to 0 during serving
items.author: enternal111
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

On a hybrid (GDN linear-attention + full-attention) model served with `--speculative-algorithm DFLASH` while grammar-constrained traffic (OpenAI `tools` + `tool_choice: "required"`) is present, an entire running batch can suddenly become "poisoned":

- **Every request in the batch — including plain-text requests with no grammar — starts emitting token id 0 (`"!"`) repeatedly** until `max_tokens` (the garbage never hits EOS/stop).
- Spec verify keeps executing (`spec_verify_calls_total` keeps increasing) but **accept rate drops to exactly 0.00 / accept length 1.00**.
- No error, no warning, no crash — **outputs are silently corrupted**.
- The state persists for each in-flight request's lifetime; newly admitted requests are healthy again once the triggering condition leaves the batch.
- The transition is a **one-step collapse** (production trace below: accept 0.48 -> 0.17 -> 0.06 -> 0.00 in three decode steps).

Two production incidents observed:
1. v0.5.20, one instance of three, poisoned for ~5 days until we rolled back (roughly 12% of traffic emitting garbage).
2. v0.5.19, one instance of four, poisoned for ~1.5 h and self-recovered when traffic mix changed. **So this is not a v0.5.20 regression — both tags are affected.**

### Reproduction

Semi-reliable (~30% per round on an instance that has recently served real mixed traffic; 0/10 on a freshly started instance). Model: a pre-release Qwen3.8-27B hybrid (GDN + full attention) with its DFlash2 draft model; launch flags:

```
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 --enable-mixed-chunk \
--enable-strict-thinking --enable-hierarchical-cache --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer \
--attention-backend flashinfer --tp 4
```

Per round (run 10 rounds, fresh content each round):

```bash
# 1) 10 grammar requests (tool_choice=required), max_tokens=600, temperature=1.0
for v in 0 1 2 3 4; do send g$v.json & send g$v.json & done   # g*.json: tool-call requests
sleep 1
# 2) 30 concurrent requests with FRESH ~50K-token prompts (multi-chunk prefills)
for i in $(seq 30); do send flood.json & done
sleep 3
# 3) plain probe (max_tokens=40), inspect output text
```

Observed (two consecutive runs on the same instance):

```
run 1: rounds 3/6/8 of 10 -> probe output '!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!'
run 2: rounds 3/5   of 10 -> probe output '!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!'
control on a freshly started instance: 0/10
```

Controls: grammar requests alone + probe (no flood) -> healthy; flood alone (no grammar) -> healthy. **Both ingredients are required**: grammar requests in the batch *and* multi-chunk admissions reshaping the batch.

Production trigger (log reconstruction of the Oct 10 incident, v0.5.19):

```
10:05:35  healthy decode: run=5, accept_len=3.38, accept_rate=0.48   (pools idle: token_usage=0.26, no retraction)
10:05:41  two admissions in the same second:
            newseq=1 new-token=8128 cached=155904   (long-prompt chunk tail)
            newseq=3 new-token=8128 cached=129792   (three requests join at once; run 5->8)
10:05:42  next decode: accept_len 3.38->1.87, accept_rate 0.48->0.17   (one-step collapse)
10:05:43  accept_rate 0.06; first victim finishes (prompt=78634, completion=62, accept_rate=0.0)
10:05:44  accept_len=1.00, accept_rate=0.00 -- stays there for ~1.5 h
```

Just before the trigger, several long-prompt / short-completion (~100-300 token output, tool-call-shaped) requests had finished — i.e. grammar-bearing requests left the batch seconds before the batch was reshaped.

Profiling captured live during a poisoned window:

- py-spy stack: `build_grammar_vocab_mask` -> `generate_token_bitmask` -> `traverse_tree`/`dfs` **inside** `forward_batch_generation` (the DFlash verify path).
- Flame graph (15 s of the poisoned verify loop): `spec_utils.dfs` = 57% of scheduler CPU, `build_grammar_vocab_mask` = 30%; the accept kernels (`accept_sampling` / `_accept_block`) < 1%.

### Environment

(Reconstructed from the incident deployment — direct `check_env` run is restricted on that host.)

```
- sglang: v0.5.19 and v0.5.20 (both affected)
- Python: 3.12.3
- GPU: 4x NVIDIA H20 96GB, driver 580.95.05, CUDA 13.0
- attention backend: flashinfer; TP=4
- model: hybrid GDN linear-attention + full-attention (~27B) + DFlash2 draft
- overlap scheduling enabled (default)
```

items.title: [Bug] PP>1 + DSA skip-topk stage boundary: 'OwedOutput' object has no attribute 'shape' during decode CUDA-graph capture
items.author: yy-fighting
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Serving a **GLM-5.3 / GlmMoeDsa** checkpoint with `--pp-size 2` crashes during **decode CUDA-graph capture at startup**:

```
AttributeError: 'OwedOutput' object has no attribute 'shape'
  File ".../sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v2.py", line 3143, in forward
    and hidden_states.shape[0] != 0
```

The fault is in the DSA skip-topk PP-boundary guard inside `DeepseekV2Model.forward`. It reads `hidden_states.shape[0]`, but the value can legitimately be an opaque `OwedOutput` handle.

This reproduces on **current `main`** (`de487f8039`, 2026-10-10), on the **2026-10-09 nightly** (`265efe5e`), and on **`v0.5.21`** — i.e. it is a regression introduced by the residual-stream refactor **#41549** ("Carry residual state across stage boundaries", merged 2026-09-29) that has not been fixed. There is no open issue for it (searching `OwedOutput` in issues returns 0 hits).

### Environment

- GPU: 8× RTX 6000D (sm_120), driver 580.159.04, docker
- Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:nightly-dev-cu13-20261009-265efe5e` (also `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21`)
- Model: GLM-5.3-NVFP4 (`architectures: ["GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM"]`, `num_hidden_layers: 78`, `index_topk_freq: 4`, `qk_rope_head_dim: 64`)
- Parallelism: `--tp-size 4 --pp-size 2`

### To reproduce

```bash
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/GLM-5.3-NVFP4 \
  --tp-size 4 --pp-size 2 \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.90 --max-running-requests 64 \
  --disable-shared-experts-fusion --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass \
  --chunked-prefill-size 8192 --context-length 270336 --max-prefill-tokens 16384 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 3 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 64 \
  --cuda-graph-bs-decode 1 2 3 4 6 8 12 16 24 32 40 48 56 64 \
  --cuda-graph-max-bs-prefill 8 \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 \
  --json-model-override-args "{\"index_topk_freq\": 4}"
```

The server dies ~4–5 min in, during `Capturing batches (bs=64 ...)`.

The essential conditions are: a GLM-5.3/DSA model with `index_topk_freq > 1`, `--pp-size 2`, and decode CUDA graph enabled. With `num_hidden_layers=78`, PP stage 0 ends at layer 38; `38 % 4 != 0` so `dsa_layer_skips_topk(config, 38)` is `True`, and the guard is entered.

### Full traceback

```
Capturing batches (bs=64 avail_mem=7.58 GB):   7%|▋ | 1/14 [01:10<15:18, 70.62s/it][PP0 TP1] Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 5950, in run_scheduler_process
    scheduler = Scheduler(server_args, port_args)
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 560, in __init__
    self.init_model_worker()
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 1099, in init_model_worker
    self.init_all_cuda_graphs()
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 1082, in init_all_cuda_graphs
    self.tp_worker.init_cuda_graphs()
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/tp_worker.py", line 425, in init_cuda_graphs
    self.model_runner.init_cuda_graphs(
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner.py", line 1131, in init_cuda_graphs
    capture = capture_cuda_graphs(
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/cuda_graph_setup.py", line 413, in capture_cuda_graphs
    decode = capture_decode_graph(model_runner=model_runner)
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/model_runner_components/cuda_graph_setup.py", line 738, in capture_decode_graph
    runner = GraphRunnerCls(model_runner)
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py", line 513, in __init__
    self.capture()
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py", line 1108, in capture
    self._capture_one_stream()
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py", line 1165, in _capture_one_stream
    self.capture_one_shape(
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py", line 1293, in capture_one_shape
    self.backend.capture_one(
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/runner_backend/full_cuda_graph_backend.py", line 145, in capture_one
    output = forward_fn()
  File ".../sglang/srt/model_executor/runner/decode_cuda_graph_runner.py", line 1257, in run_once
    out = forward(
  File ".../torch/utils/_contextlib.py", line 124, in decorate_context
    return func(*args, **kwargs)
  File ".../sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v2.py", line 3334, in forward
    hidden_states = self.model(
  File ".../sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v2.py", line 3143, in forward
    and hidden_states.shape[0] != 0
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'OwedOutput' object has no attribute 'shape'
```

### Root cause

`python/sglang/srt/models/deepseek_v2.py` (main, lines ~3135-3150):

```python
if not self.pp_group.is_last_rank:
    proxy_tensors = residual_batch.to_pp(hidden_states, forward_batch)
    if (
        self.use_dsa
        and dsa_forward_uses_topk
        and self.end_layer < self.config.num_hidden_layers

                "DSA topk_indices because the next stage starts on a "
                "skip-topk layer."
            )
```

items.title: [Bug]: Speculative decoding (mtp and dflash) silently disables prefix-cache hits for hybrid GDN models on nightly; worked on v0.24.0
items.author: cgoudie
items.body_excerpt:
(analysis by Fable 5)
### Your current environment

- DGX Spark (GB10, `sm_121`/`sm_121a`, aarch64, 128 GB unified memory), Docker `--network host --gpus all --ipc host`
- Image: `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` → reports `v0.28.1rc1.dev43+g6f7df92a8`
- Comparison baseline on the same host: `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.24.0`
- Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid GDN: 48 linear-attention + 16 full-attention layers, built-in MTP head). Also reproduced with `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` + `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (rev `dedf8df`).
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, `--max-model-len 65536`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.30`, env `CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_121a`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On the current nightly, enabling **any** speculative decoding method (built-in `mtp` or `dflash`) on a hybrid GDN model silently drops `vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total` to **0** — align-mode prefix caching engages at startup (log: `Mamba cache mode is set to 'align' for Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) but never hits, and repeated long prompts pay full re-prefill. The identical command minus `--speculative-config` hits normally. No crash, no warning — the caching is just inert, so this is easy to miss in production.

A/B on the same host, same model, same 18,219-token prompt sent twice (`max_tokens=10`):

| nightly config | TTFT req1 → req2 | `prefix_cache_hits_total` delta |
|---|---|---|
| APC only (no spec) | 9.46 s → **0.64 s** | **17,248** |
| APC + `{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` | 23.6 s → 13.9 s* | **0** |
| APC + `{"method":"dflash", ..., "num_speculative_tokens":7}` | 12.9 s → 12.5 s | **0** |

\* the MTP row also shows a large decode regression on this platform (10.5 tok/s vs 19.7 on v0.24.0 with the same flags — possibly a separate sm_121 issue; noting it for context, not the subject of this report).

**On `v0.24.0`, MTP + align-mode APC coexist correctly** on the same host/model: repeated 9,901-token prompt → 8,000 tokens hit, TTFT 7.27 s → 1.33 s, with `mtp` k=3 active. So spec+APC coexistence for hybrids existed and regressed somewhere between v0.24.0 and the current nightly.

Repro (nightly):

```bash
docker run --rm --init --network host --gpus all --ipc host \
  -v /opt/models:/models -e CUTE_DSL_ARCH=sm_121a \
  vllm/vllm-openai:nightly /models/qwen3.8-27b-nvfp4 \
  --served-model-name bench --port 10099 \
  --max-model-len 65536 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.30 \
  --max-num-seqs 1 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
# send any >3,300-token prompt twice; watch vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total stay 0
# drop --speculative-config and the second send hits ~all full blocks
```

Possibly related but distinct: #53670 (hits occur but recompute per hit), #41884 (DFlash+APC IndexError crash — we see silent zero-hit, not a crash), #26201 (tracking).

Is the suppression intentional (spec-decode + hybrid APC support not yet wired on the new path), or a regression? If intentional, a startup warning like the align-mode one would save users from silently losing their cache. Happy to run further diagnostics on this hardware.

### Instructions

Either run the commands below or download one of our [Vulkan releases](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases). If you have multiple GPUs please run the test on a single GPU using `-sm none -mg YOUR_GPU_NUMBER` unless the model is too big to fit in VRAM. If you use RADV please run with the environment variable `RADV_PERFTEST=nogttspill` as that can fix a bunch of performance issues.

items.title: Feature Request: Graceful reasoning budget termination. Avoid mid-sentence cutoff.
items.author: CleStil
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

PR #20297 (merged ~2025-03-11) added `--reasoning-budget-message`, which injects
a string at the hard token cutoff to signal the model to wrap up. The injection
still happens at exactly token N with zero warning. The model gets no time to
finish its current thought before the `</think>` boundary.

Graceful termination before the cutoff is expected to improve reasoning
performance. See Motivation and Possible Implementation for details.


### Motivation

Raw truncation of the thinking trace measurably reduces answer quality compared
to graceful termination. Muennighoff et al. (s1: Simple test-time scaling,
arXiv:2501.19393) showed that appending an end-of-thinking delimiter with
"Final Answer:" before the hard cut outperforms naïve truncation. This was
confirmed by follow-up work (arXiv:2505.05315), which states directly that
"the S1 approach performs better than directly truncating the full reasoning
trajectory, underscoring the importance of preserving the solution segment."

The current --reasoning-budget-message implementation injects a wrap-up message
at exactly token N, leaving the model zero tokens to actually act on it. This is
functionally equivalent to truncation with a cosmetic suffix — the model cannot
produce a meaningful conclusion within 0 remaining tokens.

### Possible Implementation

Three approaches in increasing complexity:

Option A — message offset
Inject the budget message at `budget - offset` instead of `budget`, giving the
model `offset` tokens to act on the wrap-up signal. The s1 paper
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393) shows this outperforms raw truncation.
Change in the COUNTING state of reasoning-budget.cpp:

    if (ctx->remaining <= ctx->warn_offset)  // was: <= 0

Files: reasoning-budget.cpp, reasoning-budget.h, common.h, arg.cpp,
sampling.cpp. Default 0 preserves current behavior.

Option B — separate budgeting
Split total budget into thinking (t) and conclusion (s) phases, t + s = budget.
Force `</think>` at token t, leave s tokens for a conclusion before the answer.
Follow-up work on s1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05315) shows this outperforms
the basic offset approach. Would add a second parameter, e.g.
--reasoning-budget-conclusion M.

Option C — logit biasing toward `</think>`
Ramp up the logit weight of `</think>` as the budget runs low, then force it at
the hard limit. No dependency on an injected phrase, model-agnostic. NVIDIA NIM
uses this approach with a 10% extension window for sentence completion. More
invasive (sampler changes) but cleanest long-term.

Options A and B build on the existing message injection architecture. Option C
is a parallel approach that could coexist with either.

Happy to test on ROCm/gfx1100 (Qwen3.5-27B) and contribute a draft of Option A
or B if there is interest.

items.title: [Bug]: Timed-out put is revoked while its queued slices are still pending; they later overwrite the next object at that address
items.author: yubofredwang
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

#### Summary

When a Store put times out (60 s, hardcoded), the client returns `TRANSFER_FAIL (-800)` and revokes the object. The master frees the replica immediately, and the next put can get the same address. The timed-out transfer is not cancelled: slices still in the transfer engine queue are posted later and overwrite the new object. Nothing reports an error.

#975 / #993 added `discarded_replicas_` for this hazard ("the faulted client ... is still writing data to discarded replicas"). `PutRevoke` doesn't use it.

#### Environment

- `mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13==0.3.13.post1`; source checked at `e5598b0` (`v0.3.13-rc1`). Same code on current `main`.
- Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel `6.8.0-1047-nvidia`, `OFED-internal-25.10-1.2.8`, rdma-core `2510.0.10-1`.
- `mlx5_4` (InfiniBand), firmware `28.47.2526`.

#### Reproduce

Single host, RDMA (`MC_STORE_MEMCPY=0`), standalone master with defaults, one 16 MiB segment.

1. Client A: stop its two `transferWorker` threads with ptrace (RPC and heartbeat threads keep running), then put 12 MiB of `0x5C`.
2. After 60 s, A's put returns -800 and the object is revoked.
3. Client B (a separate process): put 12 MiB of `0x33` to a new key, then read it back. It lands at the same address and reads back `0x33`.
4. Resume A's workers. B's key now reads back all `0x5C`, and so does the segment memory.

Result: 8 out of 8 trials, same address every time, no crash. An earlier TCP run with a blackholed port, with no threads stopped, showed the same overwrite once the port came back.

Stopping the workers is artificial. It only stands in for anything that keeps slices queued past the timeout (e.g. a paused rail, `rdma_rail_pause_seconds` = 30, or a blocked worker). We have not reproduced it with a real link failure across two nodes.

#### Expected

A write from a revoked put should never land in memory that has been handed to another object.

#### Why

Links are pinned to `e5598b0`.

1. The timeout only stops waiting ([`transfer_task.cpp#L889-L895`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp#L889-L895)). Queued slices aren't removed or marked cancelled.
2. The destructor calls `freeBatchID` ([`transfer_task.h#L226`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/include/transfer_task.h#L226)), which returns `BatchBusy` for unfinished tasks ([`transport.cpp#L42-L50`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transport/transport.cpp#L42-L50)). The result is ignored, so the batch is leaked, and the slices stay valid to post later.
3. `PutRevoke` erases the replica right away ([`master_service.cpp#L4869`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4869)). Stale put-start cleanup ([`#L4440-L4450`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4440-L4450)) and upsert preemption ([`#L4944`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/e5598b0992cc258b06d22f24d875480e8931a28e/mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp#L4944)) move replicas to `discarded_replicas_` instead.

#### Impact

- The overwritten object belongs to another key whose put succeeded. Reads succeed and return wrong data.
- For a KV cache, every later prefix hit on that key gets the wrong KV until it is evicted.
- Slices read their source at post time. If the caller has reused its source buffer after the -800, the bytes that land aren't even the failed key's data.

#### Questions for maintainers

Before proposing a code change, we'd like your view on:

1. Have we seen other reports related to this issue in production?
2. Can it be prevented without code changes? For example, settings that keep the time a slice can spend queued well under 60 s (rail pause, retry count), or object checksum validation to catch the overwrite on read.

#### Possible fix

If you agree this is a real problem and not just a theoretical one, we'd propose a quarantine: `PutRevoke` moves the replicas to `discarded_replicas_` instead of erasing them, the same way stale put-start cleanup does. Dropping a timed-out batch's unposted slices would make that quarantine time a real upper bound. We can send a PR.

#### Related

#975 / #993 (`discarded_replicas_`), #4247 (same problem in the sync transfer API on Ascend), #3030.

### Before submitting...

- [x] Ensure you searched for relevant issues and read the documentation

items.title: [Bug]: Local hot-cache invalidation retains unbounded per-key generation metadata
items.author: jacklin78911-collab
items.body_excerpt:
### Problem

With the local hot cache enabled, invalidating a key that was never cached retains an entry in `LocalHotCache::key_generation_`. There is no per-key reclamation on the steady-state write/remove paths, so this metadata grows with all historical distinct keys rather than the configured cache capacity.

Audited main: `dcddb56c0cddc96f41eeb8dd82e5bd9f497183a2`.

### Source and affected workload

`RemoveHotKey` increments `key_generation_[key]` before checking whether the key exists. `RemoveHotKeys`, `BumpKeyGeneration`, and `BumpKeyGenerations` also create entries. Only whole-cache `Clear`/`RemoveAllHotKeys` clears the map.

- [Cache invalidation and generation tokens](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/dcddb56c0cddc96f41eeb8dd82e5bd9f497183a2/mooncake-store/src/local_hot_cache.cpp#L213-L358)
- [Client::Put invalidates before PutStart](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/dcddb56c0cddc96f41eeb8dd82e5bd9f497183a2/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L1981-L1992)
- [Client::Remove increments before the master operation](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/dcddb56c0cddc96f41eeb8dd82e5bd9f497183a2/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L3699-L3715)

A long-lived client writing many distinct object keys retains version metadata even if none of those objects is admitted to its hot cache. Failed removes also retain entries. This is separate from the bounded payload blocks and admission sketch.

### Component reproduction

I compiled the unmodified main `local_hot_cache.cpp` with its CMake flags and exercised a heap-backed cache. The unused SHM boundary was replaced with aborting link stubs; no cache logic was mocked. This is a cache-component reproduction, not a full Store memory benchmark.

```cpp
LocalHotCache cache(8192, 4096, false);  // 2 payload blocks
for (size_t i = 0; i < 200000; ++i) {
    std::string key = std::string(56, 'x') + std::to_string(i);
    if (cache.RemoveHotKey(key)) std::abort();  // no payload was ever inserted
}
if (cache.GetCacheSize() != 2) std::abort();
if (cache.AcquirePutToken(std::string(56, 'x') + "0").key_generation != 1) std::abort();
```

Linux/glibc measurements, calling `malloc_trim(0)` before each RSS sample:

| Distinct invalidated keys | Configured payload capacity | Live heap (`mallinfo2().uordblks`) | RSS |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 8,192 B | 99,184 B | 3,932,160 B |
| 100,000 | 8,192 B | 14,500,896 B | 19,677,184 B |
| 200,000 | 8,192 B | 28,900,896 B | 35,500,032 B |
| after `Clear()` | 8,192 B | 101,888 B | 6,881,280 B |

Thus only 8 KiB of payload capacity retains about 27.5 MiB of additional live heap after 200,000 distinct invalidations. The source establishes that the steady-state map has no bound; this test does not claim an observed production OOM.

### Fix constraint

Generation tracking is needed to reject detached fills after invalidation (the correctness goal of #2471). Simply erasing entries on removal would make an old generation-zero token valid again. Reclamation must preserve outstanding-fill invalidation, rather than removing the check or periodically flushing the whole cache.

Related #4334 addresses block-key access races; it does not bound this map. I found no open issue/PR covering this retention after checking the related cache-invalidation work.

items.title: [CI] Multi-rank PG CPU tests flake with ECONNRESET on the WRITE ack read
items.author: he-yufeng
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The multi-rank CPU transfer tests in `test_pg_p2p` flake on CI with TCP sessions being reset while a WRITE ack is still in flight. Two occurrences within two hours on 2026-10-09:

- main branch run: https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/37930984424
- PR run (unrelated diff): https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/actions/runs/37925444040

Both fail `test-wheel-ubuntu (ubuntu-22.04, 3.12, mooncake-wheel-ci-py312)`, which then fails CI Gate and blocks unrelated PRs.

## Failure signature

```
tcp_transport_session_impl.h:704] ClientSession: failed to read WRITE ack frame. Error: Connection reset by peer (value: 104)
mooncake_worker_thread.cpp:271] Rank N [DATA] transfer to peer 3 (global=3) failed for op 2 status=6 diff_us=23401..41808
```

The reset always arrives at the sender while it is blocked reading the WRITE ack, 20 to 40 ms after the transfer started, and always on a session toward the last global rank. That timing says the receiver side closed or tore down its end of the session mid-transfer rather than the wire dropping.

## Hypothesis

In the split-ranks / multiple-senders patterns the receiver knows how many bytes it expects per peer. If the receiver side of a session is destroyed as soon as its expected receive count is satisfied while the sender still has the final ack outstanding, the socket close lands as ECONNRESET on the sender's ack read. That would make this an ordering bug in session teardown, not test-environment noise, and would also explain why it only flakes under CI host scheduling jitter.

## Impact

Every red occurrence fails CI Gate for the whole matrix, so all open PRs pay the retry cost.

## Next step

I intend to reproduce this locally with the CPU multi-rank tests under `taskset`-style scheduling pressure and pin down the teardown ordering. Filing this so the failure has a tracking home in the meantime; if someone else is already looking at the worker-thread suite, happy to leave it to them.

AI assistance disclosure: this analysis was prepared with AI assistance; the log evidence and the reproduction plan were verified by the human submitter against the linked CI runs.

items.title: [RFC]: [Store] Cold-Tier Storage Device Control Plane, Phase 2: Fault Isolation and Device-Level Graceful Drain
items.author: zxpdemonio
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

RFC #4561 proposed a cold-tier storage device control plane for Mooncake Store, and Phase 1 landed in PR #4560: device metadata, a derived health state machine (UNKNOWN / HEALTHY / DEGRADED / FAILED / UNMOUNTING), a maintenance planner, and read-only admin observability.

Phase 1 made cold-tier device health **visible**. It deliberately left the reaction of the master unchanged: after `nof_heartbeat_failures_threshold` consecutive probe failures the heartbeat thread unmounts the segment, and nothing happens in between. There is also no operator-facing way to stop writing to a device, or to migrate its contents off it.

This RFC covers **Phase 2**, which turns that health signal into action:

1. **Fault isolation (cordon / uncordon)** - fence a device against new allocations without unmounting it, and return it to service automatically once probes recover.
2. **Device-level graceful drain** - bind the existing segment `DrainJob` machinery to a device identity so that `maintenance_plan` output can actually drive evacuation.
3. **Admin write endpoints** - `isolate`, `unisolate`, `drain`, `drain_status`.

Reference implementation: #4566 (stacked on #4560). Related: #4431 (cross-client move/migration control plane), which owns the `DrainJob` lifecycle this phase builds on.

---

## Motivation

### The window between DEGRADED and unmount is unused

With threshold `N` and probe interval `I`, Phase 1 reports DEGRADED after `N/2` failures, while the alive timeout unmounts at roughly `N * I`. That window currently exists only in the reported health - the master takes no action inside it. For a cold tier this is the worst of both outcomes:

- New evictions keep landing on a device that is already failing probes, so the objects written during the window are precisely the ones most likely to be lost when the segment is finally unmounted.
- The unmount itself is a cliff. The segment disappears, its allocator is torn down, and objects whose only remaining replica was cold become unrecoverable until they are re-fetched or re-evicted.

### No operator action short of unmount

Today there is no way to express "stop writing to this target, keep its data readable, and let me migrate it". Node maintenance, NVMe target firmware upgrades, and predicted disk failures all need exactly that, and all of them currently have to be done by pulling the client out from under the master.

---

## Proposed design

### 1. Fence state machine

Phase 2 adds one reversible action between HEALTHY and the terminal unmount:

```text
   HEALTHY
      |  consecutive probe failures >= N/2
      v
   DEGRADED ---- auto-isolate (fence) ----+
      |                                   |
      |  probe succeeds                   |  probes keep failing
      v                                   v
   HEALTHY  <---- auto-unisolate       FAILED
                                          |  alive timeout (N * I)
                                          v
                                       UNMOUNT   (unchanged terminal rule)
```

Two properties matter:

- **Fencing is not terminal.** `IsolateSegment()` detaches the allocator registration of the segment and moves it to `DRAINING`. The segment stays mounted, its `buf_allocator` is untouched, and no read path in the master gates on `SegmentStatus::OK`, so cold replicas already on the device remain readable and migratable.
- **The alive-timeout unmount rule is unchanged.** Fencing never weakens or delays it. A device that never recovers is still unmounted at exactly the same point as before this change.

Note that fencing at DEGRADED rather than at FAILED is what gives the mechanism a window to act: FAILED is derived from the same threshold as the alive timeout, so a device that is only fenced at FAILED is unmounted in the same heartbeat iteration.

### 2. Fenced devices keep being probed

The heartbeat probe set is defined by one predicate, shared with on-demand probing:

```cpp
// OK: serving allocations. DRAINING + isolated: fenced for maintenance.
// UNMOUNTING / GRACEFULLY_UNMOUNTING / DRAINED: leaving the cluster.
static bool IsNoFSegmentProbeCandidate(SegmentStatus status, bool isolated);
```

This is load-bearing for two reasons:

- Auto-recovery is only possible if a fenced device is still probed. On the first successful probe the heartbeat thread clears the fence and re-registers the allocator, unless the cordon is manual or a drain job is still active.
- Without it, a cordoned device would drop out of the probe set, its heartbeat accounting would be discarded, and its reported health would silently collapse back to UNKNOWN - exactly when an operator is watching it.

Manual cordons are never lifted automatically; only entries in `auto_isolated_devices_` are.

### 3. Device-level drain

`DrainStorageDevice(device_id, target_segments, max_concurrency)`:

1. Resolves the device to its mounted NoF segment and rejects devices that are already unmounting or already draining.
2. Cordons the device (manual isolation) so that no new allocation lands mid-migration.
3. Delegates to the existing `CreateDrainJob()` over that segment. No second migration lifecycle is introduced.
4. Records `device_id -> job_id` so device listings and `maintenance_plan` can report drain progress.

The whole operation is serialised by a dedicated mutex, so two concurrent admin requests cannot both pass the "already draining" check and orphan a job.

`maintenance_plan` integration:

| Condition | Plan bucket | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| health DEGRADED / FAILED | recovery_candidates | `probe_degraded` / `probe_failed` |
| isolated, no active drain | recovery_candidates | `device_isolated` |
| active drain job | gc_candidates | `draining` |
| drain finished, segment DRAINED | gc_candidates | `unmounting` |

### 4. Isolation and drain must not fight over segment status

Both fencing and draining are expressed as `SegmentStatus::DRAINING`, and the existing drain cancel and drain fa

items.title: torch.autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16) runs cuDNN LSTM/GRU in float16
items.author: KeithG33
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

As title says, using autocast with bf16 runs LSTM/GRU layers in fp16. There's a forum post and tiny repro script  [here](https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/why-nn-lstm-still-use-float16-in-hidden-state-even-if-set-to-bfloat16-or-float32-already/207172). Did a search and couldn't find this reported, apologies if I missed something. 

This bug is specifically for the autocast cuDNN path as shown by code, comments, and output below (generated by Claude):

```python

import torch

lstm = torch.nn.LSTM(64, 64, batch_first=True).cuda()
x = torch.randn(4, 20, 64, device="cuda")

# 1. bf16 autocast: cuDNN path returns fp16; non-cuDNN path returns bf16
for cudnn in (True, False):
    torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = cudnn
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        out, (h, c) = lstm(x)
    print(f"autocast(bf16), cudnn={cudnn}: output {out.dtype}, h {h.dtype}, c {c.dtype}")
torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = True

# 2. cuDNN itself runs bf16 RNNs when called with bf16 directly
m = torch.nn.LSTM(64, 64, batch_first=True).cuda().to(torch.bfloat16)
out, (h, c) = m(x.to(torch.bfloat16))
print(f"direct bf16 (no autocast), cudnn=True: output {out.dtype}, h {h.dtype}, c {c.dtype}")

# 3. the cell APIs follow the autocast dtype
for cls in (torch.nn.LSTMCell, torch.nn.GRUCell):
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        out = cls(64, 64).cuda()(x[:, 0])
    print(f"{cls.__name__} under autocast(bf16): {(out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out).dtype}")
```

Output (nightly 2.16.0.dev20261010+cu130, cuDNN 9.26, RTX 3090; same on 2.11.0+cu128 and 2.13.0+cu130):
```
autocast(bf16), cudnn=True: output torch.float16, h torch.float16, c torch.float16
autocast(bf16), cudnn=False: output torch.bfloat16, h torch.bfloat16, c torch.bfloat16
direct bf16 (no autocast), cudnn=True: output torch.bfloat16, h torch.bfloat16, c torch.bfloat16
LSTMCell under autocast(bf16): torch.bfloat16
GRUCell under autocast(bf16): torch.bfloat16
```

Asked Claude to do mini investigation when I found this problem, so here's the specific code/cause:

**Cause:** the autocast kernel for _cudnn_rnn, at::autocast::_cudnn_rnn_cast_reflatten (aten/src/ATen/cudnn/AutocastRNN.cpp), casts input, hx, cx and the weights to at::kHalf regardless of the autocast dtype. It dates from #42385, when autocast was fp16-only. Since #164411, cuDNN >= 9.13 supports bf16 RNNs, but this wrapper was not updated. The ROCm wrapper added in #121539 (miopen_rnn) copies the same hard-coded at::kHalf.

items.title: Use atomic_cas inside a loop
items.author: giorgio-arena
items.body_excerpt:
Hi, I'm experimenting with a simple kernel that reduces a rank-3 tensor on its last dimension. The kernel uses atomics to sum across one tensor row (I know it's not efficient, this is just a simple reproducer). I'm using two versions of the atomics, the first using atomic_add, and the second using the lock-like mechanism with atomic_cas and atomic_xchg.

```
@triton.jit
def _sum_kernel(X, Locks, O, width: tl.constexpr, use_atomic_add: tl.constexpr):
  in_off = tl.program_id(0) * width
  out_off = tl.program_id(0)

  for w in range(0, width):
    x = tl.load(X + in_off + w)
    if use_atomic_add:
      tl.atomic_add(O + out_off, x)
    else:
      while tl.atomic_cas(Locks + out_off, 0, 1) == 1:
        pass
      tl.store(O + out_off, tl.load(O + out_off) + x)
      tl.atomic_xchg(Locks + out_off, 0)


def _sum_fn(a, use_atomic_add):
  b, h, w = a.shape
  locks = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=torch.int32, device='cuda')
  out = torch.zeros([b, h], dtype=a.dtype, device='cuda')
  _sum_kernel[(b * h,)](a, locks, out, width=w, use_atomic_add=use_atomic_add)
  return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
  x = torch.empty((8, 64, 128), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda").normal_()
  ref = torch.sum(x, axis=-1)
  rtol = 1e-03

  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, True), rtol=rtol))
  print(torch.allclose(ref, _sum_fn(x, False), rtol=rtol))
```

Unfortunately for the second version I get
```

  File "/usr/local/home/giorgio/triton/python/triton/compiler.py", line 741, in visit_For
    assert for_op_region.size() == 1, "We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block"
AssertionError: We use SCF, so the loop body should only have one block
```

Any help would be appreciated, thanks.

Hi, I doubt this is a duplicate of https://github.com/openai/triton/issues/1058 because I am not overflowing on the program ids (largest PID should be `cdiv(8192, 16) * cdiv(8192, 32) = 131072` in my case).

I extended https://github.com/openai/triton/blob/main/python/triton/ops/matmul.py to support 4D tensors, e.g. of shapes (2, 8, 1024, 1024) and (2, 8, 1024, 512).

items.title: Calculate tl.dot, the output is the matrix of col major, but the result is wrong
items.author: yushinliu
items.body_excerpt: My test code is following: ``` def test_dot(M_, N_, K_, num_warps_): @triton.autotune( configs=[triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': M_, 'BLOCK_N': N_, 'BLOCK_K': K_}, num_stages=1, num_warps=num_warps_)], key=[] ) @triton.jit def matmul_kernel( a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M, N, K, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr ): offs_am = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M) offs_bn = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N) offs_k = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K) a_ptrs = a_ptr + (offs_am[:, None] * K + offs_k[None, :]) b_ptrs = b_ptr + (offs_k[:, None] * N + offs_bn[None, :]) a = tl.load(a_ptrs) b = tl.load(b_ptrs) c = tl.dot(a, b, allow_tf32 = False) c_ptrs = c_ptr + 1 * offs_am[:, None] + M * offs_bn[None, :] tl.store(c_ptrs, c) def matmul(a, b): c = torch.empty((M_, N_), device = a.device, dtype = a.dtype) c = torch.as_strided(c, (M_, N_), c.stride()[::-1]) grid = lambda META: ( triton.cdiv(M_, M_) * triton.cdiv(N_, N_), ) matmul_kernel[grid]( a, b, c, M_, N_, K_, ) return c torch.manual_seed(0) a = torch.randn(M_, K_, dtype = torch.float).cuda() b = torch.randn(K_, N_, dtype = torch.float).cuda() triton_output = matmul(a, b).cpu() torch_output = torch.matmul(a, b).cpu() assert triton.testing.allclose(triton_output, torch_output), (triton_output, torch_output) ``` But when M!=N, the triton output will be different with torch_output. If `c_ptrs = c_ptr + N * offs_am[:, None] + 1 * offs_bn[None, :]`, which means the output of tl.dot is row major, the results are equal. I checked the generated ttgir, to confirm that the output of tl.dot is col major or the order is {0 ,1}:

items.title: [Discussion] Use Isolated MLIR Symbol Namespace and TypeIDs for Out-of-Tree Backends
items.author: hongziqi
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

An out-of-tree plugin that shares the host `MLIRContext` hits one of two link failures. Both come from one MLIR rule: **within a single process, each MLIR C++ type may have only one `TypeIDResolver<T>::id`**.

- **Undefined symbol.** The plugin references a TypeID that `libtriton.so` never defined. `dlopen` fails.
- **Conflicting definition.** The plugin defines a TypeID the host already defined, or a second LLVM/MLIR is loaded beside `libtriton.so`. MLIR then treats one class as two identities.

`PluginInfo` / `TRITON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION` fixes neither case. That version only describes the callback table (`AddPassCallback`, `RegisterDialectCallback`, `AddOpCallback`). It cannot create a TypeID, and it cannot merge two of them.

What `TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1` does today is re-export the MLIR symbols already linked into `libtriton.so`. On nightly `3.8.0+gitf893845b` that set includes Builtin, Func, Arith, SCF, MemRef, Affine, and LLVM. It does not include `linalg::LinalgDialect` or `tensor::TensorDialect`. A plugin that references those two TypeIDs fails `dlopen` with `undefined symbol`.

This proposal: **an out-of-tree backend compiles its own MLIR in a separate symbol namespace, fully isolated from the host TypeIDs. Dialects the host does not provide are defined by the backend. The host and the backend pass modules as MLIR text and do not share an `MLIRContext`.**

## Problem

`TRITON_EXT_ENABLED=1` only controls symbol visibility. **It does not change the libraries linked into `libtriton.so`.** Visibility and the link line are separate:

- Off: `-fvisibility=hidden` plus a version script. The only exported symbol is `PyInit_libtriton`.
- On: the visibility hide and the version script are removed, so every symbol already linked into `libtriton.so` is exported.
- `TRITON_LIBRARIES` in `CMakeLists.txt` does not change with the option. It contains NVVM, LLVM, GPU, SCF, Math-to-LLVM, and Triton's own libraries. It does not contain `MLIRLinalgDialect` or `MLIRTensorDialect`.

An MLIR TypeID must be unique in the process. A plugin that shares the host `MLIRContext` has only two layouts, and each one fails:

| Layout | What the plugin binary does | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| The host owns TypeID `T` | The symbol is undefined (`U`) in the plugin. `dlopen` binds it to the single global instance in `libtriton.so` | The host binary never linked a definition of `T`. Loading the plugin reports `undefined symbol` (for example the LinalgDialect TypeID) |
| The plugin owns TypeID `T` | The plugin uses `MLIR_DEFINE_EXPLICIT_TYPE_ID`, defines the dialect itself, and registers it | Two TypeIDs exist for one type. MLIR asserts at runtime |

The first failure cannot be fixed inside the plugin alone. If the plugin statically links the missing MLIR dialect archives to fill in the IR dependency, it falls into the second failure.

## Proposal

An out-of-tree backend needs Linalg, Tensor, and whatever dialects come after them. Those dialects are not linked into `libtriton.so` today. The 2026-07-08 meetup listed the following responses to the symbol problem:

| Approach | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| Split LLVM/MLIR into its own library (not recommended) | This only moves symbols. `TRITON_LIBRARIES` does not contain Linalg, so after the split the host still has no TypeID for it. |
| Symbol namespace isolation (recommended) | The backend compiles a private MLIR in its own namespace. Same-named symbols no longer bind to `libtriton.so`, which removes conflicts. Dialects the host lacks are provided by the backend library, which removes undefined symbols. A type in that namespace cannot be inserted into the host `MLIRContext`, so the module crosses the boundary as textual IR. |

The backend defines `TypeIDResolver<T>::id` inside its own namespace. At backend link time those symbols belong to the backend's static libraries. MemRef, Arith, and the other host types stay the host's symbols. The two names stay distinct, so loading both into one process does not merge them. **An op defined in the backend namespace cannot be registered into the host `PassManager`.**

### Recommended boundary

The host serializes the MLIR module to textual IR before handing it to the backend. The backend shared library follows three rules:

- Do not link `libtriton.so`. There is no `DT_NEEDED` on MLIR symbols.
- Compile the private MLIR in its own namespace, so `mlir::detail::TypeIDResolver<...>::id` is a different symbol from the host's.
- Accept and return only textual IR. Do not pass C++ objects such as `mlir::Value` or `PassManager*` across the boundary.

The backend statically links the smallest MLIR subset its lowering needs (Linalg, Tensor, and the transitive dependencies it actually references) and ships that subset in its own wheel. Adding a dialect later means updating the backend's link line, not shipping a new Triton.

```text
# Host: only dialects Triton already has, then serialize.
ttir_text = str(host_module)
# Backend: private MLIRContext, parse the text, lower, return text.
out_text = backend.compile_text(ttir_text)
```

## Questions

1. When an out-of-tree backend needs a dialect the host does not include, is **a separate MLIR symbol namespace, with those dialects defined by the backend, and modules passed as textual IR** the approach upstream recommends?
2. This path does not use `passes.plugin.extend_with` to inject a Linalg pass into the host `PassManager`. Does upstream accept this backend shape, or must every backend share one `MLIRContext`? Is there a better alternative?

items.title: Loop-carry detection skips `prev = cur` when both start as the same value, silently keeping the pre-loop value instead of carrying it
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** `CodeGenerator._find_carries` decides which variables of a `for` or `while` loop become `iter_args` by comparing IR values after one dry run of the body, instead of asking whether a value can differ between iterations. If `prev` and `cur` are the same IR value before the loop and the loop runs `prev = cur`, `prev` looks unchanged and is not carried, so it keeps its pre-loop value in every iteration and after the loop. Regression from #7200, first in 3.5.0 (3.4.0 is right). Possible fix: also carry every name that is assigned in the loop (as 3.4.0 did), or only those that share their initial IR value with another name.

**Why one dry run misses it.** `_find_carries` ([L485-L524](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L485-L524), the comparison is [L513](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L513)) runs the body once with every name bound to its pre-loop value. When `prev = cur` runs there, `cur` is still at its pre-loop value, so `prev` is bound to the value it already had. In the real body `cur` is a block argument, so `prev = cur` is a different value in every iteration. Seeing that takes a second pass that already knows `cur` is carried.

The smallest example. `prev` is `cur`'s value at the start of each iteration; `SAME=False` is the control, where `prev` is equal to `cur` but a different IR value:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(out_ptr, n, SAME: tl.constexpr):
    cur = 0
    if SAME:
        prev = cur          # prev and cur are the same IR value
    else:
        prev = cur + 0      # control: equal to cur, but a different IR value
    for i in range(n):
        prev = cur          # prev is cur's value at the start of the iteration
        cur = cur + 1
    tl.store(out_ptr, prev)      # expected n - 1
    tl.store(out_ptr + 1, cur)   # expected n


n = 5
for same in (True, False):
    out = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    k = kernel[(1, )](out, n, same)
    print(f"SAME={same!s:5} prev, cur = {out.tolist()}, expected {[n - 1, n]}")
    print("   ", [l.strip() for l in k.asm["ttir"].splitlines() if "scf.for" in l][0].split(" : ")[0])
```
```
SAME=True  prev, cur = [0, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %cur = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32)
SAME=False prev, cur = [4, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %prev:2 = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur = %c0_i32, %prev_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32, i32)
```
With `SAME=True` only `cur` is an `iter_arg`. 3.4.0 has two `iter_args` in both cases and returns `[4, 5]`. Without an `iter_arg`, `prev` is still bound to its pre-loop value when the body starts, and `enter_sub_region` restores that binding when the loop ends ([L146](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L146)).

**Why since 3.5.0.** Up to 3.4.0 every name that is assigned in the loop and live before it was carried ([visit_For](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1114-L1115), [visit_While](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1153-L1154)). #7200 (2025-06-23, "Improve detection of loop carries", for builtins that modify their arguments) replaced that with the comparison of IR values; v3.5.0 is the first tag that contains it. The existing tests for shared initial values (`test_loop_carry_shared_initial_value` and its while and tuple variants in test_frontend.py, #11369) update the aliased variables independently (`a = a + 1`, `b = b + 2`), so none has a copy between them.

**Possible fix.** Two variants, both tested as source patches on main @6fe3348e6.

Carry every name that is assigned in the loop, as 3.4.0 did, and keep the comparison:
```diff
--- a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
+++ b/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py
@@ -493,6 +493,9 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
         self.scf_stack.pop()
         block.erase()
 
+        # A name that is assigned in the loop may have copied another one, which an unchanged handle doesn't show.
+        assigned = {n.id for n in ast.walk(node) if isinstance(n, ast.Name) and isinstance(n.ctx, ast.Store)}
+
         # If a variable (name) has changed value within the loop, then it's
         # a loop-carried variable. (The new and old value must be of the
         # same type)
@@ -510,7 +513,7 @@ class CodeGenerator(ast.NodeVisitor):
 
                 live_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([live_val])
                 loop_handles = flatten_values_to_ir([loop_val])
-                if live_handles != loop_handles:
+                if name in assigned or live_handles != loop_handles:
                     names.append(name)
                     init_tys.append(live_val.type)
                     init_handles.extend(live_handles)
```
The comparison was added by #7200 for builtins that modify their arguments in place. #8832 (2025-11-25) removed that case ("now that we ban mutations") together with its tests, attribute and item assignment raise, and aggregates cannot be assigned to after construction, so a name whose IR value changes is a name that is assigned. In test_frontend.py and the Gluon frontend tests, 57 of the 181 (name, loop) pairs that `_find_carries` looked at had a changed IR value, and all 57 are assigned in the loop. The set of assigned names comes from the AST, so it does not depend on what the dry run did; that also covers a branch that only the lowering takes (see below). It over-carries assigned names whose value does not change (`x = x`); they become `iter_args` and the canonicalizer in `make_ttir` removes them (the TTIR of t

items.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

items.title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

comments.author: yyihuang
comments.body:
Root cause: the test's last check relied on the torch profiler reporting CUDA kernel names for the graph replay (`assert names and not any("FillFunctor" in n for n in names)`). In the GB300 `cu129` job (`flashinfer-ci-cu129:20260930-b1420f1`, torch 2.13.0+cu129, `nvidia-cuda-cupti-cu12` 12.9.79) CUPTI reports **no CUDA events at all**, so `names == []` and the assertion fails on the empty list; every behavioural assertion before it passed (the capture never touched the generator, the offsets advanced, the replay was bitwise reproducible). The same stack reports CUDA events on B200, and the cu130 / cu134 GB300 jobs report them too, which is why only `unit_test_gb300: [*, cu129]` failed. The sampling kernels and the host route are not involved.

Fix: the test now takes its witnesses from CPU-side evidence (dispatcher-level `aten::fill*` events, the generator's host state across replays, an `aten::clone` sentinel proving the profiler recorded the window) and keeps the kernel-name check only as additional evidence where CUPTI reports the replay.

- `main`: fixed by #6143 (merged 2026-10-08, commit `3121b2831` of that PR), so the next `main` pipeline should be green on GB300 / cu129.
- `release-v0.7.2`: cherry-pick in #6247.

Verification so far, in the CI image (`flashinfer-ci-cu129:20260930-b1420f1`, torch 2.13.0+cu129, `nvidia-cuda-cupti-cu12` 12.9.79, driver 580.159.03) on a GB300 node: a fresh-process profiler probe prints `function cbapi.getCuptiStatus() failed with error CUPTI_ERROR_INVALID_DEVICE (2)` / `CUPTI initialization failed - CUDA profiler activities will be missing`, records 0 CUDA events with `activities=[CUDA]`, and records the CPU ops (including `aten::clone`) with `activities=[CPU, CUDA]`; the fixed test passes there (`1 passed`, 246 s including the first-use JIT build) with the same warning in its stderr. The other tests of the file were not affected in the failing job (53 passed, 1 failed in its `test_cake_sampling.py` batch).

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [TransferEngine] TcpTransport benchmark note: VRAM-backed transfers pay per-chunk staging; original "2x host-path loss on USE_CUDA" was a benchmark-config artifact
items.author: n-WN
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report / Performance

**TcpTransport throughput drops ~2x when the build enables USE_CUDA, even for pure host-memory transfers** — measured on loopback with `transfer_engine_bench` (write, 4 threads × batch 32, duration 3–4 s, same box, same commit `f1f5e40`, only the build flag differs):

| block size | build without CUDA | build with `-DUSE_CUDA=ON` |
|---|---|---|
| 64 KB | 0.99 GB/s | 0.84–0.88 GB/s |
| 256 KB | 2.10 GB/s | 1.09–1.28 GB/s |
| 1 MB | **3.41 GB/s** | **1.53–1.64 GB/s** |

All buffers are plain DRAM (`numa_alloc`/`malloc`); no GPU memory is involved in the transfer.

### Root cause (from reading `tcp_transport.cpp`)

Under `USE_CUDA` (and the other accelerator macros), both `ClientSession::writeBody`/`readBody` and `ServerSession::writeBody`/`readBody` call `getCudaDeviceId(addr)` → `cudaPointerGetAttributes()` **once per 64 KB chunk** (not once per request), on both ends of the connection. For a 1 MB transfer that is 16 chunks × 2 sides = 32 CUDA runtime calls per request; `cudaPointerGetAttributes` costs on the order of a microsecond and serializes on CUDA runtime internals, which is enough to halve throughput at these block sizes. The result of the lookup cannot change between chunks of one request — the address range is fixed at submit time.

### Suggested fix

Resolve the memory type **once per request** (at header processing / `initiate`) and carry `cuda_device` through the chunk loop, instead of re-querying per chunk. That is a small, behavior-preserving change; a further step could consult the registered-buffer metadata (the engine already knows the location string of registered memory) and skip the CUDA query entirely for buffers registered as `cpu:*`.

Happy to pick this up as a follow-up to my in-flight TCP work if nobody else wants it — the benchmark setup above reproduces it in a couple of minutes on any CUDA-build machine.

### Environment
- main @ `f1f5e40`; x86_64 Linux with a recent GCC/CUDA toolchain; loopback P2PHANDSHAKE metadata.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Confirmed the root cause from a read of `tcp_transport.cpp`. In the server read path, `getCudaDeviceId(addr)` is called inside the per-chunk block (around line 261) — and `addr` is the constant buffer base, only `total_transferred_bytes_` advances between chunks. So every 64 KB chunk re-runs `cudaPointerGetAttributes` on the same pointer, which is exactly the overhead you measured; a CUDA build pays it once per chunk instead of once per transfer.

The fix is to resolve the device id once when the transfer starts and reuse it for every chunk. The same per-chunk `getCudaDeviceId(addr)` pattern appears at the other transfer sites (~192, ~399, ~503), so they'd want the same treatment.

I verified this by reading, not benchmarking (no GPU on hand), so the throughput numbers are yours — but the redundant call is clearly on the hot path. Happy to review a PR that hoists it.

comments.author: n-WN
comments.body:
**Correction: I re-ran the attribution today and the original report does not hold up. The ~2x delta was a benchmark-configuration artifact, not a host-path regression.** @he-yufeng — the code fact you confirmed (the query really is per-chunk and redundant) is true, but measurements show it cannot be the cause; details below.

**1. The per-chunk call is ~0.3%, not ~50%.** Microbenchmark on the same H100 box (context initialized, 200k iters):

| pointer class | `cudaPointerGetAttributes` per call |
|---|---|
| plain `malloc` (unregistered host — the class the TCP path queries) | 0.125 µs |
| `cudaMallocHost` / `cudaHostRegister` / `cudaMalloc` | 0.07–0.10 µs |
| unregistered host, different page every call (defeats driver caching) | 0.126 µs |

At 64 KB per chunk that is ~0.3% of chunk wire time even counting both ends — two orders of magnitude short of explaining 2x.

**2. The original A/B compared VRAM buffers against host buffers without knowing it.** `transfer_engine_bench` defines `use_vram` **only under the accelerator macros, with default `true`** — the flag does not even exist in a non-CUDA build (passing it errors out). So with the flag omitted from both command lines, the CUDA build silently benchmarked **`cudaMalloc` VRAM buffers** (per-chunk staging: `new` + synchronous `cudaMemcpy` + `delete` on every 64 KB), while the non-CUDA build used `numa_alloc` host memory. My "all buffers are plain DRAM" claim in the report was wrong for the CUDA column. Same binary, same box today: VRAM 1.32–1.66 GB/s vs `--use_vram=false` 1.73–2.13 GB/s @ 1 MB.

**3. With the configuration fixed, there is no USE_CUDA host-path regression.** Equal-flags rebuild (only `-DUSE_CUDA` flipped, same commit), host memory both sides, interleaved runs on the same box:

| block | non-CUDA build | CUDA build, `--use_vram=false` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 MB | 2.44–2.83 GB/s | 1.95–2.32 GB/s |
| 256 KB | 1.92–2.09 GB/s | 1.77–2.16 GB/s |

Overlapping ranges, within run-to-run variance (absolute numbers differ from the original report — different day/load on a shared box — but the interleaved comparison is internally controlled).

**Consequence:** given these numbers, the hoist I offered in the description would be measurable-benefit-free churn, so I won't send one. The honest disposition is to close this as not-a-bug (mislabeled benchmark configuration), or retitle it as a note that VRAM-backed TCP transfers pay a per-chunk staging cost — which is the real (and expected) difference the numbers were showing. Maintainers' call; apologies for the noise, and thanks @he-yufeng for engaging — the reading was right, the magnitude was not.
