items.title: [Bug]: `/metrics` (iteration-stats) route blocks the serve event loop — a 2 s Prometheus scrape inflates request latency 5–60× and cuts prefill throughput ~5× (4× RTX 5060 Ti TP4, Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN NVFP4 27B, 1.3.0rc29)
items.author: sean640112
items.body_excerpt:
> **Update (2026-10-09): the root cause is not sm120.** The "fixed" per-request cost comes from the `/metrics` iteration-stats route blocking the serve event loop: a 2 s Prometheus scrape inflates request latency 5–60× and cuts prefill throughput ~5×. Controlled A/B, py-spy stacks and the Prometheus-side numbers are in the [follow-up comment](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/issues/19623#issuecomment-6076428189) below.

# ~6 s fixed per-request latency floor on sm120 (4× RTX 5060 Ti, TP4) with a Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN 27B NVFP4 checkpoint

## Summary

On a 4× RTX 5060 Ti (sm120) box serving a **dense hybrid GDN + full-attention 27B** NVFP4 checkpoint with `trtllm-serve` (PyTorch backend, TP4), we measure a **~6 s per-request floor on time-to-first-token that is independent of prompt length**. A 212-token request takes **6.06 s** to first token (8.0 s total), and the floor persists at every length we tested (212 → 59,571 tokens). Requests are reproducible to ±5 ms across 12 measurements in 3 separate server starts.

The same hardware, same checkpoint, same prompt, same client, served by SGLang gives **0.26–0.30 s** for the identical request. `trtllm-serve` therefore looks ~20× slower on short requests, while its *marginal* prefill throughput is only ~2.6× lower (~2,143 tok/s vs ~5,600 tok/s).

We have ruled out MTP/spec-decode, scheduler policy, `max_seq_len`, chunked prefill, the CUDA caching allocator, and thinking-mode as causes (details below). We would like to know whether this per-request floor is **expected on sm120 for hybrid GDN models**, or a bug — and which knob/diagnostic we should look at next. We are happy to run any instrumentation you suggest.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | 4× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, compute capability **12.0 (sm120)**, TP=4 |
| Driver | 610.57.04 |
| CUDA toolkit | 13.3 (`nvcc` 13.3, `CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3`) |
| OS / Python | Linux, Python 3.12.11 (venv) |
| TensorRT-LLM | **1.3.0rc29.dev202609240000** (nightly from 2026-09-24; PyPI 1.2.1 does not contain `modeling_qwen3_5.py`, hence nightly) |
| torch | 2.14.0+cu132 |
| flashinfer-python | 0.6.18 |
| triton | 3.8.0 |
| nvidia-cutlass-dsl | 4.8.0.dev0 |
| tensorrt / tensorrt_cu13 | 10.14.1.48.post1 |
| MPI | OpenMPI 5.0.10 (`mpi4py` bootstrap path) |
| Model | `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` — `architectures: ["Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration"]`, `model_type: qwen3_5`; 64 layers, hidden 5120, 24 Q heads, 4 KV heads |
| Quantization | ModelOpt `MIXED_PRECISION`: **FP8 per-tensor on 208 layers** (`block_size` absent) + **NVFP4 `group_size: 16` on 193 layers**, `kv_cache_quant_algo: null` |

Note on the attention backend: your hardware support matrix lists sm120 as supporting NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 (per-tensor) / FP8 KV cache, which covers this checkpoint's formats — so the quantization scheme itself should be fully supported on sm120.

## How to reproduce

Server (the `mpirun -n 1` wrapper and `OMPI_MCA_*` are needed on this host because `import tensorrt_llm` otherwise blocks in the mpi4py `MPI.COMM_WORLD` initialization, and this host's own hostname resolves to loopback only):

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3
export OMPI_MCA_btl_tcp_if_include=lo OMPI_MCA_oob_tcp_if_include=lo
mpirun -n 1 --oversubscribe trtllm-serve serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1234 --tp_size 4 \
  --max_seq_len 140000 --max_batch_size 8 \
  --served_model_name qwen3.8-27b \
  --free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.80 \
  --extra_llm_api_options opts.yaml
```

`opts.yaml`:
```yaml
enable_chunked_prefill: true
max_num_tokens: 8192
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: MTP
  max_draft_len: 3
  speculative_model: /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
```

Client — a minimal stdlib-only streaming client (this is the "probe" used for every number below; it measures the first chunk that carries `choices[0].text`/`delta.content`):

```python
import json, time, urllib.request
prompt = open("/path/to/corpus.txt").read()[:600]          # → 212 tokens
body = {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, "stream": True}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/completions",
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
t0 = time.time(); ttft = None
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
    for raw in r:
        s = raw.decode().strip()
        if not s.startswith("data: "): continue
        if s[6:] == "[DONE]": break
        d = json.loads(s[6:])
        ch = d.get("choices") or []
        if ch and ch[0].get("text"):
            ttft = time.time() - t0; break
print("TTFT", ttft)
```

## Measured results (same probe, same prompts, same box)

| prompt tokens | path | TRT-LLM stream TTFT | TRT-LLM non-stream total | SGLang stream TTFT | SGLang non-stream total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **212** | completions | **6.053–6.062 s** (n=5) | 7.995–8.035 s | **0.262 s** | 0.304 s |
| 222 | chat (medium template) | 12.11 – **22.21 s** (unstable across restarts) | 14.06 – 26.19 s | 0.268 s | — |
| 7,172 | completions | 10.10 s | 12.02 s | 0.243 s *cached* | 1.84 s *cached* |
| 12,131 | completions | 12.12 s | 14.06 s | — | — |
| 28,008 | completions | — | 20.13 s | — | 6.15 s *cached* |
| 59,571 | completions | — | 36.26 s | — | — |
| 65,032 | chat | 56.52 s | 56.45 s | — | — |

*("cached" = the SGLang side hit its radix prefix cache on the shared corpus prefix, so those cells are not a like-for-like prefill comparison.)*

Least-squares fit of the completions path (`total = C + N/R`, 5 points spanning 212 → 59,571 tokens):
**C = 8.10 s, R = 2,143 tok/s, R² = 0.9966** — i.e. a very large constant plus a modest rate term. (The streaming TTFT is ≈ 1.9 s lower at every point, i.e. TTFT ≈ 6.1 s + N/2143.)

For reference, an independent client (vLLM's `bench serve` against the same server) measured prefill throughput of **453 / 1,014 / 1,302 tok/s** at 8K / 32K / 64K with meanTTFT 16.15 / 29.28 / 46.44 s, i.e. the same

comments.author: LaelaZorana
comments.body:
Probe done, single GPU numbers below. This isolates the GDN prefill cost independent of the TP4, mpirun and NVFP4 27B variables.

Env is TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, torch 2.14.0, single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell sm120. Model is Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B, qwen3_5, same hybrid GDN family, served via trtllm-serve at TP1.

Results, TTFT over 5 runs

With FlashInfer prefill on, the default, the 212 tok prompt with max_tokens 1 took 16.1 to 17.5 ms and the 4096 tok prompt took 49.6 to 53.9 ms. With FlashInfer prefill off, TLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_GDN_PREFILL=0, they took 17.8 to 19.1 ms and 49.9 to 52.5 ms.

Stream closes within 0.1 ms of TTFT, single token responses. FlashInfer is the default, see the server log.

Takeaways

On one card, GDN prefill is measured in milliseconds, nowhere near the 6.1 s floor. That floor comes from the TP4 path, the mpirun loopback setup, or something about the NVFP4 27B ckpt.

FlashInfer toggle moves latency only about 2 ms either way here.

Server log also flags an Autotuner cache miss, falling back, for nvfp4_gemm on shape 4 by 2560, which fits a small M shape, just FYI.

Next steps to nail down the 6.1 s

Serve the same 2B at TP4 on the same box, which shows if it is the TP4 path.

Short nsys capture around a single 212 tok request, where GPU busy vs. wall clock shows GDN kernels vs. gaps.

If the GPUs are idle for about 6 s, py-spy dump on rank 0 should show exactly where the wall clock goes.

comments.author: sean640112
comments.body:
**Follow-up: the per-request latency floor and the prefill throughput cap are both caused by scraping the `/metrics` route, not by sm120**

Thanks for the earlier guidance. Following it, we ran controlled A/Bs on the same binary and found that the "fixed per-request cost" comes from the **Prometheus scrape of `/metrics`**, and that it degrades more than first-token latency.

Setup: TRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29, sm120, 4× RTX 5060 Ti 16G, TP4, `Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid GDN), `mpirun -n 1 trtllm-serve ... --tp_size 4`.

**A. Short requests** (212-token prompt, reproducible ±5 ms)

| | engine on `127.0.0.1:1234` (Prometheus scrapes every 2 s) | same engine on `127.0.0.1:1235` (nothing scrapes it) |
|---|---|---|
| 212-token, non-stream | **7.74 / 8.07 / 8.07 s** | **0.137 / 0.137 / 0.178 s** |
| stream TTFT | **6.060 / 6.060 / 6.060 s** | **0.139 / 0.138 / 0.140 s** |

**B. Prefill throughput** (canonical `vllm bench serve`, `--dataset-name random`, 2 prompts, concurrency 1, output len 1)

| input len | scrape active | not scraped |
|---|---|---|
| 8,192 | 488 tok/s (Mean TTFT 14,996 ms) | **2,514 tok/s (2,911 ms)** |
| 32,768 | 1,081 tok/s (27,476 ms) | **2,386 tok/s (12,449 ms)** |
| 65,536 | 1,452 tok/s | **2,177 tok/s** |

So a 2-second monitoring scrape costs anywhere from ~5× to ~60× depending on the request shape.

Prometheus side (`job_name: llm`, `scrape_interval: 2s`, `scrape_timeout: 1500ms`, `metrics_path: /metrics`), its own `scrape_duration_seconds{job="llm"}`:

* with our TRT-LLM server up: every scrape **times out at 1.5003–1.5012 s** (`up=0`)
* with our SGLang server on the same port: 0.060–0.063 s (`up=1`)

Mechanism: the single serve event loop is blocked inside the `/metrics` handler, which awaits engine stats through a blocking RPC. py-spy from the frontend process shows the same stack at 0.6 s / 3 s / 6 s into a request:

```
get_iteration_stats (serve/openai_server.py) -> get_stats_async (llmapi/llm.py)
  -> aget_stats (executor/proxy.py) -> _call_sync (executor/rpc/rpc_client.py) -> Future.result()
```

TTFT ≈ 3 × 2.02 s and non-stream total ≈ 4 × 2.02 s — the scrape interval *is* the quantum. It also explains why the engine looked idle while requests were slow: GPUs at ~0% util, rank 0's executor parked in `queue.get()`, and the other ranks spinning in the per-iteration request-count broadcast — the request had not reached the engine yet.

Mitigations we tested:

1. **Not scraping the port** → full recovery (tables above).
2. `enable_iter_perf_stats: true` in the extra LLM API options → **short requests recovered** (0.184 s / TTFT 0.140 s) while Prometheus kept scraping every 2 s, **but prefill did not** (8K stayed at 488 tok/s vs 2,514 clean). So that flag is not a substitute for fixing the route.

The underlying hazard looks like the stats route awaiting a blocking RPC on the serve event loop (the source comment in that path mentions nvbug 6102381). Making `/metrics` non-blocking by default — or documenting that Prometheus should scrape `/prometheus/metrics` rather than the JSON stats route — would prevent a monitoring scrape from inflating latency and prefill cost by 5–60×.

Happy to share py-spy dumps, full server args, or run a patched build on this exact setup (4× sm120 consumer cards, TP4) if that helps.

Thanks again, @LaelaZorana — this was filed half expecting it to go unanswered, so your reply was a pleasant surprise, and it is what led us to run the A/B that found the real cause.

### CuTe DSL
* New features
  - Initial Rubin support to accelerate dense GEMMs. The following features are available:  
    - CuTe DSL and CuTe extensions
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions
      - B collector reuse 
      - Extended TMEM size from 512 COL to 576 COL
      - Larger shared memory allocations (328KB)
      - Enhanced mixed precision throughput (FP8/FP4)
      - Softmax acceleration related features
    - Primitives
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions
      - B collector reuse
      - Extended TMEM size from 512 COL to 576 COL
      - Larger shared memory allocations (328KB)
      - Enhanced mixed precision throughput (FP8/FP4)
      - Softmax acceleration related feature
      - 2:4 sparsity support for FP4

  - CuTe DSL extensions has several new features:
    - CTA-V maps are now inferred automatically for `cute_ext` TMA load, store, multicast, and reduce-store operations. Explicit CTA-V maps remain supported as overrides.
    - Added asynchronous atomic TMA reduce-store and sparse MMA operations.
    - Added reusable `cute_ext` GEMM mainloop and TMA epilogue helpers.
    - Added opt-in TMEM accumulator-buffer planning, including overlapping ping-pong storage for capacity-constrained kernels.
    - Improved device-side TMA descriptor updates and grouped GEMM performance through SMEM-staged updates, workspace reuse, and reduced prologue and synchronization overhead.
  - This release includes an opt-in preview of the CuTe DSL extensions (`cute_ext`) compiler pipeline for ordinary Cute DSL kernels. This pipeline lets user mix `cute_ext` APIs directly into `@cute.jit` and `@cute.kernel` code and is required for kernels that mix the two API surfaces. You may test this feature with the following:
  `CUTE_DSL_USE_EXTENSION_COMPILER=1 python your_program.py`
The pipeline is expected to preserve program behavior and performance, but generated PTX/SASS may differ.  Note that this pipeline will become the default in the future, no earlier than 4.10.
  - Added examples for better control over Primitives' compiler warnings/errors introduced in 4.7.0.  See the `CuTeDSL/experimental/compiler_diagnostic/` directory.
  - IKET Profiler Tool
    - Rubin kernels (sm107) can now be profiled.
    - It is now possible to only dump timing data for a specific cluster to reduce profiling overhead.  Previously all clusters were profiled.
    - Task Scheduling can instrument the schedule with IKET ranges when constructing TaskManager objects (`iket_enable_profiling=True`).  Task execution will generate an IKET range and individual pipeline stages in a schedule may generate separate ranges (`iket_profiling_stages`).
  - A number of new examples were added in this release:
    - Rubin (CuTe):
      - Dense GEMM for legacy data type with B collector reuse as applicable
      - Grouped GEMM with B collector reuse
      - Dense blockscaled GEMM with FP4/FP6/FP8 mixed precision and UE5M3 / block-32 scale-factor support
      - Grouped blockscaled GEMM with B collector reuse as applicable
      - Blockwise GEMM
    - Rubin (CuTe extension):
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) blockscaled GEMM with UE5M3 scale-factor
      - Grouped GEMM with B collector reuse
    - Blackwell (CuTe extension):
      - Dense GEMMs
        - Back-to-back GEMM
        - Blockscaled GEMM
        - Persistent GEMM with alpha/beta scaling
        - CLC scheduler/dynamic persistent GEMM
        - GLU GEMM
        - Mixed input GEMM
        - Planar complex GEMM
        - Input transform GEMM
        - GeForce pingpong dense GEMM
        - Blackwell Ultra blockscaled GEMM
      - Dense Convolutions
        - Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - Blocksclaed Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - GeForce Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - GeForce Blockscaled Implicit-Gemm Fporp Conv 
      - Attention
        - GQA Decode
      - Grouped GEMM
        - Unscaled and blockscaled grouped GEMM
      - Top-K
    - Ampere (CuTe extension):
      - SIMT GEMM
  - CuTe DSL now supports x86_64 Windows
  - CuTe DSL AoT now supports new host target: QNX8.0 
  - Notebooks are restructured under examples/python/CuTeDSL/cute/notebooks and new notebooks for primitives will be added under examples/python/CuTeDSL/notebooks 
  - Numpy is now not a default dependency

* Bug fixes and improvements:
  - `nvidia-cuda-nvdisasm` is now an optional dependency of `nvidia-cutlass-dsl` via the optional `[sass]` extra. SASS dumping (`CUTE_DSL_KEEP=sass` / KeepSASS) now resolves `nvdisasm` from the bundled wheel (recommended since its version matches the DSL toolchain) or from a local CUDA Toolkit (`CUDA_HOME`/`CUDA_PATH`). A locally-provided `nvdisasm` must come from a CUDA Toolkit at least as new as the toolchain that produced the CUBIN. Installations that never dump SASS are unaffected.
  - Reduced the protobuf version requirement of IKET profiler from 6.30 to 4.21.  This should make protobuf an easier requirement to satisfy in preparation for transioning IKET to an optional extra.

## Bug: qwen4exp graph builder aborts (ggml_abort) on DGX Spark (SM121) under sustained load

**Model:** Qwen3.8-Flash-Next UD-IQ4_XS (unsloth GGUF, 93.7G)
**Hardware:** DGX Spark (GB10, SM121, 128GB unified)
**Build:** PR #27742 branch, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121 -DGGML_CUDA_FA=ON`
**Serve:** `llama-server -m <gguf> -ngl 99 --flash-attn on --ctx-size 32768`

## Symptom

The server **aborts (SIGABRT) during sustained multi-request load** — specifically during a tool-calling benchmark battery. It handles single/short requests fine (coherent output, tool calls, structured output, long prompts all work), but **aborts deterministically at a specific scenario** (~scenario 20 of the battery, reproduced 3×).

## Backtrace (from the abort)

```
#0  __GI___wait4
#1  ggml_print_backtrace ()
#2  ggml_abort ()
#3  llama_model_qwen4exp::graph::graph(llama_model const&, llm_graph_params const&)
#4  llama_model_qwen4exp::build_arch_graph(llm_graph_params const&) const
#5  llama_model::build_graph(llm_graph_params const&) const
#6  llama_context::process_ubatch(...)
#7  llama_context::decode(llama_batch const&)
#8  llama_decode ()
#9  server_context_impl::decode(...)
```

## Analysis

`ggml_abort()` is called from inside the **qwen4exp graph constructor** (`llama_model_qwen4exp::graph::graph`). This is a **deterministic abort on a specific batch shape** (a token count / batch size the benchmark sends), not a memory-pressure or OOM issue. The graph builder hits an unsupported path and hard-aborts.

## Repro

Run a sustained multi-turn tool-calling benchmark against the server (e.g. tool-eval-bench). It aborts at a specific scenario, reproducibly. I could not isolate the exact shape with targeted single requests (tool calls, structured output, long prompts, multi-turn all work individually) — it only triggers under the benchmark's specific batch pattern.

## Environment

- DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), 128GB unified
- llama.cpp PR #27742 branch, build 10656, commit 035e22731
- `-ngl 99 --flash-attn on --ctx-size 32768`

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

@juney-nvidia

Load Kimi Linear or Kimi K3 in the release container (or a fresh environment with only the wheel's runtime requirements):

`tensorrt_llm/_torch/modules/kimi_kda/kimi_kda_mixer.py` imports `fla.modules.ShortConvolution` at load time (line 26 in 1.3.0rc28). Short prefill and the decode / verify fallbacks also call `fla.ops.kda.chunk_kda` and `fla.ops.kda.fused_recurrent_kda`.

Fix proposed in #19837: add `fla-core==0.5.2` to `requirements.txt`. It is the same version `requirements-dev.txt` already installs (via `flash-linear-attention==0.5.2`) and is MIT-licensed. The new-dependency license/vulnerability scan still needs the maintainers' tooling.

items.title: moe_cute_util.cuh: util_convert_type returns a tensor that points at a local array
items.author: BwL1289
items.body_excerpt:
In `cpp/tensorrt_llm/cutlass_extensions/include/cutlass_extensions/gemm/kernel/moe_cute_util.cuh`:

```cpp
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
return cute::make_tensor(cute::make_rmem_ptr<To_type>(&frag), tensor.layout());
```

The returned tensor is a view of `frag`, a local of `util_convert_type`. `frag` is gone once the function returns, so
reading the result is undefined behaviour. Both routines in `fused_moe_kernel_routine.cuh` read it
(`util_convert_type<...>(accum)`, then the copy to shared memory).

With nvcc this happens to work. With clang (device code at -O3, sm_121a) the conversion and the SwiGLU that feed it are
removed, ptxas then removes the MMAs whose results are no longer used, and the kernel stores registers nothing wrote.
SASS counts (HMMA / LDSM / F2FP / FMUL) for the bf16 32x128x64 SwiGLU instantiation of
`fused_moe::run_global<Fused_Moe_Kernel_sm80<...>>`:

- nvcc (NVIDIA's flashinfer-jit-cache 0.7.0+cu130 wheel): 96 / 64 / 12 / 72
- clang: 64 / 40 / 0 / 48
- clang with the change below: 96 / 64 / 12 / 72

A bf16 or fp16 MoE call through this kernel (DeepSeek-V2-Lite shapes, 256 and 8192 tokens) then gets every row wrong
(NaN or values up to 1e37), and the output changes from call to call. With the change, the output matches the nvcc build
to every printed digit (max abs error against a float32 reference: 1.6e-05 for bf16 at 256 tokens, as with nvcc).

Suggested change, which returns a fragment that owns its registers (same layout, same element order):

```cpp
static_assert(cute::cosize_v<Layout> == numel, "util_convert_type: the fragment must be contiguous");
auto frag = convert_op(*reinterpret_cast<cutlass::Array<From_type, numel> const*>(tensor.data()));
auto out = cute::make_tensor<To_type>(tensor.layout());
CUTLASS_PRAGMA_UNROLL
for (int i = 0; i < numel; ++i) {
  out.data()[i] = frag[i];
}
return out;
```

To see the lifetime problem without a GPU: compile the function against small stand-ins for the CuTe/CUTLASS types it
uses, read the returned tensor after the call, and run it under AddressSanitizer with
`ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1`. The current code is reported as a stack-use-after-return; the change
above is not.

FlashInfer's own `include/flashinfer/attention/hopper/utils.cuh` (`convert_type`) has the same pattern.

items.title: [Bug] calculate_nvfp4_global_scale returns wrong per-token scales for hidden sizes above 8192 that are not multiples of 8192
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.2.1 wheel, torch 2.9.1+cu130, A100 80GB PCIe (driver 610.57).
- The kernel is unchanged on main `b031dbe`: `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/quantization.cu` and `cpp/tensorrt_llm/common/reduceKernelUtils.cuh`.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`torch.ops.trtllm.calculate_nvfp4_global_scale(x, None)` on a bf16 `x` of shape `[m, n]` should return `448 * 6 / max|x[i]|` for each token. When the hidden size is above 8192 and not a multiple of 8192, many tokens get a wrong scale once a CTA handles more than one token (for a 2-D input, `m` above the SM count).

A minimal script:

```python
import torch
import tensorrt_llm  # registers torch.ops.trtllm

m = 512
torch.manual_seed(0)
rows = torch.arange(m)
amp = 2.0 ** ((rows * 5) % 11 - 3) * (1 + (rows * 3 % 8) / 8)  # per-token maximum
for n in (12288, 8192):
    x = (torch.rand(m, n) - 0.5) * amp[:, None]
    x[rows, torch.randint(n, (m,))] = amp
    x = x.bfloat16().cuda()
    ref = 2688.0 / x.double().abs().amax(1, keepdim=True)
    got = torch.ops.trtllm.calculate_nvfp4_global_scale(x, None)
    bad = ((got.double() - ref).abs() > 1e-4 + 2e-6 * ref.abs()).sum().item()
    print(f"n={n}: {bad} of {m} tokens have a wrong global scale")
```

On an A100 (SXM4 80GB) it printed:

```
n=12288: 309 of 512 tokens have a wrong global scale
n=8192: 0 of 512 tokens have a wrong global scale
```

Results with the 1.2.1 wheel:
- each call was checked in full against a float64 reference;
- a call counts as wrong if any token's scale is non-finite or off by more than 1e-4 + 2e-6 · |ref|.

| x shape (bf16) | wrong calls | wrong tokens in sampled calls |
|---|---|---|
| [512, 12288] | 914302 / 914302 | 301–318 of 512 |
| [256, 28672] | 920766 / 920766 | 101–114 of 256 |
| [512, 8192] | 0 / 924832 | |
| [1024, 4096] | 0 / 914518 | |

For example, in the first call at [512, 12288], token 3 got 28.0 instead of 42.0.

### Expected behavior

Each token's global scale is `2688 / max|x[i]|`, for any `n` the operator accepts. The launcher checks only `n % 256 == 0`.

### actual behavior

In `computePerTokenGlobalScaleForFP4QuantizationKernel` (`quantization.cu:351–374`), `getMaxAbs` calls `blockReduceMaxV2`, which contains a `__syncthreads()`, inside the per-thread loop:

```cpp
for (int vecIdx = threadIdx.x; vecIdx < n / ElemsPerVec; vecIdx += blockDim.x)
{
    float4 vec = reinterpret_cast<float4 const*>(input + tokenIdx * n)[vecIdx];
    float maxAbsVal = getMaxAbs<T>(vec);   // blockReduceMaxV2 -> __syncthreads()
    perTokenMaxAbsVal = cuda_max(perTokenMaxAbsVal, maxAbsVal);
}
```

The launcher uses `blockDim.x = min(n / 8, 1024)`. When `n / 8` is above 1024 and not a multiple of it, threads with `threadIdx.x < (n / 8) % 1024` run one more iteration per token than the others. CUDA requires a `__syncthreads()` in conditional code to be reached by all threads of the block, and here it is not.

The warps with fewer iterations run ahead. Each barrier instance then joins warp 0's reduction of one token with the other warps' reductions of later tokens handled by the same CTA. After those warps exit, it joins with the values they left in shared memory. The reduced maximum mixes tokens. In a standalone copy of the kernel, run without Compute Sanitizer, every wrong value matched the one predicted from this pairing.

A second, smaller problem: `blockReduceMaxV2` has no barrier between warp 0's read of `shared[lane]` (`reduceKernelUtils.cuh:281`) and the next call's write of `shared[wid]` (line 269). On the standalone copy, Compute Sanitizer racecheck reports hazards between these two lines at every shape we tested, including `n` = 4096 and 8192. Under racecheck or synccheck, those two shapes also returned wrong scales (one launch each), though they were correct in every plain run.

### additional notes

Suggested fix: reduce once per token, after the loop, followed by a barrier.

```diff
@@ -343,7 +343,6 @@ __device__ float getMaxAbs(float4& vec)
     {
         absMaxVal = static_cast<float>(cuda_max(absMaxVec.x, absMaxVec.y));
     }
-    tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&absMaxVal);
     return absMaxVal;
 }
 
@@ -365,6 +364,11 @@ __global__ void computePerTokenGlobalScaleForFP4QuantizationKernel(
             float maxAbsVal = getMaxAbs<T>(vec);
             perTokenMaxAbsVal = cuda_max(perTokenMaxAbsVal, maxAbsVal);
         }
+        // Reduce once per token, outside the per-thread loop: threads make different numbers of loop iterations
+        // when n / ElemsPerVec is not a multiple of blockDim.x.
+        tensorrt_llm::common::blockReduceMaxV2<float, 1>(&perTokenMaxAbsVal);
+        // blockReduceMaxV2's shared slots are rewritten by the next token's reduction.
+        __syncthreads();
         float globalScaleVal = 448.f * 6.f / perTokenMaxAbsVal;
         if (threadIdx.x == 0)
         {
```

A standalone copy of the kernel with the equivalent change gave no wrong scales on A100 and A40, and is clean under racecheck and synccheck.

**Reach.** Callers in the tree:
- the opt-in NVFP4 low-precision MoE combine in `nccl_ep.py:460` (`use_low_precision_moe_combine`, default off). It requires NVFP4 and a hidden size that is a multiple of 512, so sizes such as 10240 or 12288 can reach it. Its input is `[ep_size, max_tokens_per_rank, hidden]`, so a CTA handles several tokens once a rank receives more than SMs / `ep_size` tokens;
- `deep_ep_low_latency.py:386`, which runs this combine only for hidden sizes 4096, 6144 and 7168, and is not affected;
- `visual_gen/.../cute_dsl/fmha.py:626`, which caps rows at 8192 and is not affected; its comment calls 8192 "the largest dimension compatible with the same routine".

The operator's unit test (`test_fp4_calculate_global_scale.py`) use

items.title: Example 64 (Ada FP8 grouped GEMM) refuses capable GPUs via exact CC 8.9 gate
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

examples/64_ada_fp8_gemm_grouped/ada_fp8_gemm_grouped.cu (~line 1107) gates execution on exactly compute capability 8.9:

```cpp
if (!(properties.major == 8 && properties.minor == 9)) {
    std::cerr << "... requires a device of compute capability 89." ...
```

The grouped FP8 kernels here compile cleanly for newer architectures, and the sibling example 58_ada_fp8_gemm uses the inclusive form:

```cpp
if (properties.major < 8 || (properties.major == 8 && properties.minor < 9))
```

On an RTX 5060 Ti (sm_120a, CUDA 12.8.1) the stock binary exits immediately with the capability message; with the gate relaxed to the sibling's form the example builds and runs to completion including device-reference verification (`Passed`). Example 64 is therefore refusing capable hardware for no functional reason.

### Suggested fix

Use the same `major*10+minor < 89` / `major < 8 || (major == 8 && minor < 9)` inclusive check as example 58.

A clear and concise description of what the bug is.

`cute.arch.store` documents `val` as "scalar Numeric or vector ir.Value". Storing a `TensorSSA` vector works for f32, bf16, f16, u8, i8 and i16, for example `cute.arch.store(ptr, x.load().to(BFloat16))`; each lowers to a single `st.global.v8.b32`. With an fp8 element type (`Float8E4M3FN` or `Float8E5M2`), the same call passes tracing, but backend compilation fails with an internal error:

```
error: NVVM backend compilation failed
error: libNVVM failed while compiling generated device IR.
       LLVM Translation failed for operation: builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast
       Failed creating the llvm::Module.
```

It is not about bit width: 8-bit integer vectors work, and so does the same fp8 vector after `.bitcast(Uint8)` (also a single `st.global.v8.b32`). It looks like a vector of fp8 has no type conversion in the LLVM lowering of the store. `Tensor.store()` of the same fp8 vector does work, but it emits extra byte shuffles (`PRMT`) compared with the bitcast path.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
Follow this guide http://matthewrocklin.com/blog/work/2018/02/28/minimal-bug-reports to craft a minimal bug report. This helps us reproduce the issue you're having and resolve the issue more quickly.

Compile-only (no GPU run needed):

```python
# CuTeDSL MRE: cute.arch.store of an fp8 vector fails in the NVVM backend.
#
# cute.arch.store documents `val` as "scalar Numeric or vector ir.Value". An
# f32 / bf16 / u8 / i8 TensorSSA stores fine (one st.global.v8.b32), but an
# fp8 one (x.to(Float8E4M3FN) or Float8E5M2) traces and then fails while
# lowering:
#   LLVM Translation failed for operation: builtin.unrealized_conversion_cast
# Not a bit-width issue: the same fp8 vector bitcast to Uint8 stores fine.
#
# Compile-only; prints one line per variant.
#   python arch_store_fp8_vector.py
import importlib.metadata

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass import BFloat16, Float8E4M3FN, Float8E5M2, Float32, Int8, Uint8

N = 32  # elements per thread


def make(dtype, via_u8):
    @cute.kernel
    def kernel(out: cute.Tensor):
        tid, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
        x = cute.make_rmem_tensor(N, Float32)
        for i in cutlass.range_constexpr(N):
            x[i] = Float32(tid + i)
        v = x.load().to(dtype)
        dst = out[tid, None].iterator
        if cutlass.const_expr(via_u8):
            cute.arch.store(cute.recast_ptr(dst, dtype=Uint8), v.bitcast(Uint8))
        else:
            cute.arch.store(dst, v)

    @cute.jit
    def run(out: cute.Tensor):
        kernel(out).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(32, 1, 1))

    return run


print("nvidia-cutlass-dsl", importlib.metadata.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl"))
for dtype, via_u8 in (
    (Float32, False),
    (BFloat16, False),
    (Uint8, False),
    (Int8, False),
    (Float8E4M3FN, False),
    (Float8E5M2, False),
    (Float8E4M3FN, True),
):
    t = cute.runtime.make_fake_tensor(dtype, (32, N), stride=(N, 1), assumed_align=32)
    name = f"{dtype.__name__:13s} {'bitcast->u8' if via_u8 else 'direct'}"
    try:
        cute.compile(make(dtype, via_u8), t)
        print(f"  {name}: ok")
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        msg = " ".join(str(e).split())
        key = "unrealized_conversion_cast"
        print(f"  {name}: FAILED ({key if key in msg else msg[:200]})")
```

Output on 4.8.0:

```
nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0
  Float32       direct: ok
  BFloat16      direct: ok
  Uint8         direct: ok
  Int8          direct: ok
  Float8E4M3FN  direct: FAILED (unrealized_conversion_cast)
  Float8E5M2    direct: FAILED (unrealized_conversion_cast)
  Float8E4M3FN  bitcast->u8: ok
```

**Expected behavior**
A clear and concise description of what you expected to happen.

`cute.arch.store(ptr, fp8_vector)` lowers to a vector store of the packed bytes, the same as the `Uint8` bitcast path. If fp8 vectors are intentionally unsupported, the DSL should raise a clear error at trace time, not an ICE in libNVVM.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: [Bare-metal, Docker, Cloud(specify cloud provider)] 

 - Environment location: Bare-metal
 - GPU: NVIDIA GB300 (sm_103a), driver 610.43.02
 - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (aarch64), Python 3.12.13
 - nvidia-cutlass-dsl: 4.8.0

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

items.title: [inductor][cpu] `torch.std`/`var` accumulate in float32: inf/NaN for 1e30-scale inputs, and **zero output with an all-zero gradient** for 1e-30-scale inputs (eager and float64 are correct)
items.author: cuiliaomei-beep
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** `torch.std`, `torch.var`, `var_mean` and `std_mean` on CPU do not give the same numbers in eager and under torch.compile: eager accumulates in double and matches a float64 reference, while Inductor accumulates in float32, so 1e-30-scale inputs give a variance of 0 with an all-zero gradient, 1e30-scale inputs give inf, and values distributed as N(1e5, 1) give a variance with relative error 3e-3 instead of 5e-8 (torch 2.14.0 and nightly). A user sees no error; training on such data stalls or drifts silently, and CUDA eager shows the same float32 behaviour, so the divergence is specific to CPU eager versus compiled. Because the accumulation precision is chosen by the backend rather than by the program, the same code produces different statistics before and after compilation.

On CPU, eager `torch.std` / `torch.var` / `var_mean` / `std_mean` accumulate float32 inputs in double, so they are correct over the whole float32 range. Under `torch.compile(backend="inductor")` the variance is accumulated in float32:

- inputs of magnitude ~1e30 → `std` / `std_mean` return **inf or NaN** (eager: 1.02e30, equal to the float64 truth). (`var` overflows to inf in eager as well because 1e60 does not fit in float32, so only `std`/`std_mean` disagree there.)
- inputs of magnitude ~1e-30 → `std` returns **0** (eager: 8.2e-31) and, more importantly, the **gradient is all zeros** while eager and float64 give the correct O(1) gradient `(x - mean) / ((N-1)·std)`. A model whose activations are tiny therefore trains in eager and silently stops learning under compile.

`backend="aot_eager"` matches eager in both cases; the deviation enters at Inductor.

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)

# 1. large values -> inf / nan
x = torch.randn(4, 8) * 1e30
print("eager   :", torch.std(x))                              # tensor(1.0223e+30)  (float64: 1.0223e+30)
torch._dynamo.reset()
print("inductor:", torch.compile(torch.std)(x))               # tensor(inf)   (nan for other inputs, e.g. 5 values ~1e30)

# 2. small values -> zero output and zero gradient
def grads(fn, x):
    xx = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y = fn(xx)
    (g,) = torch.autograd.grad(y, xx)
    return y.item(), g

x = torch.randn(5) * 1e-30
print("eager   :", grads(torch.std, x))            # (8.19e-31, tensor([-0.0371,  0.2498, -0.1366, -0.3250,  0.2489]))
print("fp64    :", grads(torch.std, x.double()))   # same values
torch._dynamo.reset()
print("inductor:", grads(torch.compile(torch.std), x))   # (0.0, tensor([-0., 0., -0., -0., 0.]))
```

Also reproduces for `std_mean`, `correction=0`, and dim-wise `std(dim=1)`.

| | eager | float64 | inductor |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std` of `(4,8) * 1e30` | 1.0223e30 | 1.0223e30 | **inf** |
| `std_mean` of the same | (1.0223e30, 6.592e27) | same | (**inf**, 6.592e27) |
| `std` of 5 values `* 1e30` | 8.19e29 | 8.19e29 | **nan** |
| `var` of `(4,8) * 1e30` | inf (1e60 overflows fp32 output) | 1.045e60 | inf (same as eager) |
| `std` of `(5,) * 1e-30` | 8.19e-31 | 8.19e-31 | **0.0** |
| grad of `std` w.r.t. `(5,) * 1e-30` | `[-0.037, 0.250, -0.137, -0.325, 0.249]` | same | **all zeros** |

`backend="aot_eager"` gives the eager column in every row.

Also on Linux CPU (Kaggle, torch 2.10.0+cu128): `std` of 1e-30 values eager 1.16e-30 / inductor 0.0, gradient eager `[0.139, 0.215, -0.382, 0.153, -0.125]` / inductor all zeros; `std` of `(4,8)*1e30` eager 9.15e29 / inductor inf. On CUDA (T4) eager itself accumulates in float32 and returns 0 / inf as well, so this is a CPU-eager-vs-Inductor discrepancy — which is exactly where users move models between.

A third, more everyday instance of the same accumulation difference: `x = torch.randn(4, 100003) + 1e5` (values ~N(1e5, 1)). `x.var(-1)` in eager has relative error 5.6e-8 against a float64 reference, the compiled version 3.0e-3 (e.g. eager 1.000474 vs compiled 1.002948, truth 1.000474); `std`, `var_mean` and `std(correction=0)` behave the same, and `F.group_norm` on the same data is 10x less accurate compiled (2.7e-3 vs 2.7e-4). With `x = 1 + 1e-4 * randn` (`var` ~ 1e-8) the compiled error is 1000x eager's. Sweep: `scripts/large_reduce_sweep.py` (837 op x value x dtype cases; every flagged case is a variance-family op or an fp16 `prod`). The same sweep on the 2026-09-11 nightly flags exactly the same 26 cases, so the recent reduction-codegen change (#196371) did not affect this.

Still present on nightly torch 2.15.0.dev20260911+cu130 (nightly, git fb8ff0f1, Kaggle: Tesla T4 + Linux CPU), Linux CPU: `std` of 1e-30 values eager 1.16e-30 / inductor 0.0, gradient eager O(0.1) / inductor all zeros; `std` of `(4,8)*1e30` eager 9.15e29 / inductor inf.

Expected: finite `std` for 1e30 inputs; non-zero `std` and the correct gradient for 1e-30 inputs — as eager and float64 give. If float32 accumulation is the intended trade-off, the CPU eager kernel and Inductor should at least agree; a silent all-zero gradient is the worst possible failure mode for training.

Related: #173793 (open) reports the same overflow for `LayerNorm` on CUDA with 1e37 inputs; #173989 fixed the LayerNorm CPU path only. `std`/`var` themselves, and the gradient consequence, are not covered there.


### Error logs

No error is raised; the values differ as shown above.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A

OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
GCC version: Could not collect
Clang version: Could not collect
CMake version: Could not collect
Libc version: N/A
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64 (used by Inductor's C++ backend)

Python version: 3.14.7 (tags/v3.14.7:823f032, Aug  5 2026, 10:51:32) [MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)] (64-bit runtime)
Python platform: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0
Is CUDA available: False
CUDA runtime version: No CUDA
GPU models and configuration: No CUDA
Is XPU available: False
Is XNNPACK av

The diagnostic made one GET, disabled redirects, read only the 17-byte error response and stopped. It performed no installation. A minimal equivalent request is:

```python
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

class NoRedirect(urllib.request.HTTPRedirectHandler):

items.title: torch.compile: complex sgn decomposition overflows on tiny inputs which causes NaN gradients in abs backward
items.author: Shakil-Muhit
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

According to the documentation, `torch.sgn` returns values with "absolute values (i.e. magnitudes) of one" for non-zero complex inputs. But when I use `torch.compile`, non-zero complex inputs with magnitude below about 2.94e-39 (≈ 1/FLT_MAX for complex64) give `inf`/`nan` instead, while eager `torch.sgn` on CUDA returns the correct values for the same tensor.

My audio source separation model's training setup has an L1 loss on STFT residuals. Because the derivative of `abs` is `grad * self.sgn()`, a compiled loss built on `abs()` of a complex tensor like mine can have a finite value but NaN gradients. My model trains cleanly when run in eager mode but gets intermittent NaN gradients under `torch.compile`. I traced the failing `abs` backward to a single STFT residual element of magnitude 1.4e-45 and the repro below shows the same failure without the model. I made an experiment of two runs with that model by freezing weights and one captured sample. The first run tracked 75 of 200 replayed backward passes being non-finite and the second one tracked 95 out of 200 non-finite backward passes. But after removing only `aten.sgn` from Inductor's decomposition table, all of them out of 600 were tracked finite. A workaround that works fine is to keep the loss outside the compiled region (`torch.compiler.disable`), so `sgn` runs in the eager CUDA kernel.

**Repro** (the same failure without the model or data):

The reproducer below was written by an AI coding agent at my direction. I reviewed it and ran it myself. The output after it is from my run.

```python
import torch

def cases(device):
    return torch.tensor([-1e-39 + 0j, complex(0, -1e-39), complex(1e-39, 1e-39),
                         -1.4e-45 + 0j, -1e-30 + 0j], dtype=torch.complex64, device=device)

def show(label, t):
    print(f'  {label:<28}', [complex(round(v.real, 4), round(v.imag, 4)) for v in t.tolist()])

def run(device):
    print(f'== {device}  torch {torch.__version__}')
    z = cases(device)
    show('native torch.sgn', torch.sgn(z))
    show('torch.compile(torch.sgn)', torch.compile(torch.sgn)(z))
    a = z.clone().requires_grad_(True); a.abs().sum().backward()
    show('eager abs().backward() grad', a.grad)
    b = z.clone().requires_grad_(True); torch.compile(lambda x: x.abs().sum())(b).backward()
    show('compiled abs() grad', b.grad)

run('cuda')
```

Output on 2.16.0.dev20261009+cu132, RTX 5090:

```
== cuda  torch 2.16.0.dev20261009+cu132
  native torch.sgn             [(-1+0j), -1j, (0.7071+0.7071j), (-1+0j), (-1+0j)]
  torch.compile(torch.sgn)     [(-inf+nanj), (nan-infj), (inf+infj), (-inf+nanj), (-1+0j)]
  eager abs().backward() grad  [(-1+0j), -1j, (0.7071+0.7071j), (-1+0j), (-1+0j)]
  compiled abs() grad          [(nan+nanj), (nan+nanj), (nan+nanj), (nan+nanj), (-1+0j)]
```

Expected in every row: `-1, -1j, 0.7071+0.7071j, -1, -1` (the last input is a normal-range control). Same output on 2.8.0+cu128.

**Which stage introduces it.** `torch.compile(torch.sgn, backend=...)` on `-1e-39+0j`, CUDA:

```
== cuda  input [(-1.0000002153053333e-39+0j)]
  eager [(-1+0j)]
  aot_eager [(-1+0j)]
  aot_eager_decomp_partition [(-inf+nanj)]
  inductor [(-inf+nanj)]
```

The failure can be noticed with Inductor's decomposition table even after bypassing Inductor's kernel code generation (`aot_eager_decomp_partition`). No issue is there with `aot_eager` which doesn't apply the decompositions.

**Cause.** `aten.sgn` decomposes to `torch._refs.sgn`:

```python
def sgn(a):
    if utils.is_complex_dtype(a.dtype):
        a_abs = a.abs()
        return torch.where(a_abs == 0, 0, a / a_abs)
```

Even though `a_abs` is real, `a / a_abs` is subtly cast to complex ÷ complex division and the code calls `aten.div.Tensor` with a complex64 result. PyTorch's complex division multiplies by the reciprocal `1 / (c + d·(d/c))` which is `1/|z|` here. Below about 2.94e-39 the reciprocal overflows to `inf` and then `(-tiny)·inf = -inf` and `0·inf = nan`. The `== 0` guard only catches exact zeros. The CUDA eager kernel divides by the real magnitude (`z / std::abs(z)`) and so it never forms the reciprocal. complex128 fails the same way below about 5.6e-309 (checked on CPU).

**Suggested fix.** Divide each component by the real magnitude, as the CUDA kernel does:

```python
        return torch.where(
            a_abs == 0, 0, torch.complex(a.real / a_abs, a.imag / a_abs)
        )
```

After I made this change in the nightly above, the two compiled results of the repro produced expected values at the printed precision on both CPU and CUDA. A standalone test of compiled `sgn` and compiled `abs()` gradients on tiny real, imaginary and mixed inputs also passes on CPU and CUDA for complex64 and complex128 (atol 1e-4 and 1e-12). I have not run PyTorch's own test suites with the change. The exact unit magnitude is not produced for the very smallest mixed inputs, as `|z|` itself is rounded. The change removes the overflow which was the objective.

**Related: CPU eager.** The CPU kernel's scalar path (`sgn_impl` in `aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/zmath.h`) shows the same overflow behaviour as it divides by `zabs(z)` which returns the magnitude as a complex number. The vectorized path works fine as it divides by the real magnitude. On an AVX-512 machine, `torch.sgn(torch.full((19,), complex(-1e-39, 0), dtype=torch.complex64))` gives `-1` at indices 0–15 and `-inf+nanj` at 16–18. The analogous fix would be `z / std::abs(z)`. This could be a separate issue if preferred.

I directed AI coding agents to run the experiments and also help me investigate. I reviewed the analysis and after the agents ran the scripts, reran the repro, the backend comparison, the patched run and the standalone test myself. AI also helped me make adjustments to this write-up. I take the whole accountability.

If this approach looks right, I would like to make a PR for the `_refs.sgn` change with regression tests.

### Error logs

None. No error is raised. The values

items.title: float8_e8m0fnu: float32 -> E8M0 cast rounds every exact tie up, never to the even code
items.author: sw23
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This bug was identified by comparing floating point number conversion results across a few open-source implementations. The FP32-to-E8M0 code and test naming suggest that the intention was to round ties to even, but the code as implemented always rounds up. Feel free to cancel if this is expected/intended.

Below is the full AI-generated summary:

`fp8e8m0fnu_from_fp32_value()` says it implements "round to nearest, with ties to even" (the comment above its guard/round/sticky logic), and its test is `test_float8_e8m0fnu_rne_rounding`, but every exact tie rounds **up**. E8M0's values are the powers of two, so ties sit at 1.5·2ⁿ, and half of them land on the odd code:

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([0.75, 1.5, 3.0, 6.0, 12.0], dtype=torch.float32)
print(x.to(torch.float8_e8m0fnu).view(torch.uint8))
# tensor([127, 128, 129, 130, 131], dtype=torch.uint8)
# expected [126, 128, 128, 130, 130] (each tie to the even code)
```

3.0 lies exactly halfway between 2.0 (code 128) and 4.0 (code 129) and gives 129. Over all 254 ties 1.5·2ⁿ (n = −127…126), **254 round up and 127 land on the odd code**, so the cast's round-to-nearest-even gives the same results as ties-away. `torch.compile` on CPU matches eager. CUDA not checked (no GPU here).

**Cause:** in `torch/headeronly/util/Float8_e8m0fnu.h`:

```cpp
  // in casting to e8m0, LSB is the implied mantissa bit. It equals to 0 if the
  // original float32 is denormal, and to 1 if the original float32 is normal.
  uint8_t lsb = exponent > 0;
```

Ties-to-even tests the least significant bit **of the result**. E8M0 stores no mantissa, so the result's LSB is the exponent's LSB, the bit the round-up carries into. The implied mantissa bit is not part of the result, and for a normal input it is always 1, so every tie rounds up. (For a subnormal input `lsb` is 0, but there `g=1, r=0, s=0` only occurs for exactly 2⁻¹²⁷, which is representable, so the 0 never decides a tie.) A one-line fix for normal inputs is `uint8_t lsb = exponent & 1;`.

`test_float8_e8m0fnu_rne_rounding` in `test/quantization/core/experimental/test_floatx.py` computes its expected values with the same `lsb = biased_exponent > 0` rule, so it can't catch this.

**Why "even" means the even code here.** IEEE 754's "even least significant digit" is degenerate when the precision is 1, because both neighbours have significand 1.0. Two references resolve it the same way:

- **OCP OFP8 Revision 1.1, Appendix A** settles OCP ties by the parity of the **destination encoding's** LSB (E4M3: 464 → 448 because 448's mantissa LSB is 0; E5M2: 61,440 → overflow because 57,344's mantissa LSB is 1). With no mantissa field, that LSB is the exponent's.
- **ml_dtypes** has the same round-up behaviour and its maintainers agreed it is a bug to fix on both the host and the XLA side: [jax-ml/ml_dtypes#398](https://github.com/jax-ml/ml_dtypes/pull/398) ("I think I agree with the PR author that we need to round to nearest even so this is a bug we should fix in both places"). gfloat, the P3109 group's reference implementation, already rounds these ties to the even code.

Numerically this matters less than #199708 (a tie is equally far from both neighbours), and the OCP MX scale algorithm uses `floor`, not round-to-nearest. But the code says nearest-even and doesn't do it, and JAX/XLA is moving to the even code. If both libraries keep the same rule, a scale tensor gets the same codes in each.

**Related to #199708 / draft #199718.** That PR sets `lsb = 1` and its new test asserts 1.5·2⁻¹²⁷ → code 1. Under ties-to-even that tie goes to code 0, so the special case would be `magnitude_bits > 0x00600000` rather than `>=`. It would be good to decide the tie rule before that test lands.

Use the following links to see the expected conversion results:

- [0.75 (binary32) → E8M0](https://sw23.github.io/fp-conv/?in=fp32&out=e8m0&val=0.75)

items.title: `torch.compile fails during fake-tensor propagation on deprecated uint8 mask indexing that eager still accepts`
items.author: tinywisdom
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Indexing a tensor with a `uint8` index (the deprecated "byte tensor as boolean mask" form) is still accepted in eager — it emits a deprecation warning and returns the masked result — but under `torch.compile` it fails during fake-tensor propagation with `TorchRuntimeError: RuntimeError when making fake tensor call` on both `aot_eager` and `inductor` (so the fault is in the shared fake-tensor/meta layer, not Inductor codegen). The equivalent `bool` mask compiles successfully even under `fullgraph=True` (which forbids graph breaks, so this is genuine in-graph compilation, not an eager fallback), and ordinary `int64` indexing compiles too — so this is specific to the uint8-as-mask path in `aten._unsafe_masked_index` (whose handling is bool-only), not the general data-dependent-output-shape limitation.

```python
import torch
def fn(t, idx): return t[idx]
t   = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0], dtype=torch.float16, device='cuda')
idx = torch.tensor([0, 2], dtype=torch.uint8, device='cuda')

fn(t, idx)                                                         # eager: tensor([2.], ...)  (+ uint8-indexing-deprecated warning)
torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager", fullgraph=True)(t, idx)     # TorchRuntimeError: RuntimeError when making fake tensor call
torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor",  fullgraph=True)(t, idx)     # same

# Controls — compile in-graph (fullgraph=True forbids graph breaks / fallback):
torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager", fullgraph=True)(t, torch.tensor([False, True], device='cuda'))        # -> tensor([2.], ...)
torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager", fullgraph=True)(t, torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int64, device='cuda'))  # -> tensor([1., 2.], ...)
```

**Expected:** since uint8 mask indexing is still accepted by eager as deprecated compatibility behavior, `torch.compile` should either preserve that behavior or fall back / report it as unsupported cleanly, rather than failing through an internal fake-tensor/decomposition error.

items.title: [RFC][Data] Add Apache Gravitino catalog provider for Ray Data
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

This RFC proposes Apache Gravitino as a Ray Data catalog provider for organizations that manage their Hadoop and Spark data estate in Gravitino. Ray jobs would resolve table names and access paths through Gravitino's own metadata and services.

The intended outcome is for these users to keep Gravitino as their metadata control plane when they add Ray training, preprocessing, and batch inference. The initial implementation slice is existing Iceberg table reads and writes plus registered external Delta table reads. Delta writes, Parquet table access, and storage-access guarantees remain explicit capability gaps.

## Why Ray needs Gravitino

For many Hadoop and Spark-centered enterprises, particularly in China, the relevant starting point is an existing Hive and Iceberg catalog estate. Apache Gravitino is designed to manage these catalogs and provides a Spark connector for them. Ray Data should consume the same cataloged data for AI workloads instead of requiring a separate metadata system or repeated physical-path configuration.

Ray's DatabricksUnityCatalog provider connects to a Databricks workspace and cannot resolve Gravitino tables. Ray therefore needs a Gravitino-native path through its existing format-specific APIs.

The integration would give Ray users a consistent table name across Spark and Ray, keep table discovery in their existing Gravitino deployment, and let Ray's distributed readers and writers operate on data they already manage.

## Proposed coverage

| Ray workflow | Gravitino path | Acceptance gate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Iceberg read and write | Resolve through the dynamic catalog configuration provider of Gravitino's Iceberg REST service (`catalog-config-provider=dynamic-config-provider`) and use Ray's existing PyIceberg paths. | Existing-table read and write, authorization, and storage access pass real integration tests. |
| External Delta read | Resolve format and location from Gravitino Generic Lakehouse metadata and use `read_delta`. | Driver and distributed workers read successfully with a documented storage identity, including denied-access tests. |
| External Delta write | Use `write_delta` only after defining how Delta changes update registered metadata. | Schema and partition changes cannot silently leave Gravitino metadata stale. |
| Parquet read and write | Evaluate Gravitino-managed Hive or Glue Parquet tables against Ray's existing Parquet APIs. | Format, partition, location, write, and credential semantics are specified and tested before support is claimed. |
| Gravitino-only operation | Use Gravitino endpoints and documented authentication and storage-access mechanisms. | Supported workflows run in an environment without Unity Catalog. |

Iceberg and Delta reads form the initial implementation. Delta writes and Parquet are follow-on capability gaps. Gravitino can meet these goals through its own mechanisms; the provider does not copy another catalog's internal protocols.

## Proposed integration

`GravitinoCatalog` would implement Ray's existing `Catalog.resolve(table, reader, mode)` contract. Reads use `CatalogAccessMode.READ`; Ray write paths call the same method with `CatalogAccessMode.WRITE`. The configured metalake and logical table identifier select the Gravitino catalog.

The Gravitino main API and Iceberg REST service have distinct endpoints and authentication. The provider must configure them explicitly. The optional `apache-gravitino` Python client is imported only when used, and credentials must not appear in serialized Catalog state, representations, or logs.

For external Delta tables, the provider validates the Generic Lakehouse catalog, table format, external-table marker, and declared location. Gravitino 1.3.0 does not support `ALTER` for these tables and does not list Generic Lakehouse Delta in its credential-vending support. Delta writes and storage access therefore require their own design and validation.

## When both catalogs are present

When an organization also has Unity Catalog, Ray would be able to consume data from each catalog through its own provider once both providers are available. Gravitino's Iceberg REST backend can proxy another Iceberg REST catalog, and Unity Catalog exposes an Iceberg REST endpoint. This suggests a possible Iceberg interoperability path that must be tested for naming, authentication, credentials, reads, writes, and metadata freshness. These sources do not establish reverse-direction or general bidirectional metadata synchronization.

## Non-goals

- Creating, dropping, or altering catalogs, schemas, or tables through Ray Data.
- Automatically supporting every Gravitino catalog type or SQL view.
- Treating two Ray catalog providers as proof of cross-catalog synchronization.
- Replacing Ray's existing execution engine or table-format readers.

## Questions for Ray Data maintainers

1. Should this start as a Gravitino-maintained external connector using Ray's public alpha Catalog API, with a Ray documentation link, or should Ray accept `GravitinoCatalog` as an alpha public provider?
2. Is the proposed Gravitino-only Iceberg and external Delta scope the right first implementation boundary?
3. Should the Gravitino-to-Unity Catalog Iceberg REST proxy path be treated as follow-on interoperability work after the standalone Gravitino workflow is validated?

## Validation plan

- Unit-test table-name resolution, CatalogAccessMode handling, catalog and format checks, permission errors, missing locations, unsupported operations, and secret-safe behavior.
- Use real Gravitino 1.3.0 services to test Iceberg and external Delta with multiple Ray read tasks. Test Iceberg writes, denied access, and a supported object store.
- Run supported workflows in a Gravitino-only test environment and record exact Ray, Gravitino, client, PyIceberg, deltalake, and storage versions.
- Close the Delta-write and Parquet rows in the coverage table with real metadata and storage tests before claiming broad provider coverage

items.title: [Data] Actor-pool scale-down leaves primary object-store pins, so worker nodes never go idle
items.author: carlpayne
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

Ray Data actor-pool scale-down drops the actor handle and does not call `ray.kill` (`ActorPoolMapOperator._release_running_actor`: remove references so lineage can still reconstruct outputs). The actor then dies with `The actor is dead because all references to the actor were removed.` Primary copies of its returns stay in that worker's object store. `LocalResourceManager::UpdateAvailableObjectStoreMemResource` starts the idle clock only when `used == 0.0`; any leftover byte clears it. `GetResourceIdleTime()` then returns nullopt, so `idle_duration_ms` stays 0 and node activity is only `Resource: object_store_memory currently in use.` CPU is free and there are no workers, so an autoscaler idle timeout never starts.

Expected: once the pool has released the actor and nothing downstream will read its outputs, those `ObjectRef`s are dropped, object-store use hits 0, and the existing idle timeout removes the node.

A byte threshold, or `ray.kill` on idle scale-down, would drop the only copy of an object the driver still references. The next fetch fails, or reconstruction runs against an actor that is already dead (constructor args in plasma, #53727). #17718 closed as working as intended: destroying the actor when it goes out of scope can lose objects it owned, so the node should stay until those refs are actually gone.

Reproduced on 2.56.1 with the script below, while the dataset was still at 16/17 with one actor alive:

```
3 actors DEAD, death cause contains "all references to the actor were removed"; 1 ALIVE

emptied worker: cpu_used=0, object_store_memory used=13639977, idle_duration_ms=0
node_activity=["Resource: object_store_memory currently in use."]
```

Same pattern on a KubeRay cluster, Ray 2.56.1, during a long `map_batches`. The pool had scaled from thousands of actors down to a few dozen. Hundreds of worker pods had no Python workers and free CPU, with about 1–3 MiB of primary copies (sample: 7 pinned objects, 1,923,463 primary bytes, `is_idle: 0`). `idle_duration_ms` was 0 on every node. Requested CPU stayed ~13k while CPU in use had fallen to ~300. The driver still held the finished returns (`LOCAL_REFERENCE`, task `FINISHED`). `iter_batches` discards each batch; the refs live in Ray Data / the core worker until the dataset finishes. `scheduler_report_pinned_bytes_only` is true, so these are primary copies, not the secondary-copy case in #21870 / #22020.

### Versions / Dependencies

Ray 2.56.1, Python 3.12. Repro on macOS. Production observation on Linux, KubeRay, same Ray version. The two functions above are unchanged on master and in the 2.59.0 sources. The script was run on 2.56.1 only.

### Reproduction script

```python
import threading
import time

import ray
from ray.autoscaler.v2.sdk import get_cluster_resource_state
from ray.cluster_utils import Cluster
from ray.data import ActorPoolStrategy
from ray._private.state import actors as gcs_actors

HOLD_S = 45

class Encode:
    def __call__(self, batch):
        if 0 in [int(i) for i in batch["id"]]:
            time.sleep(HOLD_S)
        return {"blob": [bytes(1 << 20) for _ in batch["id"]]}

def used(total, avail, key):
    return float(total.get(key, 0)) - float(avail.get(key, 0))

cluster = Cluster()
cluster.add_node(num_cpus=1, include_dashboard=False)
cluster.add_node(num_cpus=2, resources={"encode": 2}, include_dashboard=False)
cluster.add_node(num_cpus=2, resources={"encode": 2}, include_dashboard=False)
ray.init(address=cluster.address)
ctx = ray.data.DataContext.get_current()
ctx.autoscaling_config.actor_pool_util_upscaling_threshold = 0.8
ctx.autoscaling_config.actor_pool_max_upscaling_delta = 4
ds = ray.data.range(17, override_num_blocks=17).map_batches(
    Encode, batch_size=1, num_cpus=1, resources={"encode": 1},
    compute=ActorPoolStrategy(min_size=1, max_size=4, initial_size=4),
)
release = threading.Event()

def consume():
    for batch in ds.iter_batches(batch_size=1, batch_format="numpy"):
        release.wait(timeout=HOLD_S + 30)
        del batch

threading.Thread(target=consume, daemon=True).start()
deadline = time.monotonic() + 20
while time.monotonic() < deadline:
    time.sleep(2)
    state = get_cluster_resource_state(ray._private.worker.global_worker.gcs_client)
    for node in state.node_states:
        total, avail = dict(node.total_resources), dict(node.available_resources)
        if float(total.get("encode", 0)) <= 0:
            continue
        print(
            "cpu", used(total, avail, "CPU"),
            "obj", used(total, avail, "object_store_memory"),
            "idle_ms", node.idle_duration_ms,
            "activity", list(node.node_activity),
        )
    for info in gcs_actors().values():
        if "MapWorker" in info["ActorClassName"]:
            print(info["State"], info["DeathCause"])
release.set()
ray.shutdown()
cluster.shutdown()
```

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: [RFC]: Normalize the token_load decode score by each pod's KV capacity
items.author: hengguangcui11-cyber
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The `token_load` decode score (#2842, with output growth from #2852 and the cross-replica ledger from #2868) counts the tokens each decode pod holds. It compares those counts across pods as if every decode pod had the same KV capacity. When capacities differ, for example in a heterogeneous GPU deployment (`docs/source/features/heterogeneous-gpu.rst`), the smaller pods fill up first and overflow. In simulation, `token_load` then does worse than the default `load_balancing` on long-output workloads. This RFC proposes dividing each pod's `token_load` score by its KV capacity in tokens, read from metrics the engines already expose (`vllm:cache_config_info`). With equal capacities the ranking is unchanged.

## Motivation

`load_balancing` reads `KVCacheUsagePerc`, which is already relative to each pod's capacity. `token_load` replaced that stale signal with an exact ledger, but in absolute tokens: 60k tokens on a 100k-token pod is 60% full, and on a 200k-token pod 30% full, yet both score the same.

Decode pods with different KV capacities are a supported setup, not an edge case:

- **Heterogeneous GPUs.** The same model deployed on several GPU types (one Deployment per type, sharing `model.aibrix.ai/name`) gives decode pods different KV capacities.
- **Different engine settings** on pods of the same model: vLLM sizes its KV cache from `gpu_memory_utilization` unless `kv_cache_memory_bytes` or `num_gpu_blocks_override` sets it directly.
- **Per-engine KV limits** set by ModelClaim on shared cards (#2795) are another source, discussed under open questions.

In the simulation below, with four 200k-token and four 100k-token decode pods, `token_load` has 65× the excess KV it has with equal capacities on steady chat traffic. On long-output workloads it is worse than `load_balancing`.

## Proposed Change

**Capacity per decode pod.** Read each pod's KV capacity in tokens during the regular metric scrape:

- vLLM: `vllm:cache_config_info`, an info gauge whose `num_gpu_blocks` and `block_size` labels give `capacity = num_gpu_blocks × block_size`. AIBrix already reads label values this way (`QueryLabel`, as for `max_lora` from `vllm:lora_requests_info`).
- SGLang: `sglang:max_total_num_tokens`, a gauge of the KV pool size in tokens that the engine sets once at startup.
- The capacity is fixed for an engine process, so a missing or unparsable value just leaves the pod without one.

**Score.** Under `token_load`, a decode pod's score becomes the fraction of its capacity in use:

```
decode_score = (local tokens + local growth + remote tokens + remote growth) / capacity
```

The ledger, growth and cross-replica sharing are unchanged; only the final division is new. `finalPDScore` already normalizes decode scores by the maximum in the run, so the unit change doesn't affect how prefill and decode scores combine.

**Missing capacities.** A pod without a known capacity uses the mean capacity of the candidates that have one. If none has one, the score stays in absolute tokens, which is today's behavior. With equal capacities, dividing by a constant doesn't change the ranking.

**Switch.** `AIBRIX_DECODE_TOKEN_LOAD_CAPACITY_AWARE`, default `true`, since it changes nothing for pools with equal capacities. Only the `token_load` decode policy reads it.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Fall back to `load_balancing` when capacities differ.** It is capacity-relative, but brings back the stale-scrape herding that `token_load` removed (chat, bursty: 69.40 vs 4.17 excess KV below).
- **A configured capacity per pod or per GPU type.** It drifts from the engine's actual configuration, and operators would have to keep it in sync. The engines already report it.
- **Normalize by the scraped `KVCacheUsagePerc` instead** (combine the ledger with the scraped fraction). It reintroduces the 1 s staleness for the part of the signal that matters during bursts, and needs capacity in tokens anyway to combine the two.

## Evidence (simulation, not engine measurements)

The same simulation as #2849 and #2867: it drives the real `filterPrefillDecodePods` (fast paths, scoring, ledger with growth) against a per-pod KV model with load-dependent decode speed and a 1 s metric scrape. Eight decode pods: four with 200k tokens of KV and four with 100k. A prototype passes each pod's capacity to the router. The metric is excess KV: time-averaged demand above each pod's capacity, summed, as % of the mean pod capacity (lower is better). Spread is the time-averaged max − min utilization across pods.

| workload | load | seeds | `load_balancing` | `token_load` | `token_load` / capacity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| chat (outputs 256) | steady | 10 | 27.74 (±5.10) | 16.99 (±5.24) | **0.82** (±0.56) |
| chat | bursty | 10 | 69.40 (±11.82) | 36.68 (±7.34) | **4.17** (±2.38) |
| long outputs (40% generate 2k–16k) | steady | 30 | 0.83 (±1.37) | 4.66 (±4.54) | **0.50** (±0.88) |
| long outputs | bursty | 30 | 7.65 (±5.34) | 16.01 (±9.65) | **1.85** (±1.89) |

- Spread on chat, steady: 88.8% / 66.4% / 28.6%.
- **Control:** with eight 150k-token pods (same total capacity), `token_load` and `token_load` / capacity give identical results in all four rows (for example 0.26 and 2.50 on chat, steady and bursty), as expected from dividing by a constant.
- On long outputs, steady, the capacity-aware score and `load_balancing` are within noise of each other. The clear results are that today's `token_load` is worse than `load_balancing` there, and that the capacity-aware score is better under bursts.

Limitations: this is a model (no engine preemption or queueing, assumed step times), and capacities are given to the router exactly. Two capacity tiers are one example; the effect grows with the ratio between them.

## Open Questions

1. Should the switch default to `true`? It changes nothing with equal capacities, but it is a new input to the score.
2. With ModelClaim on shared cards, an engine's effective KV limit can be lower than `num_gpu_blocks × block

items.title: [Bug] /v1/completions returns 400 when prompt is an array of strings or token ids
items.author: ptimizeroracle
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`validateCompletionRequest` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/util.go`) unmarshals `prompt` into a go `string`, so a `/v1/completions` request whose `prompt` is an array is rejected by the gateway with 400 `error processing request body` before it reaches the engine

the openai completions api takes four shapes for `prompt`: a string, an array of strings, an array of token ids, an array of token id arrays. vllm accepts the same four. only the first one gets through the gateway, measured on main @ 4a8be31:

| prompt | gateway status |
|---|---|
| `"hello"` | ok |
| `["hello","world"]` | 400 |
| `[1,2,3]` | 400 |
| `[[1,2],[3]]` | 400 |

the comment above the struct says this was a workaround for `CompletionNewParamsPromptUnion` not unmarshaling in openai-go v0.1.0-beta.10. go.mod is on openai-go v3.32.0 now, so the workaround may no longer be needed, i did not check that part

clients that batch prompts or send pre tokenized input (some eval harnesses do) work against vllm directly and fail once aibrix is in front

### Steps to Reproduce

drop this in `pkg/plugins/gateway/` and run `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway -run TestCompletionsPromptShapes -v`

```go
package gateway

import (
	"fmt"
	"testing"

	"github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/utils"
)

func TestCompletionsPromptShapes(t *testing.T) {
	cases := []struct{ name, prompt string }{
		{"string", `"hello"`},
		{"string array", `["hello","world"]`},
		{"token ids", `[1,2,3]`},
		{"token id arrays", `[[1,2],[3]]`},
	}
	for _, c := range cases {
		_, msg, _, _, errRes := validateRequestBody("r", "/v1/completions", []byte(`{"model":"m","prompt":`+c.prompt+`}`), utils.User{})
		code := 0
		if errRes != nil {
			code = int(errRes.GetImmediateResponse().GetStatus().GetCode())
		}
		fmt.Printf("%-16s status=%d len(message)=%d\n", c.name, code, len(msg))
	}
}
```

output

```
string           status=0 len(message)=5
string array     status=400 len(message)=0
token ids        status=400 len(message)=0
token id arrays  status=400 len(message)=0
```

### Expected behavior

the gateway accepts the four documented shapes and passes the body through. for the routing text, joining the strings looks natural for the string array case. for token ids i am not sure what you would want in `routingCtx.Message` (empty, or the ids as text), so asking before sending a pr

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

items.title: [Bug] PendingLoadProvider.GetConsumption returns success when the profile has no latency data
items.author: AlSh007
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`PendingLoadProvider.GetConsumption` (`pkg/cache/pending_load_provider.go`) looks up the profile's throughput and latency separately:

```go
lambda, err1 := profile.ThroughputRPS(signature...)
meanLatency, err2 := profile.LatencySeconds(signature...)
if err1 != nil || err2 != nil {
    return 0.0, err1
}
```

When only the latency lookup fails, `err1` is nil, so the function returns `(0, nil)`: a success that says the request consumes no load. That happens for a profile that has throughput data but no `e2e` table (`ErrProfileNoE2E`), and for an `e2e` table that is too small for the request's signature ("signature out of bound").

The callers treat `(0, nil)` as real. `packLoadRouter` and the pulling `leastLoadRouter` add 0 to the pod's utilization, so a pod whose profile cannot estimate the request looks as if it had spare capacity and is preferred; `cache_trace.go` records a pending load of 0 for it. With a real error they log it, skip the pod, and fall back to the others.

### Steps to Reproduce

A unit test shows it without a cluster:

1. Build a `PendingLoadProvider` over a cache whose `GetModelProfileByPod` returns `&ModelGPUProfile{Indexes: ..., Tputs: ...}` with no `E2E`.
2. Call `GetConsumption` with a routing context that has an output predictor.
3. It returns `(0, nil)`. The same happens with an `E2E` table smaller than `Tputs`.

### Expected behavior

`GetConsumption` returns the latency error, so the routers skip the pod instead of counting it as free.

### Environment

Found by reading the code on `main` (00d62a59); no cluster needed. A fix and test are ready, and I'll open the PR with this issue.
