items.title: [Feature] compute-mamba-ratio skill: plain-spec D is off the slot budget; admission clamp needs a +1 slot margin
items.author: junliu-mde
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Two sizing corrections for the `compute-mamba-ratio` skill (#32763, #32789), found while sizing GLM-5.3-Flash on 8×H100 (TP8 + `--enable-dp-attention` dp8, NEXTN `D=6`, `extra_buffer`, overlap on, image `0.0.0.dev1+g033446bb05`). This is feedback on the sizing guidance, not a bug report against the runtime.

#### 1. Plain spec: `D` is no longer a slot-pool cost — same accounting as the ReplaySSM caveat

The skill computes `r* = (S + D) · token_equiv · dcp / L` and pins `--max-mamba-cache-size = target_concurrency · S` (joint-solving `(S+D)` per request with spec).

On current main, plain EAGLE/NEXTN allocates the per-draft intermediate states in a dedicated buffer sized by `max_running_requests`, outside the slot pool:

- `memory_pool.py`: `intermediate_ssm_state_cache` shape `(layers, spec_state_size + 1, D, ...)`
- `kv_cache_configurator.py`: `mamba_spec_state_size=sizes.max_running_requests`

So the slot-pool cost per running request is `S`, and `D` is a fixed deduction from `rest` scaled by `max_running_requests` — exactly the treatment the skill already prescribes for ReplaySSM, but it applies to plain spec too. Using `(S+D)` overestimated the state pool ~2.2× at `L≈300K` in our case.

Boot-log evidence (per rank, dp8 so pools are /8):

```
Mamba Cache is allocated. max_mamba_cache_size: 30, conv_state size: 0.15GB, ssm_state size: 2.12GB intermediate_ssm_state_cache size: 2.87GB intermediate_conv_window_cache size: 0.20GB
```

`ssm_state 2.12 GiB / 31 = 68.4 MiB/slot`; `intermediate_ssm_state_cache 2.87 GiB = (6+1 reqs) × 6 drafts × 68.4 MiB` — sized by per-rank `max_running_requests`, not by slot count. The configurator's own clamp is `mmcs // S` (30 // 5 = 6/rank), which matched observed admission.

#### 2. The pin needs a +1 slot margin: chunked-prefill stash transiently allocates before freeing

With admission exactly at the clamp (6 running/rank × S=5 = 30/30 slots, all locked), the chunk-boundary stash (`cache_unfinished_req` → `prepare_for_caching_req` → `_alloc_mamba_slot`) allocates the donate slot before the old one is released. Transient demand is `running · S + 1`. `evict_for_alloc` cannot free anything (all slots belong to running requests), the assert fires, and the scheduler exits. Under round-robin DP load all 8 ranks hit it within one second, taking the whole server down. Deterministic for us: 48 concurrent 8K-in/1K-out requests crash; 16 concurrent never do.

<details>
<summary>Crash log (same on all 8 ranks)</summary>

```
[2026-08-29 07:48:03 DP0] Prefill batch, ... full token usage: 0.12, mamba usage: 1.00, #running-req: 4, ...
[2026-08-29 07:48:03 DP0] Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../managers/scheduler.py", line 3151, in get_next_batch_to_run
    self.stash_chunked_request(self.chunked_req)
  File ".../mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py", line 927, in cache_unfinished_req
    cl = comp.prepare_for_caching_req(
  File ".../mem_cache/unified_cache/components/mamba_component.py", line 498, in _alloc_mamba_slot
    assert slot is not None, "Can not alloc mamba cache"
AssertionError: Can not alloc mamba cache
```

</details>

Suggested skill changes:

1. Add a caveat mirroring the ReplaySSM one: when the boot log shows a separate `intermediate_ssm_state_cache` allocation, use `D=0` in the slot math and account the buffer as a `rest` deduction driven by `max_running_requests`.
2. Change the pin recommendation to `--max-mamba-cache-size = target_concurrency · S + 1` (per attention-dp rank), or note that the configurator clamp sits exactly on the assert boundary.

Corrected sizing validated on the same deployment: pin 136 (17/rank = 3·S + 2 margin), `--max-running-requests 24`, rest to KV (per-rank KV tokens 359,680 → 889,536). 16× and 24× concurrent 330K-token requests all completed correctly, zero restarts.

### Related resources

- #32763, #32789 (`compute-mamba-ratio` skill)
- `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/memory_pool.py` (`intermediate_ssm_state_cache`), `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py` (`mamba_spec_state_size`), `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_cache/components/mamba_component.py` (`_alloc_mamba_slot`)

items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.

items.title: Fully-masked softmax rows exponentiate to 1 in the FMHA no-loop kernel
items.author: StephenLReed
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: 1.3.0rc23 (built from `f20ea652`); behaviour re-checked against `main` @ `fbda11f5`
- GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120), driver 595.71.05
- PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12.13
- Ubuntu 25.10, kernel 6.17.0-41-generic
- Backend: PyTorch; single GPU, no TP/PP
- Model where observed: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 with FP8 KV cache (where model-specific)

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Reproduction

In `cpp/kernels/fmha_v2/src/fused_multihead_flash_attention_kernel_noloop.h`, `CHECK_NEG_INF` is
enabled only for bidirectional sliding-window, sliding-window, and custom masks. When it is compiled
out, a row whose running maximum is still `-FLT_MAX` — every score in the row masked — evaluates
`expf(-FLT_MAX - (-FLT_MAX))`, which is `expf(0) == 1`. Each masked score therefore contributes
weight 1 instead of 0.

The requirement belongs to the softmax input state, not to a mask type: any instantiation that can
present an entirely masked row is affected, including ordinary causal and padding masks.

### Expected behavior

A fully-masked softmax row contributes zero weight to the attention output.

### actual behavior

The row's running max is still -FLT_MAX, so every masked element evaluates expf(0) == 1 and the row attends masked positions with weight 1. Silent: no error, no NaN. Presents as sequence-length-banded output corruption.

### additional notes

We can demonstrate the arithmetic directly by inspection of `apply_exp_with_mask`. We do **not** have
an isolated regression test attributing our production symptom to this line alone: the fix was
deployed alongside an unrelated kernel-enumeration change, and the evidence is a multi-day production
soak rather than a controlled A/B.

A maintainer with the fmha_v2 test harness can construct the direct case far more cheaply than we
can: any causal-mask configuration whose final Q tile is partial should show masked positions
receiving weight 1 before the change and 0 after.

**Questions for maintainers**

1. Is enabling the guard unconditionally the fix you would want, or would you prefer it gated on the
   configurations that can actually produce a fully-masked row?
2. Is there a known-good harness in `cpp/kernels/fmha_v2` you would want a regression test added to?
3. Has the performance impact of the guard on previously-unguarded instantiations been characterised
   anywhere? We have not measured it.

Per CONTRIBUTING.md this Issue Request precedes the patch, which is ready and applies cleanly to `main` @ `fbda11f5`.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

**Backward kernel GPU time**, ms (B200, bf16, head dim 128, 16 heads; median of 50; main backward kernel only, from the torch profiler; a repeat run agrees within 1% for the block-sparse rows and within 5% for the others)

| attention | 4.5.3 | 4.6.0.dev0 | 4.8.0 ¹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| full, batch 2 × 8192 | 2.039 | 2.010 (−1%) | 2.084 |
| causal, 2 × 8192 | 1.121 | 1.140 (+2%) | 1.177 |
| GQA causal (32 q / 4 kv heads), 2 × 8192 | 2.287 | 2.266 (−1%) | 2.366 |
| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

items.title: [SM121 / GB10] cutlass_fused_moe: GEMM2 FINALIZE tactics 32 and 33 fail to initialise at every M (follow-up to #4847)
items.author: Col-5555
items.body_excerpt:
This follows up a note in #4847. That PR says gemm2 tactics {32, 33} on SM120 still fail at cutlass `initialize` with real problem shapes, and leaves them as profiling-time skips. We see the same pair fail the same way on **SM121 (GB10, DGX Spark)**, with a different model shape and at every M we tried. That suggests they may never be runnable on SM12x, in which case they could be removed from the candidate list instead of being tried and skipped on every tuning pass. We have not found the root cause.

**Setup.** 2× GB10 (sm_121), TP=2. FlashInfer 0.7.0 built from source (AOT, `sm121a`), CUDA 13.0, driver 580.178.04, torch 2.13.0+cu130. Model `RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4` (288 experts, top-8, NVFP4 weights and activations).

**What we ran.** `flashinfer.fused_moe.cutlass_fused_moe` on synthetic NVFP4 inputs with our per-rank layer shapes (hidden 4096, intermediate 1024, bf16 output). We forced each autotuner candidate through `profile_ids` with GEMM1 fixed at tactic 18, and made 20 calls at each of M = 1, 24 and 256. The IDs are as numbered on our build. GEMM2 offered 32 candidates: 20–23, 26–33, 36–43, 46–53 and 56–59. The 8 IDs that #4847 reports as dispatch-rejected on SM120 (24, 25, 34, 35, 44, 45, 54, 55) were not offered.

**Result.** Tactics 32 and 33 failed at all three M with:

```
RuntimeError: [TensorRT-LLM][ERROR] Assertion failed: Failed to initialize cutlass TMA WS grouped gemm. Error: Error Internal (/workspace/build/aot-providers/sm121a/generated/cutlass_instantiations/12…
```

Our log kept only the first 200 characters, so the file and line were cut off. We can re-run to capture the full message and stack. Every other GEMM2 tactic ran at every M. In normal serving the autotuner skips 32 and 33 and carries on, so the impact is wasted tuning time and log noise, not a crash.

**Context.** 32 and 33 are in the FINALIZE (fused finalize epilogue) family. The other 14 FINALIZE tactics run but are non-deterministic run to run on our build, which is what vllm#54945 / vllm#54948 address with `use_fused_finalize=False`. With that switch, neither 32 nor 33 is offered.

**Suggestion.** If the failure is architectural, filtering these configs on SM12x in `get_valid_tactics` (or in the candidate config list) would save the tuning attempts. One guess is a shared-memory limit, given that SM12x has 99 KB per block and FINALIZE adds epilogue storage, but we have not checked that against the configs. If the cause depends on the shape after all, remembering an init failure per (tactic, problem shape) would at least stop it being retried.

We can test a candidate fix on 2× GB10 in a maintenance window if that helps. Related: #4847, #2077, vllm#54948.

_Drafted with Claude Code from our own run logs; every number checked against the raw results._

items.title: Feature Request: add SYCL / oneAPI detection and prebuilt install support
items.author: Sjoerd
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

I would like `llama.app` / the unified `llama` installer workflow to support the SYCL backend on Linux, in addition to CUDA, ROCm and Vulkan.

At the moment, the installer probes CUDA, ROCm and Vulkan and then falls back to CPU. SYCL is not probed or selectable, even though `llama.cpp` itself already has an official SYCL backend and official releases provide prebuilt Linux SYCL binaries.

My system is an Intel Arc Pro B50 (Battlemage G21) running with the `xe` kernel driver. The Intel oneAPI / Level Zero stack is installed and the GPU is detected correctly:

```text
$ sycl-ls
[level_zero:gpu] Intel(R) oneAPI Unified Runtime over Level-Zero V2, Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B50 Graphics 20.1.0 [1.14.37020]
```

However, installing through:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh
```

does not offer or detect SYCL.

I expected the unified installer to be able to select an appropriate official SYCL build when a supported Intel GPU and SYCL runtime are available, or at least provide an explicit way to request the SYCL backend.


### Motivation

The new `llama.app` installer and unified `llama` CLI provide a much simpler way to install and use llama.cpp. It would be useful if Intel GPU users could use the same installation and update workflow instead of having to manually download SYCL release archives or compile llama.cpp from source.

SYCL is already an established llama.cpp backend and is particularly relevant for Intel Arc GPUs. Vulkan is also available on these GPUs, but SYCL and Vulkan can have different performance characteristics, supported optimizations and runtime behavior.

For users who specifically want to use Intel's oneAPI / Level Zero stack, the current installer creates an unnecessary gap: the backend exists, official binaries exist, and the hardware/runtime may already be correctly configured, but the normal `llama.app` installation path cannot select it.

Adding SYCL support would make the unified llama.cpp experience more consistent across supported GPU backends and would make Intel Arc setups significantly easier to deploy and maintain.


### Possible Implementation

One possible implementation would be to add a SYCL probe to the Linux installer, similar to the existing CUDA, ROCm and Vulkan probes.

For example, the installer could:

1. Check whether the Intel SYCL / oneAPI runtime is available.
2. Detect whether a compatible Level Zero GPU is present.
3. Prefer or offer the official Linux SYCL FP16 build for supported Intel GPUs.
4. Fall back to Vulkan or CPU if SYCL is unavailable.
5. Optionally provide an explicit backend override for users who want to choose between SYCL and Vulkan.

Conceptually, the detection order could be something like:

```text
CUDA -> ROCm -> SYCL -> Vulkan -> CPU
```

An explicit override would also be useful, for example:

```bash
LLAMA_BACKEND=sycl curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh
```

The exact syntax is of course up to the project.

Since llama.cpp releases already publish prebuilt Ubuntu SYCL FP16/FP32 binaries, this may mainly require adding the corresponding installer probe, artifact selection and runtime detection rather than adding a new backend to llama.cpp itself.

I am happy to test this on an Intel Arc Pro B50 / Battlemage Linux system.

items.title: qwen4exp: multi-seq split replay corrupts recurrent state when rs rollback is enabled (why the arch is excluded from llm_arch_supports_rs_rollback?)
items.author: netmana808
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`LLM_ARCH_QWEN4EXP` is excluded from `llm_arch_supports_rs_rollback()`, so `n_rs_seq` clamps to 0 for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and hybrid-recurrent batched rollback never engages. Force-enabling it shows why: **`test-recurrent-state-rollback` fails `test_multi_seq_split_replay` with a logits max diff of 9.25** — single-seq checkpoint restore passes, multi-seq split replay corrupts state. If the exclusion is deliberate, this issue documents the concrete gap (and asks what state is missing snapshot coverage); if it's an oversight, the repro below should make it easy to chase.

### Repro (~2 min on top of loading the model)

On `master` @ `cc231cb0d`:

1. Add the arch to the rollback allowlist:

```diff
--- a/src/llama-arch.cpp
+++ b/src/llama-arch.cpp
@@ bool llm_arch_supports_rs_rollback(const llm_arch & arch) {
         case LLM_ARCH_QWEN35:
         case LLM_ARCH_QWEN35MOE:
+        case LLM_ARCH_QWEN4EXP:
         case LLM_ARCH_DEEPSEEK4:
```

2. Run the existing test against a Qwen3.8-Flash-Next GGUF (tested with an IQ4_XS quant, CPU backend):

```
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" ./bin/test-recurrent-state-rollback \
  --model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00003.gguf -ngl 0
```

3. Output:

```
main : recurrent rollback checkpoint restored successfully
test_multi_seq_split_replay : multi-seq split replay logits mismatch (max diff 9.25491, first at seq 0 pos 16)
```

A diff of 9.25 in the logits is state corruption, not numerical noise.

### Suspected cause

qwen4exp carries extra per-row recurrent state beyond the gated-delta-net state that the snapshot planes cover for the allowlisted archs:

- the **PLE conv history** (`ple_layer_ids: [2]` — the PLE module sits on a layer that is also a delta-net layer, so both keep conv state in the same recurrent row), and
- possibly **QSA indexer** state.

If those aren't widened into the `(1 + n_rs_seq)` snapshot groups, an equal-split replay would restore the GDN state but replay over stale conv/indexer state — consistent with the mismatch appearing early (pos 16) on seq 0.

### Why it matters

On hybrid-recurrent archs, server spec decode with `--parallel N` currently pays a large serialization cost without rollback snapshots. Measured on a GB10 (Grace-Blackwell, 128 GB unified, CUDA sm_121) with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ4_XS + `--spec-type ngram-map-k4v --parallel 3`: three concurrent streams reach only ~50 tok/s aggregate on rewrite-style workloads vs ~66–70 with speculation disabled — speculation *inverts* under concurrency. Batched rollback is the structural fix, and it's blocked on this arch by the missing snapshot coverage.

Secondary observation while in this code: `common_params_speculative::need_n_rs_seq()` only arms `n_rs_seq` for the draft-model spec types (MTP/EAGLE3/DFLASH/DSPARK). Is there a reason the `ngram-*` types are excluded? They hit the same partial-acceptance rollback path.

### Offer

Happy to test patches on GB10 hardware — the repro takes ~2 minutes here and I can also run before/after server throughput numbers (`--parallel 3`, ngram spec) on the same box.

items.title: [RFC]: Mooncake Data Plane Model Distribution, Phase 1
items.author: XucSh
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed ## Summary This RFC proposes a Phase 1 model distribution capability inside Mooncake's data plane. In this design: - Mooncake Store is the storage and transfer substrate for model weights. - `mooncake_master` exposes HTTP APIs for model distribution orchestration. - node-side `mooncake_client` executes data movement tasks. - initial external acquisition is handled by a new `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` task. - follower replication continues to use Mooncake's existing object copy path. Phase 1 ends when a model is `Staged` on the requested nodes. It does not include runtime model loading, warmup, or serving readiness. ## Motivation Mooncake already has the right primitives for model distribution: - object-based storage - replica-aware transfer - task orchestration - node-side execution What is missing is a model-aware orchestration path that can do two things in sequence: 1. download model data from an external source onto one seed node and publish it into Mooncake Store 2. fan out the same data to follower nodes through Mooncake's internal replication path This should be solved inside Mooncake's data plane, not by introducing a new node-level service. ## Goals Phase 1 must provide the following: 1. `mooncake_master` accepts a model distribution job over HTTP. 2. Mooncake can determine whether a seed node already has the required objects. 3. If not, Mooncake can issue a `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` task to the seed node. 4. The seed node can download model files from a given source and write chunked objects into Mooncake Store. 5. After seed data is available, Mooncake can issue copy tasks to follower nodes. 6. Mooncake can return aggregated job and placement state over HTTP. 7. The terminal success state for Phase 1 is `Staged`. ## Non-Goals Phase 1 does not attempt to solve: - runtime model load into serving engines - runtime warmup - serving readiness - scheduler integration - artifact deletion and GC workflows - complex multi-source fallback - cross-cluster distribution ## Scope Boundary This RFC is intentionally about Mooncake only. It defines: - Mooncake's HTTP contract for model distribution - Mooncake's internal task model - Mooncake's data movement behavior - Mooncake's job and placement state model It does not define the external control plane in detail. An external control plane, such as `smg`, may call Mooncake's HTTP APIs, track its own higher-level lifecycle state, and present operator-facing workflows. That integration is an example, not the subject of this RFC. ## Terminology ### Model Manifest An immutable description of one model version, keyed by: `model_id + revision + format + provider` The manifest uses file-level semantics, while Mooncake stores the payload as chunked objects. ### Distribution Job A Mooncake-managed request to stage one model version on a set of target nodes. ### Placement The per-node staged state of one model version. ### Seed Node The node responsible for initial external acquisition when the requested objects are not already present. ### Follower Node A target node that receives the model through Mooncake's internal replication path after seed data becomes available. ## Architecture Overview ```mermaid flowchart LR CP[External Control Plane
example: SMG] MM[mooncake_master
distribution orchestrator] S[Seed mooncake_client] F[Follower mooncake_client] MS[(Mooncake Store objects)] NV1[(Seed local NVMe)] NV2[(Follower local NVMe)] CP -->|Create / Query distribution job| MM MM -->|MODEL_DOWNLOAD task| S S -->|publish chunked objects| MS MM -->|copy tasks| F MS -->|replicate objects| F S --> NV1 F --> NV2 ``` ## Component Responsibilities ### `mooncake_master` `mooncake_master` is the data plane orchestration entrypoint. It is responsible for: - exposing model distribution HTTP APIs - validating create/query job requests - checking whether the seed node already has all required objects - issuing `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` tasks when seed acquisition is needed - issuing copy tasks to follower nodes after seed data is available - computing aggregate job and placement state ### node-side `mooncake_client` The existing Mooncake client process is responsible for execution. It is responsible for: - executing `MODEL_DOWNLOAD` - reading the source file or URL - writing chunked objects into Mooncake Store - executing existing copy tasks - materializing staged model data on local storage ### External Control Plane An external control plane is out of scope for this RFC, but a typical caller is expected to: - build or store the model manifest - select target nodes - choose the seed node - create a distribution job in Mooncake - poll Mooncake for job state `smg` is one example of such a caller. ## Why There Is No Standalone Model Agent We explicitly reject a separate node-level model agent for Phase 1. Reasons: - it adds one more process and deployment artifact on every node - it duplicates logic that already belongs in Mooncake's task execution path - it creates another operational boundary for storage and transfer behavior The simpler model is: - `mooncake_master` orchestrates - `mooncake_client` executes ## End-to-End Workflow ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant CP as External Control Plane participant MM as mooncake_master participant Seed as Seed mooncake_client participant Store as Mooncake Store participant Follower as Follower mooncake_client CP->>MM: POST /api/v1/model-distribution/jobs MM->>MM: Check if seed already has all objects alt Seed already has objects MM->>MM: Skip initial download else Seed missing objects MM->>Seed: Submit MODEL_DOWNLOAD task Seed->>Seed: Download source file Seed->>Store: Publish chunked objects end MM->>Follower: Submit copy tasks Follower->>Store: Pull / materialize objects CP->>MM: GET /api/v1/model-distribution/jobs?job_id=.

items.title: [RFC]: TENT Local Transfer Admission Queue
items.author: zbchi
items.body_excerpt: ### Changes proposed ## Summary This RFC proposes a local transfer admission queue inside `TransferEngineImpl`. The queue orders logical transfers and applies backpressure before work is handed to `Transport::submitTransferTasks()` or `ProxyManager::submit()`. This covers the local-runtime part of the Transfer Queue roadmap item in #1883, before adding distributed pressure signals or receiver credits. It does not replace transport or ProxyManager execution. RDMA slice scheduling, CQ/QP handling, staging state machines, retries, and KVCache placement remain owned by their existing layers. Phase 1 keeps the normal submit path direct and adds a private queue model plus compatibility tests. Distributed pressure and receiver credits can be added later as inputs to local admission; this RFC does not propose a cluster-wide per-transfer executor. ## Motivation The current path is optimized for direct submission: ```text submitTransfer() -> merge requests -> resolve transport or staging -> allocate SubBatch -> assign sub_task_id -> Transport::submitTransferTasks() or ProxyManager::submit() ``` This is fast when the process is not overloaded. Under heavy load, background prefetch or migration traffic and foreground Store `get` traffic can enter transport queues through the same direct path. By the time foreground work is visible to the runtime, transport-side queues may already contain background work. Transport execution and ProxyManager staging remain owned by their existing layers. This RFC adds an earlier runtime admission point in `TransferEngineImpl::submitTransfer()`, so accepted work can be capped and latency-sensitive requests can be ordered before handoff. ## Current Code Shape The queue would be inserted into the current `submitTransfer()` path: ```text Current direct-submit shape Application / Store | | allocateBatch(batch_size) v TransferEngineImpl::submitTransfer(batch_id, requests) | | merge requests | append public TaskInfo entries to Batch::task_list | allocate SubBatch state and assign sub_task_id | +-- direct path --> Transport::submitTransferTasks() | -> RDMA / TCP / SHM / NVLink / GDS execution queues | +-- staged path --> ProxyManager::submit() -> shard queue with TaskInfo* -> stage buffers / internal batches / engine callbacks Status and lifetime side paths getTransferStatus() -> expects valid transport state for non-staging tasks -> treats UNSPEC as retry/fallback, not as "queued" freeBatch() -> currently recycles through caller-thread-local state -> async queueing needs explicit engine-owned lifetime ``` In the direct path, public task state is published before any queue admission point. The queued path must therefore: - Introduce explicit queue metadata instead of overloading `UNSPEC`, `TaskInfo::xport_priority`, or transport `sub_task_id`. - Admission capacity is charged by public request/task ids. Merged or derived task ids resolve through an owner map instead of becoming independent queue items. - Production async dispatch needs the engine to own batch lifetime and pin local buffers such as `Request::source`. `BatchID` is effectively a `Batch*`, and `SegmentTracker::ref_count` is not a transfer pin. - Transport and ProxyManager keep execution ownership; the queue only controls admission and scheduling before handoff. Production staged queueing also needs stable task addresses because `ProxyManager::submit()` stores `TaskInfo*`. ## Architecture The queue sits between caller submit and transport/proxy execution. L2 signals are inputs to the queue, not executors: In Phase 1, the normal submit path stays direct; the new code only exercises the queue model, side-table state, and owner mapping to ensure direct-path compatibility. ## Runtime Queue Design ### Data Model A queue item represents one logical transfer owner. It is not an RDMA slice and does not copy payload data. The first implementation can keep this as a private model, but the model should already reflect production boundaries such as batch ownership, derived-task mapping, byte charge, priority class, route plan, queue state, and reserved internal work. The logical owner is the single queued task for a merged request. Derived public task ids resolve to that owner and are not independently queued, dispatched, retried, or charged. An implementation can start with a private shape like this: ```cpp struct QueueOwner { QueueOwnerId id; BatchRef batch; // model id first; engine-owned ref later size_t owner_task_id; std::vector derived_task_ids; Request request; // metadata only, no payload copy size_t task_charge; size_t byte_charge; PriorityClass priority; RoutePlan route; // transport or staging decision QueueState state; uint64_t attempt_generation; TimePoint enqueue_time; CreditReservation credits; bool internal_staging_work; }; ``` The key point is to keep queue state in this private model instead of encoding it in `TaskInfo` fields. ### Admission For the production queued path, queue admission for one `submitTransfer(batch_id, request_list)` call is all-or-nothing. If every logical owner derived from the call can be admitted, it returns `Status::OK`. If admission would exceed hard limits, it returns `Status::TooManyRequests` and leaves no partial submission behind. Transport execution can still fail later and report failure through status, matching the existing asynchronous contract. When the production queued path is enabled, `Status::OK` means the work was published to the runtime queue, not necessarily that a transport has already accepted it. Applications may observe `PENDING` for tasks that have not reached `Transport::submitTransferTasks

items.title: torch.fx.Tracer.record_stack_traces is broken in torch 2.4.0
items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:

        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected op` in backward-slice when `tl.gather` feeds `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
A `tl.gather` result used as a `tl.dot` operand inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts the `NVGPUWarpSpecialization` pass at `WSDataPartition.cpp:330` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected op")`) during backward-slice partitioning — `tt.gather` is not in the op whitelist. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        idx = tl.full([M, K], 1, tl.int32)
        a = tl.gather(a, idx, axis=1)          # gather result feeds tl.dot
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:330!
```

## Root cause
`getBackwardSliceToPartition`'s op whitelist does not include `tt.gather`; reaching it hits `llvm_unreachable` rather than a graceful "unsupported" diagnostic. The identical kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()` with `tl.atomic_add` after `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
`tl.atomic_add` on the dot accumulator written **after** `acc += tl.dot` inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts at `WSDataPartition.cpp:775` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()")`) — the atomic carries a task-id count the sliceOp dispatch does not handle. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
        tl.atomic_add(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)   # atomic AFTER dot, on acc
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:775!
```

## Root cause
Inside `WSDataPartition.cpp`'s `sliceOp`, the per-task-id dispatch assumes a fixed set of `asyncTaskIds.size()` values; the atomic-on-accumulator produces a count outside the handled set and hits `llvm_unreachable`. The kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [AMD] CoalesceAsyncCopy produces a layout the direct-to-LDS lowering cannot coalesce when a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension
items.author: bogdan-petkovic
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

### Describe the bug

`TritonAMDGPUCoalesceAsyncCopy` can rewrite an async copy into a src layout that the direct-to-LDS lowering then rejects on GFX9. It happens when the blocked order and the shared order differ and a warp has more lanes than the fastest shared dimension has elements.

For a swizzled shared encoding the pass distributes the lanes and warps along the shared order and then rebuilds the blocked encoding with the original blocked order (added in #10928). The order of a blocked encoding also decides how the lanes are linearized, so once the lanes span more than one dimension, the first lanes walk along the dimension that is strided in LDS and the writes are no longer coalesced. This only works while all lanes of a warp fall in the fastest shared dimension, like the 64x2 tile in the tests of #10928.

The existing test `async_copy_different_order` in `test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir` already shows it. Its expected layout, `threadsPerWarp = [32, 2], warpsPerCTA = [1, 4], order = [1, 0]` for an `order = [0, 1]` shared layout, fails the same way when it is lowered.

### Reproducer

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad. No GPU needed, this is a compile failure.

`repro.mlir`, a 16x4 f32 copy with 2 warps on gfx950:

```mlir
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [2, 1], order = [1, 0]}>
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [0, 1]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 2 : i32, "ttg.target" = "hip:gfx950", "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 64 : i32} {
  tt.func @copy(%input: tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> {tt.contiguity = dense<[1, 4]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.divisibility = dense<[16, 16]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.constancy = dense<[1, 1]> : tensor<2xi32>},
                %view: !ttg.memdesc<16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>) {
    %token = ttg.async_copy_global_to_local %input, %view : tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> -> <16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```
triton-opt repro.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx950 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

```
repro.mlir:7:14: error: cannot lower 'ttg.async_copy_global_to_local' to a direct-to-LDS copy: the resulting writes into shared memory are not coalesced for a vectorization of 1 element(s). Adjust the blocked or shared encoding so each warp writes a contiguous range.
```

CoalesceAsyncCopy rewrites the src to `#ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [1, 0]}>`. Lanes 1 to 3 then take the next columns, 16 elements apart in LDS. The same tile with `order = [0, 1]` lowers to a single buffer load to LDS:

```
sed 's/warpsPerCTA = \[2, 1\], order = \[1, 0\]/warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [0, 1]/' repro.mlir > shared-order.mlir
triton-opt shared-order.mlir --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

And the existing test case:

```
awk 'BEGIN{RS="// -----\n"} /async_copy_different_order/' test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir > different-order.mlir
triton-opt different-order.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx942 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx942
```

fails with the same error.

### How we hit it

In rocmlirTriton (https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) a non-power-of-two K tile is split into power-of-two segments, so a K tile of 36 has a last segment of 4. For f32 convolutions on gfx950 with an M tile of 16 or 32 the copy of that segment is a 16x4, 32x2 or 16x8 tile, which is exactly this case. Our weekly tuning ran into it on 677 configs. We disabled those tile sizes on gfx950 for now.

In our tree, falling back to the shared order when the rebuilt encoding cannot be lowered fixed all of them and left the code of every config that already compiled unchanged. We did not send that as a PR because it calls `canLoadDirectToLDS` from the pass, and a fix that builds the right layout up front seems preferable. Happy to test any fix.


### Environment details

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad, built from source with CMake (TritonRelBuildWithAsserts, nvidia and amd backends, only the triton-opt target) against the prebuilt LLVM from cmake/llvm-info.json (b010a18d2b648cab83c83967ff26b8fde11acdc6). Ubuntu 22.04.5 on x86_64, GCC 11.4.

No GPU is needed, this is a compile failure in triton-opt and the target comes from gfx-arch (gfx950 for the reproducer, gfx942 for the existing test case). We first hit it compiling f32 convolutions for gfx950 in rocmlirTriton, whose vendored Triton has the same CoalesceAsyncCopy code.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Picking this up. I read the pass and the mechanism checks out: the swizzled branch distributes lanes along the shared order and then stamps the original blocked order back on, which re-linearizes the lanes. Once a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension, consecutive lanes walk a dim that is strided in LDS, and the rewritten copy is exactly what the direct-to-LDS lowering rejects.

Fix I am testing: after building the blocked-order candidate, check it with canLoadDirectToLDS (the same predicate the lowering uses, already called from this pass) and keep the shared-order distribution when the candidate would not lower. That matches what you validated in rocmlirTriton, and leaves every config whose rewritten layout already lowers byte-identical. Will add lit coverage for both the pass output and the end-to-end lowering of your 16x4 repro.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body: PR up: #12159. The pass now checks the re-stamped encoding with `canLoadDirectToLDS` and keeps the shared-order distribution when the src order cannot lower. Your 16x4 reproducer lowers cleanly with it, and `async_copy_different_order` turned out to have the same latent problem, its expected layout changes to the shared order as well.

items.title: [Bug]: Helix all-to-all receive path: restored payload words reach the outgoing bulk copy without a proxy fence
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

Source analysis of `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/` (`helixAllToAll.cu`, `ll128Proto.cuh`, `cudaAsyncOps.cuh`) at main `b031dbe`; these files are unchanged since `a1f562a`. Hopper or later (bulk async copies); no runtime environment involved.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [ ] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

Found by checking a slice from the restore to the bulk store (a one-warp kernel that calls the shipped `protoUnpack`) against the PTX memory model with our own PTX-level checker; not reproduced on hardware.

On the receive path of the Helix all-to-all (`helixAllToAll.cu`):
1. after the incoming copy completes (`smemBarWait`, line 534), `LL128Proto::protoUnpack` (539–540) has the lanes with `halfLaneId < 15` restore the payload word displaced by each 128-byte block's flag, with an ordinary shared-memory store (`ll128Proto.cuh:140`);
2. `s2gAllFields` (543) then has lane 0 issue `cp.async.bulk.global.shared::cta` (`cudaAsyncOps.cuh:166`) to copy the fields out, and this bulk copy reads those bytes.

No proxy fence lies between the restoring stores and the bulk copy's read. The `__syncwarp()` at `ll128Proto.cuh:144` is a warp barrier, and the `cp_async_bulk_wait_group_read` at 545 follows the issue.

### Expected behavior

The bulk copy reads the restored payload words. PTX requires a proxy fence for that. PTX ISA 9.4 §8.6: "A proxy fence is required to synchronize memory operations across different proxies." §9.7.10.28.2: bulk copies are performed in the async proxy, and "Accessing the same memory location across multiple proxies needs a cross-proxy fence." The completion of the incoming copy makes its data visible to the generic proxy; it does not publish later generic stores to the async proxy.

### actual behavior

Without the fence, PTX allows the outgoing bulk copy to read a block's flag word instead of its restored payload word, so the received field would carry a stale value at that position, with no error. Field 0 is always bulk-copied, so block 0's restored word is read whenever field 0 has at least 128 bytes; field 1 is affected only with `USE_BULK_FIELD1` (variable field 1 allowed and 16-byte aligned). Lane 0's own restore is also unordered with its own bulk read, so this is not only a cross-lane issue. We have not observed a failure on hardware.

### additional notes

Suggested fix: every restoring lane, including the issuing lane, executes `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` after its restore and before the bulk copy. It can go just before the `__syncwarp()` at `ll128Proto.cuh:144` (a shared header), or in `helixAllToAll.cu` right after the `protoUnpack` call (line 540), executed by all lanes and followed by a `__syncwarp()`, so that lane 0's copy is ordered after every lane's fence. With a fence in every lane, the same slice passes the check.

A related site not covered by that check: the next entry's incoming bulk load into the same shared bytes also follows these generic stores without a proxy fence.

items.title: rank_2k_universal and symm_universal Arguments constructors discard batch_stride_B
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The `Arguments` constructors of two kernels discard their `batch_stride_B` parameter and store 0 instead:

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/rank_2k_universal.h:176
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(0),

// include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/symm_universal.h:173
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(0),
```

`trmm_universal.h:158` stores its parameter (`batch_stride_B(batch_stride_B)`), which makes the intent clear; these are copy-paste typos. Confirmed by constructing `Arguments` for both kernels in a host program and printing the stored field: passing 200 stores 0.

Consequences:

1. `Params` construction copies `args.batch_stride_B`, so downstream code always sees stride 0.
2. Both kernels' `transposed_problem()` does `std::swap(args.batch_stride_A, args.batch_stride_B)` on an `Arguments` built by that constructor (`rank_2k_universal.h:189`), so after the swap the *stored* `batch_stride_A` becomes the dead 0 too: for the transposed path both batch strides are wrong, not just B's.

Additional observation while tracing this: neither kernel body ever reads `params.batch_stride_A` or `params.batch_stride_B` (unlike `gemm_universal.h`, which advances both pointers per batch), so batched operation through these kernels keeps A and B fixed across batches regardless of the arguments. The typo is provable on its own; the unused-stride observation may deserve separate attention.

### Suggested fix

Store the parameter in both places:

```cpp
batch_stride_A(batch_stride_A), batch_stride_B(batch_stride_B),
```

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL 4.7/4.8 regression: FlashAttention-4 SM100 forward kernel spills registers (0 -> 176 B) vs 4.5.1, ~3% slower on B300
items.author: zpcore
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With identical kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.7.x/4.8.0 generates PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 forward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_fwd_sm100.FlashAttentionForwardSm100`) that spills registers, where CuTe DSL 4.5.1 generated PTX that does not. The kernel is at the 128-register cap in both cases (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory spills. The varlen causal fwd+bwd step is about 2–3% slower on B300.

The regression is in the generated PTX, not in ptxas: the 4.8.0 PTX still spills when assembled with the older ptxas 13.2, while the 4.5.1 PTX assembled with that same ptxas does not.

**Resource usage, same FA4 source (`fa4-v4.0.0.beta16`), same quack-kernels 0.4.1, sm_103a**

| Kernel | CuTe DSL 4.5.1 | CuTe DSL 4.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| `FlashAttentionForwardSm100` | 128 regs, 0 B stack, 0 spill stores/loads, 5272 SASS instr | 128 regs, **112 B stack, 176 B spill stores / 176 B spill loads** (44 STL / 33 LDL), 5768 SASS instr |
| `FlashAttentionBackwardSm100` | 128 regs, 8 B stack, 1 STL / 5 LDL | 128 regs, 24 B stack, 24 B spill stores / 60 B spill loads (4 STL / 13 LDL) |

MMA (`UTCHMMA`/`UTCQMMA`), `MUFU`, and packed FP32 (`FFMA2`/`FMUL2`/`FADD2`) instruction counts in the forward kernel are identical between the two versions, so the difference is spill traffic rather than different math.

**PTX vs ptxas cross-check (forward kernel PTX from `CUTE_DSL_KEEP=ptx`)**

| PTX from | assembled with | Result |
|---|---|---|
| CuTe DSL 4.5.1 (PTX ISA 9.1) | ptxas 13.1 and 13.2 | 0 B stack, 0 B spills |
| CuTe DSL 4.8.0 (PTX ISA 9.4, `.version` lowered to 9.2) | ptxas 13.2 | 112 B stack, 176 B spill stores / 176 B spill loads |

Neither PTX contains `.local` declarations, so the spills are introduced by ptxas from register pressure in the 4.8.0 PTX.

`CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}"` with `CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 reports the spills for both forward and backward, and marks `flash_attn/cute/tile_scheduler.py:923` (the varlen scheduler's `_get_num_m_blocks`, loading `cu_seqlens`) as the likely pressure region.

**Timing (B300, varlen causal, bf16, head_dim 128, fwd+bwd, median of 20 steps after 3 warmups, runs interleaved on one GPU)**

| Shape | CuTe DSL 4.5.1 | CuTe DSL 4.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| 8192 tokens × 32 heads, 4 docs | 1.206–1.245 ms | 1.222–1.234 ms |
| 32768 tokens × 32 heads, 8 docs | 5.300–5.329 ms | 5.486–5.488 ms (+3%) |
| 32768 tokens × 16 heads, 1 doc | 12.35–12.38 ms | 12.71–12.84 ms (+3%) |

CuTe DSL 4.7.0 and 4.7.1 (measured with quack-kernels 0.6.5) show the same slowdown as 4.8.0. The current FA4 release (`fa4-v4.0.0.beta32`) with quack-kernels 0.6.5 on CuTe DSL 4.8.0 is within noise of beta16 on 4.8.0, so the difference tracks the DSL version, not the FA4 or quack version. I could not test 4.5.3 or 4.6.x with this FA4 source (import errors unrelated to the kernel), so the regression landed after 4.5.1 and by 4.7.0.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

1. Environment: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (sm_103a), driver 590.48.01, PyTorch 2.11 (CUDA 13.0), Python 3.12.
2. FA4 source: `Dao-AILab/flash-attention` at tag `fa4-v4.0.0.beta16`, installed with `pip install --no-deps --no-build-isolation flash_attn/cute`.
3. Install `quack-kernels==0.4.1` (`--no-deps`) and one of:
   - `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.1` with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu13==4.5.1` (apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.6)
   - `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.8.0` with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu13==4.8.0` (apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.11)
4. Run the script below with `CUTE_DSL_KEEP=ptx,cubin CUTE_DSL_DUMP_DIR=<dir>`, then `cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage <dir>/*flash_fwd_sm100*.cubin`.

quack-kernels 0.4.1 annotates with `cute.core.ThrMma`/`ThrCopy`, which 4.8.0 exposes only on `cute`; the script aliases them so the same quack source imports on both DSL versions.

```python
import importlib.metadata as md
import json
import sys

import torch
import cutlass.cute as cute

for _name in ("ThrMma", "ThrCopy", "TiledMma", "TiledCopy"):
    if not hasattr(cute.core, _name) and hasattr(cute, _name):
        setattr(cute.core, _name, getattr(cute, _name))

from flash_attn.cute.interface import flash_attn_varlen_func


def bench(total, heads, head_dim, docs):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    q, k, v = (
        torch.randn(total, heads, head_dim, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True) for _ in range(3)
    )
    cu = torch.linspace(0, total, docs + 1, device="cuda").round().to(torch.int32)
    max_seqlen = int((cu[1:] - cu[:-1]).max())

    def step():
        out = flash_attn_varlen_func(
            q, k, v, cu_seqlens_q=cu, cu_seqlens_k=cu, max_seqlen_q=max_seqlen, max_seqlen_k=max_seqlen, causal=True
        )
        out = out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out
        out.float().square().mean().backward()

    for _ in range(3):
        step()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(20):
        start, end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        start.record()
        step()
        end.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        times.append(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return round(sorted(times)[10], 3)


shapes = [(8192, 32, 128, 4), (32768, 32, 128, 8), (32768, 16, 128, 1)]
print(json.dumps({
    "cutlass_dsl": md.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl"),
    "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(),
    "median_ms": {f"{t}x{h}h_d{d}_{n}docs": bench(t, h, d, n) for t, h, d, n in shapes},
}))
```

**Expected behavior**

CuTe DSL 4.8.0 generates PTX for this unchanged kernel source with register pressure comparable to 4.5.1, so the forward kernel does not spill and runs at 4.5.1 speed. If this is a deliberate lowering change, guidance on a compile option or kernel-side change that avoids the spill would help.

**Environment details**

- GPU: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (sm_103a), driver 590.48.01
- CuTe DSL: 4.5.1 (good), 4.7.0 / 4.7.1 / 4.8.0 (spills), CUDA 13 libs
- ptxas used in the cross-check: 13.1, 13.2
- PyTorch 2.11, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.

comments.author: LaelaZorana
comments.body:
Managed to reproduce this with the forward kernel by compiling the PTX for each arch and checking the ptxas -v output. Used varlen causal bf16 with head dim 128 and 32 heads, 32768 tokens in 8 docs of 4096 each.

4.5.1 uses quack 0.4.1 with FA4 beta16, which seems to be your setup with 176 B.

4.8.0 uses quack 0.6.5 with FA4 beta32, but you mentioned that beta32 seems to have the same behaviour as beta16 with 4.8.0.

On sm_100a, both use exactly 128 regs and have 0 B of stack and 0 B of spill. On sm_103a, 4.5.1 uses 128 regs with 0 B spill but 4.8.0 has 112 B of stack and 156 B of spill stores and 152 B of spill loads. So for me, the spills only happen on sm_103a.

In the 4.5.1 PTX there are 89 ld.param instructions which load kernel args close to where they are used, whereas there are only 24 in the 4.8.0 PTX. 6 of them are on lines 45 to 53 so very close to the entry, and the remaining 18 are spread out between lines 192 and 6899. So it looks like the new version reloads the args much less often, which means that they stay live in registers for very long. This matches what you saw with the load of cu_seqlens in tile_scheduler.py on line 923, in the varlen scheduler. With such a long live range and a limit of 128 regs, it seems that ptxas spills regs, only on sm_103a from my side.

It would seem that the fix belongs in the DSL lowering and not in FA4, by reloading kernel params from param space at the point of use again. Does the sm_100a version of the same kernel spill for you? I can attach the 2 PTX files and the ptxas logs.

ptxas is 13.2.86 and is called with O3.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL from_dlpack rejects float8_e4m3fn tensors (dtype_map lists Float8E5M2 only)
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

`cutlass.cute.runtime.from_dlpack` rejects `torch.float8_e4m3fn` tensors:

```
KeyError: Unsupported element type in dlpack: 'Float8E4M3FN'. Supported types are:
['Bool', 'Int64', 'Int32', 'Int16', 'Int8', 'UInt64', 'UInt32', 'UInt16', 'UInt8',
 'Float64', 'Float32', 'Float16', 'BFloat16', 'Float8E5M2']
```

The runtime already decodes the DLPack type code and reports the element type as
`Float8E4M3FN` (the string comes out of `libcute_dsl_runtime.so`, which also knows
`Float8E4M3`, `Float8E4M3FNUZ`, `Float8E8M0FNU`, `Float4E2M1FN`, ...). Only the Python
lookup table in `TensorDescriptor.element_type` /
`python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/base_dsl/runtime/tensor_descriptor.py` stops at `Float8E5M2`, so
every other 8-bit float that the runtime recognizes is rejected at import time even though
`cutlass.Float8E4M3FN` is a fully supported kernel element type.

PyTorch is not the limiting side: `torch.empty(8, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn).__dlpack__()`
succeeds on torch 2.11 and the capsule round-trips through `torch.from_dlpack`.

## Steps/Code to reproduce bug

```python
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack

x = torch.empty(8, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, device="cuda")
t = from_dlpack(x, assumed_align=16)   # KeyError: Unsupported element type in dlpack: 'Float8E4M3FN'
```

## Expected behavior

`from_dlpack` returns a `cute.Tensor` with `element_type == cutlass.Float8E4M3FN`, the same
way it does for `torch.float8_e5m2`.

## Workaround in use

Callers currently export the storage as `uint8`/`int8` and overwrite `element_type`
afterwards, e.g. FlashInfer does this in `flashinfer/gemm/kernels/bmm_fp8_blackwell.py`,
`flashinfer/attention/cute_dsl/fmha.py`, and pending PR flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5533:

```python
t = from_dlpack(x.view(torch.uint8), assumed_align=16)
t.element_type = cutlass.Float8E4M3FN
```

Adding the missing names to the `dtype_map` (at least `Float8E4M3FN`; ideally the other
strings the runtime emits) would let these call sites drop the reinterpretation.

## Environment details

- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 (`nvidia_cutlass_dsl_libs_cu13-4.8.0`), and `main` as of 2026-10-07
- torch 2.11.0+cu130
- Linux x86_64, CUDA 13.0

items.title: [BUG] Grouped GEMM and grouped Rank2K kernels build operand iterators from a temporary Params
items.author: BwL1289
items.body_excerpt:
`gemm/kernel/gemm_grouped.h` builds the mainloop operand iterators from a temporary Params:

```cpp
typename Mma::IteratorA iterator_A(
  LayoutA(ldm_A),
  ptr_A, {problem_size.m(), problem_size.k()}, thread_idx, tb_offset_A);
```

`LayoutA(ldm_A)` becomes a temporary `IteratorA::Params` that is destroyed at the end of the statement, but the pitch-linear `PredicatedTileAccessIterator` keeps `Params const &params_`, so every later `++` / `add_tile_offset` reads a dead object. Same pattern in `gemm_grouped_per_group_scale.h`, `gemm_grouped_softmax_mainloop_fusion.h`, and `rank_2k_grouped.h` (spelled `typename Mma1::IteratorA::Params(ldm_A)` there). The epilogue iterators in `rank_2k_grouped.h` copy their Params, so those are fine.

nvcc's output happens not to show it. clang's (LLVM main, 24.0.0git) at -O2 does: building example 24's `GemmGrouped` kernel (half/half/float, Sm80 multistage, 128x128x32, 4 stages) for sm_121a, 30 of the 32 `cp.async` copies in the PTX take their global address from a register that is never written. Example 38's `Rank2KGrouped` kernel: 56 of 64.

Naming the Params so it lives as long as the iterator fixes it (0 of 32 and 0 of 64 after):

```cpp
typename Mma::IteratorA::Params params_A{LayoutA(ldm_A)};  // braces: with parens this declares a function
typename Mma::IteratorA iterator_A(
  params_A, ptr_A, {problem_size.m(), problem_size.k()}, thread_idx, tb_offset_A);
```

Checked against main at 0b55a2f691 with CUDA 13.4. To get main through clang at all I had to pass `-D__nv_atomic_load_n=__atomic_load_n -D__NV_ATOMIC_RELAXED=__ATOMIC_RELAXED` (subbyte_reference.h uses the nvcc-only builtin); that's a separate problem.

items.title: [RFC] CPU float16 performance optimization on eager mode.
items.author: mingfeima
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

The RFC is to improve float16 performance as well as Op coverage on PyTorch CPU backend on eager mode.

Float16 and BFloat16 are both commonly used reduced floating point types for performance improvement in neural network inference/training. On the CPU side, previous optimization efforts have been placed more on BFloat16, which leaves float16 at a relatively primitive status.

On the 4th generation Intel® Xeon® Scalable processor (Sapphire Rapids), a new fp16 instruction set architecture for Intel® AVX-512 has been added, e.g. **avx512-fp16**. The instruction set supports a wide range of general-purpose numeric operations for fp16. One the next generation of Xeon, Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) will have fp16 support, e.g. **amx-fp16**.

This proposal would help the scenario when the model is pre trained on GPU with mixed precision of float16/float32 and users intend to do deployment on the CPU side without modifying the model weights, for instance, many HuggingFace models belong to this scenario.

**This project will be targeting at:**
* Improve float16 Op coverage on PT from 52% to ~80% (for reference, BFloat16 Op coverage ratio is 83%). Torchbench models and HuggingFace models will be prioritized.
* Improve float16 performance： Since the current fp16 performance on CPU is very low, we can use fp16 v.s. fp32 speedup as the metrics here. Performance speedup will match bf16, on average a 4x-5x performance speedup will be achieved on hardware with amx-fp16 support.
* Add Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) support for float16 on CPU.
* Improve float16 numerical stability: use fp32 as accumulate type in reduction Ops, e.g. mean.

**Technically, the optimization will be carried out as below:**

Compute intensive Ops (e.g. Convolution, Gemm, and RNN):

* Rely on oneDNN for optimal performance when the hardware has float16 acceleration.
* Functional coverage will be added for hardware without float16 acceleration, no performance gain.

Generic ATen kernels:

* Extend avx256 and avx512 and vectorization utils for dtype `Half`. Add native convert intrinsics:  `_mm256_cvtph_ps`/`_mm256_cvtps_ph` (Rounding mode: RNE).
* Unary and binary Op kernels: map to fp32 for computation.
* Non arithmetic Ops: do direct memory copy (no dtype conversion), e.g. cat, index_select.
* Reduction Ops: use fp32 as accumulate type.
* NN Ops: reuse kernels of BFloat16.

**Test Plan:**
* Extend `vec_test_all_types_AVX2` and `vec_test_all_types_AVX512` for float16.
* Add OpInfo at `torch/testing/_internal/common_methods_invocations.py`.
* Provide specific test cases for reduced floating point.

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

**Previous RFC on extending AMP fp16 on CPU:**
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/96093

**Float16 support in torch inductor** working in parallel (implemented in similar method as BFloat16 support), has dependency on explicit vectorization utils of `at::vec::Vectorized<Half>`.

**Pull Requests related to this feature requests:**
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96076
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96077
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96078
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96079
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96080
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96081
* https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/96082

items.title: float8_e8m0fnu: float32 values in (2^-127, 1.5*2^-127) cast to 2^-126 (code 1) instead of 2^-127 (code 0)
items.author: sw23
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This bug was identified by comparing floating point number conversion results across a few open-source implementations. There's a small range of FP32 numbers that round to the wrong number when targeting E8M0. Feel free to cancel if this is expected/intended.

Below is the full AI-generated summary:

Casting a float32 to `torch.float8_e8m0fnu` returns code `0x01` (2⁻¹²⁶) for **every input strictly between 2⁻¹²⁷ and 1.5·2⁻¹²⁷**. The nearest E8M0 value is 2⁻¹²⁷ (code `0x00`). E8M0 is the shared scale of the OCP MX formats, so a block scale landing here is silently off by a factor of two.

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0625, 1.25, 1.375, 1.5, 2.5], dtype=torch.float32) * 2**-127
print(x.to(torch.float8_e8m0fnu).view(torch.uint8))
# tensor([0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1], dtype=torch.uint8)
# expected [0, 0, 0, 0, (tie), 1]
```

1.0625·2⁻¹²⁷, 1.25·2⁻¹²⁷ and 1.375·2⁻¹²⁷ are nearer 2⁻¹²⁷ than 2⁻¹²⁶, yet give code 1. (1.5·2⁻¹²⁷ is an exact tie, whose behavior should be discussed on its own.)

**Scope:** exhaustive over every positive float32 subnormal, **2,097,151 of 8,388,607 are wrong**, exactly the open interval (2⁻¹²⁷, 1.5·2⁻¹²⁷). The same relative position one binade up is correct (1.25·2⁻¹²⁶ → code 1). `torch.compile` on CPU gives the same results as eager. CUDA not checked (no GPU here).

**Cause:** `fp8e8m0fnu_from_fp32_value()` in `torch/headeronly/util/Float8_e8m0fnu.h` takes the guard, round and sticky bits at fixed positions:

```cpp
  // guard bit - bit 23, or 22 zero-indexed
  uint8_t g = (f_bits & 0x400000) > 0;
  // round bit - bit 22, or 21 zero-indexed
  uint8_t r = (f_bits & 0x200000) > 0;
  // sticky bit - bits 21 to 1, or 20 to 0 zero-indexed
  uint8_t s = (f_bits & 0x1FFFFF) > 0;
```

That split is right only when the significand's leading 1 is the implicit bit 23, true for normal float32 inputs. A subnormal input is never normalised first, so for it bit 22 is the leading 1, not the half-ULP guard bit, and everything above 2⁻¹²⁷ rounds up.

**A fix pattern already exists in the org:** torchao's `_f32_to_e8m0_rceil()` (`torchao/prototype/mx_formats/mx_tensor.py`) handles this boundary with `mantissa > 0x400000` when the biased exponent is 0. Its comment notes torchao bypasses `.to(torch.float8_e8m0fnu)` on purpose.

**Related:** ml_dtypes (and JAX/XLA, which agrees with it) has the identical symptom on the identical input set through a different code path

Use the following links to see the expected conversion results:

- [1.0625·2⁻¹²⁷ (binary32) → E8M0](https://sw23.github.io/fp-conv/?in=fp32&out=e8m0&hex=0x00440000)
- [1.25·2⁻¹²⁷ (binary32) → E8M0](https://sw23.github.io/fp-conv/?in=fp32&out=e8m0&hex=0x00500000)
- [1.375·2⁻¹²⁷ (binary32) → E8M0](https://sw23.github.io/fp-conv/?in=fp32&out=e8m0&hex=0x00580000)
- [2.5·2⁻¹²⁷ (binary32) → E8M0 (correct today)](https://sw23.github.io/fp-conv/?in=fp32&out=e8m0&hex=0x00A00000)

### Versions

PyTorch version: 2.14.1
Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: None
ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A
OS: macOS 26.6.2 (arm64)
Clang version: 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)
Python version: 3.12.13 (main, Mar 3 2026, 12:39:30) [Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)] (64-bit runtime)
Python platform: macOS-26.6.2-arm64-arm-64bit
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: Apple M5 Pro
Versions of relevant libraries:
[pip3] numpy==2.5.3
[pip3] torch==2.14.1
